TAIYUAN, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday launched a Long March-6C carrier rocket, placing seven satellites into space.
The rocket blasted off at 11:21 a.m. (Beijing Time) from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province and successfully sent the satellites into the planned orbit.
This launch marked the 665th flight mission of the Long March carrier rocket series, according to the launch center.
Two high-resolution Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites -- Zhongke Sat-14 and 15 -- carry dedicated space-based cloud payloads, breaking the traditional boundary between remote sensing and cloud computing to create an integrated platform that combines satellite sensing with onboard processing, according to developer GalaxySpace, a key supplier for China's internet satellite constellation project.
The company said this marks a breakthrough in space-based computing power and serves as an important step in the country's broader push for a space-based computing network.
The two satellites integrate onboard data reception, computing and analysis, delivering stable in-orbit computing power for tasks ranging from data acquisition to real-time delivery. They cut response times to minutes in flood or earthquake scenarios and significantly reduce bandwidth demand compared with traditional models, according to GalaxySpace.
GISTDA Cube Sat 1, also built by GalaxySpace, marks the company's first full-satellite and ground-system export to a Belt and Road partner country. Delivered to Thailand's Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA), it will supply land-use, agricultural, and ecological surface data while supporting Thai universities in satellite design, telemetry, and remote-sensing education.
Other satellites aboard include the JAMX01, a microsatellite developed over eight years by Shanghai teachers and students in partnership with a Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology affiliate, aimed at promoting youth science education through hands-on aerospace projects. ■

New Yellow River tunnel opens in east China, easing cross-river traffic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:48:59 CST
19:48:59 KST

JINAN, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Drivers can now cross the Yellow River, China's second-longest river, in just about five minutes, as a new tunnel opened to traffic on Tuesday in Jinan, capital of east China's Shandong Province.
Stretching about 5.75 kilometers in total, the tunnel under Huanggang Road features a shield-driven section of roughly 3.3 kilometers, bored by the "Shanhe" shield tunneling machine with a cutting diameter of 17.5 meters, the largest of its kind among underwater shield tunnels in the country.
The single-tube, double-deck structure accommodates six lanes -- three on each level -- with a design speed of 60 kilometers per hour. "This layout makes full use of underground space resources, allowing two-way traffic with just one single bore by the shield tunneling machine, which significantly improves overall cost-effectiveness," said Zhang Tiyong, project director of Jinan City Construction Group, the project's investor.
The tunnel offers an internal clearance height of 4.2 meters, Zhang added, tall enough for buses, fire engines, and maintenance and rescue vehicles, greatly boosting cross-river traffic capacity between the southern and northern banks of the Yellow River.
According to Zhou Xiang, on-site project manager from China Railway 14th Bureau Group Corporation Limited, the project's constructor, the Yellow River section in Jinan is a typical "suspended river," with its bed rising about five meters above the urban area on the southern bank and complex geological conditions lying beneath the river.
"As the diameter of the shield tunneling machine increases, the engineering challenges and construction risks grow exponentially," Zhou said. Despite the extreme difficulties, the project team used intelligent, mechanized, and green technologies throughout construction to ensure safe, efficient boring.
Qian Qihu, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said the successful application of these technologies will drive continuous progress in China's shield tunneling capabilities and mark a milestone for the country's underwater traffic tunnel construction.
The project also incorporates an intelligent rail-borne inspection robot equipped with a full suite of smart devices, including a 360-degree panoramic gimbal, infrared thermal imaging, and laser obstacle-avoidance radar, enabling fully autonomous inspection across the entire tunnel. In addition, the tunnel's fire suppression system has been upgraded with AI-powered image-based fire detection to markedly improve detection sensitivity and accuracy.
As the second major Yellow River crossing in Jinan after the tunnel under Jiluo Road, this new route is expected to further boost cross-river economic ties and accelerate the national strategy for the river's development and the construction of the city's pilot industrial transformation zone, local authorities said. ■

Across China: Millennia-old Chinese brocade weaves new threads of expression
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:48:58 CST
19:48:58 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "Irises" has found an unexpected new canvas -- a traditional Chinese Qipao dress woven in brocade.
The fabric's intricate weave renders the painting's brushstrokes. Deep blue petals sweep upward from the hem, interlaced with lush green leaves, while green trim and knotted buttons at the collar echo the flowers' hues.
The dress is among more than 130 works on display at the Touring Exhibition of the Innovative and Inherited Works of Chinese Brocade Craftsmanship in the New Century. The Beijing leg of the exhibition, held at the Xinhua News Agency Art Museum, runs from Aug. 19 to Sept. 17.
The exhibition showcases the expanding scope of artistic expression and innovation in contemporary Chinese brocade through a wide range of works, including a brocade painting that uses modern weaving techniques to recreate the texture of oil painting, a piece featuring a giant panda, and a wall hanging rich in ethnic Zhuang character.
Brocade originated in China and is regarded as one of the most sophisticated forms of silk craftsmanship. Over more than 2,000 years, different regions of China have developed distinctive brocade traditions, including Shujin, Songjin, Yunjin and Zhuangjin. In 2009, the Craftsmanship of Nanjing Yunjin brocade was inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List.
"Brocade reflects the artistic creativity and wisdom of our ancestors," said Li Jialin, curator of the exhibition and director of the research center for silk and fashion culture at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University.
For Li, keeping the ancient craft alive means more than preserving tradition. It also means drawing on the past to "create something new" -- a message he hopes the exhibition will convey.
At the heart of this transformation are ongoing breakthroughs in interweaving warp and weft threads.
In the past, brocade patterns were woven with colored warp and weft threads, but limitations in the weaving process restricted the palette to no more than a dozen colors.
Today, with advanced digital technology, more than 4,500 colors can be reproduced in brocade, allowing silk threads to capture subtler variations in hue, light and shadow and opening up new possibilities for artistic expression.
According to Li, brocade can now reach a warp density of 113 threads per centimeter and a weft density of 205 threads per centimeter, with more than 300 warp and weft threads intersecting within each square centimeter of fabric.
Meanwhile, digital platforms are helping preserve, document and share traditional patterns and techniques more systematically. Generative artificial intelligence is also giving designers greater freedom to explore new themes and forms of expression.
One abstract piece caught the attention of visitor Tao Xiaodong. It uses weaving structures of varying densities and thread types to create a naturally textured, three-dimensional surface.
"It could be a rock, bubbles or anything you imagine," Tao said while discussing the piece with a friend. For him, that openness to interpretation is part of its appeal, showing how brocade can move beyond traditional motifs and take on a freer, more contemporary form.
Li said the evolution of brocade craftsmanship has always gone hand in hand with advances in tools, technology and materials, much like a relay carried forward through the generations.
"The history of brocade offers a glimpse into the development of human civilization," he said. "What we are doing today is taking our turn in that relay." ■

China mulls law revision to accelerate national water network construction
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
18:48:55 CST
19:48:55 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers on Tuesday began reviewing a draft revision to the country's Water Law, with the latest draft incorporating provisions to speed up the development of a national water network.
The draft was submitted for its second reading to the ongoing session of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's top legislature.
The previous draft revision was submitted to lawmakers in late April this year and was later released to solicit public opinion.
Following suggestions from lawmakers and local authorities, the draft adds provisions that the country will accelerate the development of the national water network with a focus on improving water allocation, flood control and ecological systems.
To better align with the country's Ecological and Environmental Code, which came into force in early August, the latest draft adds that efforts should be made to coordinate the governance of water resources, the water environment, water ecology and water-related disasters, and to build a modern industrial system compatible with the carrying capacity of water resources.
Furthermore, the draft adds requirements for coordinating water resources regulation with flood regulation, and for stepping up efforts to treat and restore rivers and lakes facing ecological degradation.
The legislative session runs from Tuesday to Friday this week. ■

ASTANA, August 25. /TASS/. Kazakhstan will lose around 3.5 mln metric tons of oil production this year due to attacks on the infrastructure of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said at a press conference.

"As of today, the three-month plans we receive from Transneft PJSC show zero. In other words, the resumption of transit via the Druzhba pipeline is not currently envisaged for the next three months," Akkenzhenov said in response to a question about supplies of Kazakh oil to Germany via Druzhba.

Syrian Airlines will begin operating direct and regular flights from Damascus to the Austrian capital Vienna and Denmark's capital Copenhagen on Sept. 21, Syria’s civil aviation authority announced Tuesday.
Omar al-Hosari, head of Syria’s General Authority of Civil Aviation and Air Transport, told the SANA news agency that the new routes are part of continuing efforts to expand the national carrier’s international network and strengthen air links between Syria and Europe.

The first direct flight from Berlin Brandenburg Airport arrived at Damascus International Airport on Aug. 11, operated by German carrier Sundair, marking the restoration of direct air links between the Syrian and German capitals.

Report: U.S. prepares to return Mideast diplomats evacuated before Iran war, signaling renewed fighting is unlikely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:41:20 UTC
19:41:20 KST

The U.S. State Department is preparing to return diplomats to embassies in the Middle East that were evacuated before and during the war with Iran, the New York Times reported on Tuesday, citing an internal State Department document.
The return of Foreign Service officers and the scaling back of emergency measures at U.S. missions in the region could begin as early as this week, the report said.
Reuters was not immediately able to verify the report. The U.S. Department of State could not immediately be reached for comment outside regular business hours.
Embassies slated to restore higher staffing levels include those in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait, according to the report.
In a statement quoted by the New York Times, the State Department said it "continuously reviews the security posture at our diplomatic missions around the world."
"Based on our latest assessment, we are adjusting our staffing posture at certain posts in the Middle East to ensure we can continue advancing U.S. foreign policy objectives while protecting the safety and security of our personnel," it added.
According to the document, the first diplomats to return would be assigned to the U.S. Embassy in Lebanon, although staffing there would remain below full levels. Ultimately, staff would return completely to the U.S. embassies in Israel, Jordan and Oman, the report said.
Posts in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Lebanon would initially be capped at 85 percent staffing, while missions in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain would be limited to 75 percent, according to the document.
The staff reductions began in February, when Washington authorized voluntary departures of non-emergency personnel and family members from Israel amid tensions with Iran.

MOSCOW, August 25. /TASS/. Russia’s new Polye-31 (Field-31) UAV countermeasure station, designed to protect facilities, vehicles, and personnel from attack and reconnaissance drones by jamming satellite navigation channels, has started deployment in the special military operation zone, a spokesperson for the manufacturer, NPO Kilowatt Research and Production Association, told TASS.
"The Polye-31 UAV countermeasure station has begun arriving in the special military operation zone. The system is designed to protect facilities, vehicles, armored vehicles, and personnel from attack and reconnaissance drones, as well as kamikaze drones, by jamming satellite reconnaissance channels," the company stated.
The operational range of the Polye-31 system is at least two km. "The navigation systems it is capable of jamming include GPS, GLONASS, Beidou, and Galileo. The system’s operating frequency range: 1162-1300 MHz and 1550-1630 MHz," specified the Kilowatt Research and Production Association.
During deployment, the station is installed on high ground to protect military infrastructure, industrial facilities, the agricultural sector, energy facilities, and critical infrastructure from drones.

The US Navy aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln will dock in Thailand next week, following a prolonged deployment in the Middle East during the Iran war, a Thai official said on Tuesday.
The Lincoln, which left the Middle East on Saturday, has not make a port call in more than 200 days, setting a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Democrats, amid reports of concerns about mental health and deteriorating conditions aboard.
The ship, which has roughly 5,000 sailors and marines aboard, will be in Thailand for “rest and recreation after their long sea journey,” the official said, asking not to be named. A Thai Navy spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In an interview last week, the wife of a sailor onboard the USS Lincoln told the Guardian as the deployment has stretched on and on, she has noticed a change in her husband’s messages. “There’s less hope in the way he talks and less positive things that he has to say,” she said.
“He’s just exhausted,” she added. “It’s a long, long deployment and it takes a toll.”
Reports from families of crew members published in the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes military newspapers described food and water shortages, disrupted mail services, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.
The Kremlin said it had no information on a US military transport plane landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo airport earlier today, data from the flight tracking service Flightradar24 showed.
The large Boeing Globemaster had flown direct from Riga, in Latvia, and landed in Moscow at around 7am GMT, Reuters reports. The news agency was unable to verify whether it carried any cargo or passengers.
The aircraft had arrived in Riga on 23 August from the US Camp Springs airbase near Washington DC, data from Flightradar24 showed.
The last direct flight of a US registered jet to Russia from Europe took place in January this year, carrying special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner for peace talks with Vladimir Putin on Ukraine.
The Kremlin said last week that there was no information yet on another visit to Moscow by Kushner and Witkoff, as talks between the US and Russia on Ukraine have largely stalled amid the war in Iran.

“He happened to be an admiral, retired. He said, ‘I’ve been on ships that are out there much longer than that, sir. And I know people on the Lincoln, they say it’s beautifully maintained and beautifully taken care of.’ And other people went out and they found out that to be true,” said Trump.

Four arrested over Kenya elephant deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:35:41 UTC
19:35:41 KST

Four arrested over Kenya elephant deaths
Four people have been arrested in Kenya over the suspected poisoning of 18 elephants in the Amboseli ecosystem, the Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife said on Saturday.
A representative of the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said on Monday that all four suspects were later released on bail.
Preliminary laboratory tests suggest that the animals may have died after ingesting tomatoes contaminated with cyanide from farms bordering wildlife habitats. Officials said further scientific testing was needed to confirm the cause of death.
The first 15 elephant deaths were recorded June 24 to July 24 in Amboseli National Park, Kimana Sanctuary, and the Kuku Ranch area, prompting the KWS and other agencies to launch an investigation.
Ten of the elephants developed similar symptoms before dying, including partial paralysis which left them unable to stand. According to KWS, “the condition primarily affected adult females and their calves, with only one adult male” among the reported cases.
Four suspects have since been detained as persons of interest, while investigators are pursuing another individual believed to have information relevant to the case.
A search in Tikondo in Kimana, within Loitoktok Sub-County, also uncovered chemicals and other substances believed to have been sourced from a neighboring country. The potentially toxic and unlabeled materials have been sent for analysis.
The government stressed that the arrests and seized materials do not establish criminal responsibility. The authorities said the investigation is ongoing and pledged to prosecute anyone found to have unlawfully killed, poisoned, or harmed wildlife.
Earlier in August, the Kenya Veterinary Association (KVA) called for urgent testing of agricultural produce from areas around Amboseli after preliminary findings linked elephant deaths to cyanide. The group warned of potential risks to people after tomatoes were reportedly found in the animals’ stomachs and urged the authorities to determine whether contaminated produce could have entered local food supply chains.
The Amboseli ecosystem spans around 8,000 square kilometers across southern Kenya and into neighboring Tanzania, with Amboseli National Park at its core. The area is home to around 1,800 elephants.

In Poland, eight men beat three Ukrainians; the attacker wanted to give a &quot;lecture on Volhynia&quot; — media

2026-08-25
13:33:54 EEST

In Poland, eight men beat three Ukrainians; the attacker wanted to give a "lecture on Volhynia" — media
Kyiv • UNN
In Radom, eight men attacked three Ukrainians, who suffered head and facial injuries. One of the attackers faces up to five years in prison.
In Poland, eight people attacked three Ukrainians; the attacker wanted to give them a "lecture on Volhynia," reports Onet Wiadomości, writes UNN.
Details
According to reports, a drunk 34-year-old man attacked three 20-year-old Ukrainians in Radom and began asking them about their origins and the Volhynia tragedy. Seven more men then joined the Pole, and together they carried out the attack, the publication writes.
The incident occurred on August 2 between 5 and 6 a.m. on Malczewskiego Street in Radom, but the media reported it only several days later.
"Tomasz G., a 34-year-old resident of Lublin, came to Radom for a wedding, but after it ended, he began wandering around the city. He met three young Ukrainians on Malczewskiego Street. He started a conversation with them, asking where they were from. An exchange of remarks followed. However, he did not like their answer. They, in turn, reported that he wanted to give them a lecture on Volhynia. A verbal misunderstanding arose, and at that moment [...] the resident of Lublin called over three or four young men who were crossing the street and told them that they were Ukrainians. They reacted very energetically to this, and the attack began," prosecutor Cezary Ołtarzewski from the local prosecutor's office told MójRadom.
As the publication notes, "several more attackers later joined in beating the Ukrainians, bringing the total number of attackers to eight."
"The Ukrainians sustained injuries, mainly to their heads and faces. Forensic medical experts thoroughly examined them," the publication states.
In an interview with Gazeta Wyborcza, the prosecutor added that after the incident Tomasz G. "ordered a taxi and left as if nothing had happened."
According to reports, the police managed to establish the identity of the main attacker. He has already been taken to the prosecutor's office and charged with using violence or making unlawful threats for discriminatory reasons, as well as participating in a brawl or assault. He pleaded guilty and provided detailed explanations. Among other things, he stated that he had been under the influence of alcohol. He was placed under police supervision. He faces up to five years in prison.
The search for the other participants in the brawl is ongoing. Police are examining city surveillance footage. The situation is reportedly complicated by the fact that the detainee did not know the other attackers.

Optoma GT2400HDR Review: Ace Projector for Golf Simulation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

This Optoma laser projector is great for setting up a golf simulator in your living room, but mediocre video quality makes it less appealing for home entertainment.
Great for golf simulation. Continuous operation. Light and portable. Affordable. Easy to configure using the remote.
TIRED
No built-in smart TV OS. Outdated HDMI ports. Passable performance for home entertainment and gaming. Confusing remote for everything but the initial setup.
Indoor golf simulators aren't easy to set up, and they aren't inexpensive. It starts with a home cinema projector, but you also need a wide, open space for swinging clubs, a backdrop with netting, and a gaming laptop or desktop to run the software. I was on a mission to see if I could do this much more cheaply with an affordable projector.
I accomplished my goal successfully by building around the Optoma GT2400HDR short-throw projector. I skipped the most expensive components, like the backdrop and the clubs. Instead, I used a gaming laptop and controller I already owned, and played EA Sports PGA Tour, which is included with my PC Game Pass Ultimate account. While the projector isn’t a bad option for playing golf at home on the cheap, it’s not ideal for watching movies and TV shows. It also struggles with high-octane games, and it doesn’t even include a smart TV platform.
Made for Indoor Driving Ranges
Optoma describes the GT2400HDR as a laser-based short-throw projector designed for gaming, entertainment, and golf simulation (the latter being my main intention). It can project a screen size from 30 to 300 inches at Full HD 1080p (1920 x 1080) resolution. My goal in creating an indoor driving range was to keep costs as low as possible, so I planned to use my Xbox controller with a gaming laptop and play on a 100-inch screen while still feeling like I was out on the links. For a golf game, you can get by with a midrange computer or even use a golf sim app on your iPad. (To do that, you’ll need to cast to a device that supports AirPlay or connect through HDMI via an adapter.)
Photograph: John Brandon
For less than $1,300, the GT2400HDR is a reasonable option, especially since it works well as a basic golf sim and costs far less than 4K models that can run $5,000 or more. The GT2400HDR also has some interesting perks that make it ideal for long golfing sessions.
For starters, it’s rated for 24/7 continuous operation. That’s because the laser light source doesn’t need to cool down after a few hours and can last 30,000 hours total. (Optoma does recommend powering the unit off when not in use, though.) The laser light source does not use a bulb, so there is nothing to replace. Heat dissipation is amazingly good, as the projector tends to run cool, unlike some high-end models. The GT2400HDR has an IP6X dust rating, so it’s sealed better than some massive home theater projectors that cost $4,000—ironic, considering that if you’re spending that much, you would expect better dust protection.
The projector's light weight (just under 7 pounds) and portability make it a good match for golf simulation. I found it easy to position the projector on the floor and then use it on a table or even in another room without lugging it around like a massive brick.
I first had to figure out where to place it for the golf sim, though. As a short-throw projector, it should normally sit about 4 feet away from the screen. Since I wouldn’t be using actual golf clubs, I could set it on the floor in my windowless testing room; otherwise, I would have to mount it on the ceiling, away from swinging clubs. The projected image looked big enough that, when I started playing EA Sports PGA Tour, the players looked about as tall as they are in real life.
Photograph: John Brandon
I noticed Optoma offers an app to help with initial setup, but it’s a hassle to use. You have to install the app and sync over Bluetooth, but I found it was easier to just do the keystone adjustment with the included remote. (Also, Optoma did not include the required Bluetooth dongle even though it is normally part of the package.)
Fortunately, keystoning was easy with the remote because, during setup, you can just position the four corners of the image. I ran one HDMI cable for my laptop and one for an AV receiver for surround sound (I used a Yamaha RX300A). In less than 30 minutes, I had the projector running, and I was swinging with the pros at Augusta.
I will say, I had an absolute blast with the setup. I loved the massive screen for golf, and I was pleased I didn’t have to bother with golf clubs, a backdrop screen, netting, or anything else to replicate the experience. If you want to use real clubs and balls, there are quite a few golf sim apps like SkyTrak for both PC and tablets that scan your motion and render a virtual player, although the total cost can add up quickly, including the backdrop and other gear.
Even though I was using a controller to play a video game, I still felt like I was on the links because of the massive size, bright 4,200-lumen rating, and colorful picture.
Photograph: John Brandon
The GT2400HDR only runs at 1080p resolution, but it does so at low latency (only 8.4 milliseconds at 120 Hz). I wasn’t expecting home cinema quality at this price, and golf simulations don’t require subtle color variations like a theatrical movie, which might have scenes that take place at night. You need accurate greens and blues, and the GT2400HDR handled that well.
There are two HDMI ports, which is fairly common, but the projector does not support the latest HDMI 2.1 standard for eARC passthrough audio. That means no Dolby Vision, and if you connect an AV receiver, you could run into compatibility issues. For example, I tried using my Onkyo receiver and had some minor audio glitches.
The projector also doesn’t support Wi-Fi unless you add a streaming device like a Google TV or an Amazon Fire TV. It has a legacy VGA port if your device is still in the dark ages (e.g., an extremely old computer, but in reality it is still widely used for signage, in schools, and as a fail-safe port), both a 3.5-mm input and output, and (in another unusual twist) a 3D Sync port for connecting 3D glasses (which I didn’t test).
Photograph: John Brandon
The remote has one of the most confusing layouts of any projector I have used. It seems like it was designed for a bygone A/V era. There are way too many buttons, and they're very small. There are so many buttons that it all seemed like overkill, especially since you may only use those buttons occasionally. Indeed, once everything is running, I didn’t find the need to use the remote that often.
Performance off Course
Outside of golf simulation, the GT2400HDR was just average in just about every other way. I ran a few typical benchmarks, and the skin tone tests all looked bland and grayed out, as though every face looked the same. There just wasn’t enough dynamic tonal range. In a demo video, mist over a mountain scene blended into the white background and did not look distinct. In a scene involving a fence with green grass in the background—one of the best ways to test color quality—the GT2400HDR made everything look way too brown.
For movies, I watched a scene in The Batman with flares that look shockingly red on higher-end projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max. Here, the reds were too dark, lacked shadow detail, and blended too much into the dark background. In a scene from the 4K Ultra Blu-ray version of Blade Runner 2049, where the main character arrives at a protein farm, several buildings should have rendered in distinct yellows and blues. Instead, the scene looked too grayed out, like a thin veneer covered the entire screen. Of course, it didn’t help that the 4K movie had to be downgraded to 1080p resolution.
Photograph: John Brandon
I won’t harp on these detriments too much, because the GT2400HDR is not meant to compete with a movie theater. I switched to a few more games and found that Red Dead Redemption 2 on an Xbox Series X looked pretty good, if a little too atmospheric. That’s a kind way of saying the contrast is not great. At times, it seemed like the projected image had more in common with an LCD computer monitor than a home cinema projector.
The GT2400HDR disappointed in its handling of what should be impressive updated graphics in Halo: Campaign Evolved. Instead of rich, vibrant-looking trees, they looked too bland, with flat, dull greens. In Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag Resynced, the colors in a level that takes place in Havana should pop when you walk through the town, but the blue tunics, yellow fruit, and green trees lacked vibrancy.
A news broadcast looked dull and bland, as did a World Cup match I rewatched. There’s a theme here: bland and dull colors. However, I was surprised that a dark scene of a character riding a bike in the movie Awake didn’t look terrible. I could make out faces and some colors, which is saying a lot since this scene is hard to render. An entire moonlit scene in House of the Dragon, via the HBO app on a Google TV Streamer, looked completely washed out until I switched to the Vivid picture mode, which helped a bit. It was all par for the course, no pun intended.
I then watched scenes from Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 and noticed that Cinema picture mode did help punch up the colors a bit. Super Mario Galaxy lacked the color vibrancy and clarity that it normally has and looked like it was playing on a cheap computer monitor (e.g., poor contrast and less-than-vivid colors). When I switched to The Ark on YouTube TV, the colors looked much better because the show features bright, well-lit interior shots in almost every scene.
In the end, everything I tested and benchmarked on the GT2400HDR looked just OK, but I liked how well this projector works as a golf simulator. It can run all day long for multiple rounds, has low latency to make sure your controller nudges translate to accurate drives, and looks massive and bright on a large projector screen in a dark room. Sure, just about everything else is average, but if you are into golf, this is a good low-cost entry-level option.

Has there been pressure on Russian stadium to cancel planned Kanye West concerts?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

Only a week after two shows in St Petersburg were announced, Kanye West’s upcoming gigs seem to have been cancelled – as the venue hosting the concerts say it is not hosting the controversial artist. There are reports that the venue came under pressure from Moscow to cancel the shows...
Kanye ‘Ye’ West was set to become biggest western act to play in Russia since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022.
The controversial American rapper, who has mainly made headlines due to his antisemitic outbursts and cancelled European shows, was set to perform on 10 and 11 October at St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena.
Russian fans rushed to secure tickets after the shows were announced and the concerts had all but sold out.
Now, in a fresh twist, Gazprom Arena said it would not host the rapper, as no rental agreement has been signed.
In a statement on social media, the venue said: “Gazprom Arena was not and is not the organizer of this event."
“That was handled by the Moscow concert agency Say Agency. Gazprom Arena has not signed any agreement to rent the stadium for the event."
The statement added: "No such agreement exists. Accordingly, the concert cannot take place at our venue."
Previously, Gazprom Arena had posted about the concerts on social media, calling Ye "the most influential musical artist of our time".
Promoter Say Agency disputed the venue’s account, saying Gazprom Arena had approved the announcement. The company insists the concerts will still take place.
As of writing, Ye’s concert dates have been removed from the venue’s website, and there is speculation brewing that the decision follows pressure from Moscow.
While there is no official indication that authorities intervened, St Petersburg outlet Fontanka reported that the concerts had not received all the necessary approvals and were called off following a “call from above” in Moscow.
This follows opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians wishing to rid the country of any Western influence. These include conservative Russian lawmaker Vitaly Milonov, who released a video statement in which he suggested West should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist.
“Maybe after that he’ll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person,” he said.
For the time being, confusion reigns on whether the October dates will take place.
West’s anti-Semitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media which ended up getting him booted off both X and Instagram. The musician was dropped by his talent agency and fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also distanced themselves from West.
West went on to post a picture of KKK robes, rescind his previous apology to the Jewish community, declare himself “a Nazi” and assert that he has “dominion over his wife”.
In February 2025, West started selling swastika t-shirts, and in May, he released a song titled ‘Heil Hitler’, which praised the Nazi leader. This led him to be stripped of a visa to enter Australia and faced with immediate arrest in Brazil.
West apologised for his actions and took out a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal earlier this year. He addressed his past antisemitic comments, reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour" and saying that he “lost touch with reality.”
Still, many questioned the timing of his apology, considering it coincided with the release of his new album ‘Bully’ and the start of his world tour.

Can Anwar’s call for ‘freer’ filmmaking help ease Malaysia’s censorship rules?
The prime minister’s remarks come after Malaysia’s top court upheld a ban on the independent film ‘Mentega Terbang’ last month
Anwar said an industry forced to repeatedly seek official approval for individual scenes could not become more creative or competitive, calling for fewer restrictions on filmmakers at a time when Malaysian productions were outperforming Hollywood titles at home.
But his remarks came less than six weeks after Malaysia’s Court of Appeal upheld the government’s ban on the independent film Mentega Terbang, and nearly three years after Cannes-winning Tiger Stripes reached local cinemas only after cuts its director disowned.
The government is also preparing a national film policy through 2035, raising the question of whether Anwar’s call for creative freedom can translate into looser rules or remain bounded by Malaysia’s long-standing sensitivities around religion, culture and morality.
“Where is creativity if there are too many constraints and restrictions?” Anwar said on Monday at the opening of the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas), outside Kuala Lumpur.
He said filmmakers should not feel “too pressured and constrained” to the point of having to ask “five times” whether a scene would be approved.

Sam Spiegel Film Lab to take part in Venice Film Festival, will present 10 projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:29:17 UTC
19:29:17 KST

The Sam Spiegel International Film Lab will take part in the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, presenting 10 feature-film projects in development from Israel and around the world at one of the international film industry’s most prominent meeting points.
This is an especially auspicious honor at a time when anti-Israel sentiment is running high at many festivals. The Venice International Film Festival is one of the largest and most prestigious in the world, and Israeli films have been embraced there with enthusiasm in the past.
Samuel Maoz’s Lebanon, the story of a tank crew in the First Lebanon War, won the Golden Lion, the festival’s top award, in 2009, and Maoz was invited to meet Pope Benedict XVI. But in recent years, fewer Israeli films have been selected to participate.
The lab has been chosen to take part in the Venice Production Bridge, the festival’s industry platform, which connects filmmakers and producers with production and distribution companies, financiers, broadcasters, and major streaming platforms. The lab’s main event will take place on September 7 at the Hotel Excelsior on Venice’s Lido.
The 10 projects come from Austria, Brazil, Germany, Hungary, and Israel. In addition to the formal events, there will be plenty of time for the filmmakers to network at Venice, which is a major part of the development process for aspiring filmmakers. A reception for participants will be held the night before the presentation, attended by international film industry figures and festival guests.
Production prizes totaling $70,000, provided by the Beracha Foundation, will be awarded to outstanding projects.
The International Film Lab, run by the Sam Spiegel Film and Television School in Jerusalem, develops feature films by emerging filmmakers from around the world, including Israel. Dozens of films from the lab have been shown at film festivals across the globe, many of them winning major awards.
Its alumni include a number of acclaimed international filmmakers, among them László Nemes, the director of Son of Saul, which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film in 2016, as well as the Grand Jury Prize at the Cannes Film Festival.
Israeli film holds record for Ophir Award nominations
Israeli films developed at the lab have also been produced. This year, Tell Me Everything, by Moshe Rosenthal, a graduate of the lab, leads the Ophir Award nominations with a record 16 nods. Last year, The Sea, by Shai Carmeli-Pollak, another lab graduate, won five Ophir Awards, including Best Film and Best Screenplay.
“The presence of the Sam Spiegel Lab at the Venice Film Festival for the second year is testimony to the connecting power of international creation,” said Dana Blankstein Cohen, CEO and executive director of the Sam Spiegel Film and Television School.
“The lab continues to insist on intercultural dialogue and building international bridges, and to fight for freedom of expression and artistic freedom,” she said. “Cinema has a real power to shape reality, and not only to reflect it.”
Blankstein Cohen said that Sam Spiegel sees its role as providing “a place for courageous dialogue, particularly in the complex climate in which we find ourselves,” adding that open discussion and a diversity of authentic voices and stories can foster “change, growth, and deep human connection.”
Sam Spiegel attendance at Venice festival is culmination of months of development
Mor Eldar, director of the Sam Spiegel Film and Television Labs, said the Venice event is the culmination of about 10 months of development work.
“After about 10 months of development, the 10 projects that participated in the film lab will meet the international film industry at one of the three most important festivals in the field,” Eldar said. She added that she was proud of the filmmakers and confident that the intensive work would yield results, pointing to the continuing success of alumni from previous years.
The Sam Spiegel International Film Lab is supported by the Beracha Foundation, the Edmond de Rothschild Foundation, the Sam Spiegel Foundation, the Shuster Polakoff Foundation, the Austrian Film Institute, Germany’s FFA, the Hungarian Embassy, the Institut Français, and other partners.

ASTANA, August 25. /TASS/. Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry said the country’s Kondensat oil refinery will process Russian oil, with 70% of the resulting petroleum products to be shipped to Russia and the remaining 30% retained in Kazakhstan, Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said at a briefing in response to a TASS question.
"As of today, we have an agreement that up to 30% of petroleum products in demand - gasoline and diesel - will remain in Kazakhstan, while the rest will be shipped to Russia. I believe these are reasonable terms. The owner [of the company] is not included on any sanctions lists, so sanctions-related issues will not affect us," Akkenzhenov said in response to a question about agreements with the Kondensat refinery.
He noted that there are no pipelines connecting the Kondensat refinery, located in the West Kazakhstan Region, to the pipeline systems of Kazakhstan or Russia. Oil will be delivered by rail.
"If the owner wants to start supplying [the products] now, there are no obstacles. Everything depends on rail capacity. I know that they are carrying out some work to upgrade the refinery and increase its capacity. The benefits for us are additional investment in our country and the preservation of jobs," the minister explained, speaking about the timeframe for supplies from the Kondensat refinery to Russia.

The IDF and officers from Israel Police's Jordan Border Unit thwarted an attempt to smuggle weapons across the Jordanian border last night, police announced in a Tuesday statement.

During their search of the area, police discovered 10 handguns buried in a bag near the bridge.
Police transferred the suspects to the Judea and Samaria District's police headquarters for further questioning.
The incident follows an infiltration alert in the Jordan Valley region on Monday night. In response to the suspected infiltration, the IDF set up blockades in the area to locate any suspects.
Israel's border with Jordan vulnerable to terror infiltration, weapons smuggling
In July, N12 News reported that despite the ongoing construction of a new border security fence between Israel and Jordan, local residents are fearful that a Jordanian attack could face little in the way of defenses.
Central Arava Regional Council Head Meir Tzur pointed out the vulnerability presented by the current wire-fence setup.
"There's nothing behind it," he explained to N12. "There's no problem crossing this twisted fence either. Here, for example, it's completely open. There are no indicative measures on the fence. Any citizen can cross; they don't even have to jump because it's torn down."
The border was also seldom patrolled by IDF forces, Tzus stated. "You can just walk into Jordan."
"We really want the Israeli army to be stationed on the border line, and not just with remote technology," he added. "We are afraid of this technology. Every Israeli knows that what starts with a small breach may eventually lead to a failure. A fence alone or technology is not the absolute solution."
From across the border, a steady stream of illegal entrants and smuggled goods has flowed into Israel over the years, local residents stated, including illegal weapons.
One military source told N12 that the IDF catches around 50% of the smuggled weapons and goods. "If they succeed in smuggling weapons, they can also succeed in smuggling a terrorist."
Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

Foreign Service officers could begin returning to their posts as early as this week, according to the report. Emergency measures introduced at US diplomatic missions across the region could also begin to be scaled back.
The planned redeployment would mark a shift in Washington's diplomatic security posture after months in which US missions operated with significantly reduced staffing because of the conflict. The report did not indicate that all affected embassies would immediately return to normal operations.
Earlier in August, the State Department was reported to have asked US embassies across the Middle East to prepare reduced-operations plans. At the time, officials were considering a prolonged period with smaller numbers of personnel on the ground as the war with Iran continued and diplomats displaced from their assignments faced uncertainty over when they could return.
The drawdown began after the US and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran on February 28. As the conflict intensified and American diplomatic facilities faced missile and drone threats, Washington ordered nonemergency personnel and family members to leave missions in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. Israel and Lebanon had already been operating under departure arrangements before the wider regional drawdown.
Iran subsequently retaliated against targets across the Middle East, including Gulf states and US military facilities. The regional confrontation has continued despite periods of reduced military activity, with Washington maintaining military and economic pressure on Tehran.
Tensions remain unresolved as US heavily sanctions Iran
The apparent easing of restrictions on diplomatic personnel comes as tensions between Washington and Tehran remain unresolved. On Tuesday, the US imposed additional sanctions connected to Iranian military activity and petroleum exports, while US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Washington had not ruled out further military strikes around Iran or the Strait of Hormuz.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of friction. US President Donald Trump said last week that no negotiations with Iran were scheduled and that the US naval blockade remained in effect, as efforts to reach a lasting arrangement over the strategic waterway remained stalled.

Vande Mataram row: Is Congress taking a calculated gamble or walking into BJP's trap?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:27:32 UTC

Vande Mataram row: Is Congress taking a calculated gamble or walking into BJP's trap?
Kunal Varma / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 25, 2026, 16:06 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Mallikarjun Kharge, Sonia Gandhi and Rahul at Congress headquarters on Independence Day.
NEW DELHI: Is the Congress trying to send out a subtle message signalling “soft minority appeasement”? Or has the party played to BJP’s strength by lapping up a controversy that may push it into a corner?The Congress's decision to sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram at party events signalled a rare hardening of stance on an issue that the party knows could make it vulnerable to attacks over both minority appeasement and nationalism.As expected, the Congress decision, which cited a 1937 resolution, triggered sharp reactions from the BJP, with Union home minister Amit Shah accusing the Congress of repeating "politics of appeasement."Union Minister JP Nadda also slammed the Congress, alleging that the party's 1937 resolution was driven by "appeasement politics" and contributed to the circumstances that led to the Partition. In a post on X, Nadda said the Congress' decision in 1937 to divide 'Vande Mataram' into two parts fuelled the two-nation theory and ultimately led to the partition of the country.'This was followed by attacks questioning Congress’s commitment to nationalism and patriotism.Union Minister Giriraj Singh accused the Congress leadership of disrespecting the legacy of India's freedom fighters and operating under ideological pressure. "This is not just opposition to Vande Mataram but against our revolutionaries," Singh said, adding, "Now, the Congress has become the Muslim League. This is not Gandhi ji's Congress but Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi's Congress," the BJP leader said.
BJP MP Dinesh Sharma also accused the opposition leadership of harbouring "Muslim League-like thinking." He equated senior Congress leaders with Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan who spearheaded the Two-Nation Theory, to criticise the Congress party's approach toward national symbols.Later, the BJP passed a resolution condemning the Congress Working Committee's decision to sing only the first two stanzas of 'Vande Mataram' and announced a nationwide campaign to raise awareness about the history and significance of the National Song.No surprises here. All these attacks were on expected lines. Surely, the Congress would have anticipated these high-pitched narratives questioning its nationalism and accusing it of appeasement.
Congress fights back
Congress leaders defended the party's stand, saying 'Vande Mataram' was associated with the freedom struggle and held emotional significance for the Congress. They accused the BJP of politicising the issue and diverting attention from the issue of Ram Mandir donation theft."BJP was not a part of the freedom struggle. Vande Mataram was a part of the freedom struggle; it is emotional for us, but political for them (BJP)," Venugopal said, adding, "We have been reciting Vande Mataram since 1937, more than 90 years. What is new for us?"The Congress leaders alleged that political rivals led by the BJP were deliberately stoking nationalist narratives to cover up their failures. What the Congress perhaps did not realise, or chose to ignore, was that the BJP had already set the stage for bringing Vande Mataram to the centrestage of its politics.Why the 1937 reference created more problems than it solvedBankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote ‘Bande Mataram’ in the late 19th century in Sanskritised Bengali. The original version consisted of six stanzas. The song was first inserted into the pages of his novel, Anandamath, set during the late 18th century when famine and rebellion tore through Bengal.In 1950, alongside ‘Jana Gana Mana’ as the national anthem, Vande Mataram received the honour of a national song following a decision of the Constituent Assembly, under the guidance of Rajendra Prasad, considering the historic role it played in India’s freedom struggle.However, only the first two stanzas of the song were adopted as the national song.The Congress Working Committee (CWC), in a resolution of October 29, 1937, decided that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at national and public gatherings.This had followed advice from Rabindranath Tagore, who was the first to set Vande Mataram to music and publicly sing it at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. In a letter to Jawaharlal Nehru, he suggested that only the first two stanzas of the song be used for public and national gatherings.Tagore then noted that the later verses — which invoked Hindu deities like Durga within the context of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel Anandamath—could alienate non-Hindu communities.The fact that the Muslim League and M A Jinnah were among the most vociferous critics of the song made the Congress’s 1937 resolution vulnerable to Muslim appeasement attacks ever since.
BJP’s Vande Mataram push
BJP’s Vande Mataram push began in May this year when the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act and put the National Song, Vande Mataram, composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, on the same footing as the National Anthem, Jana Gana Mana.It was during the special discussion of Parliament on “150th Year of Vande Mataram” in December last year that defence minister Rajnath Singh had strongly advocated for elevating the status of Vande Mataram to match the National Anthem. Rajnath had then accused the Congress of historically communalising the song and sidelining it due to appeasement politics.Earlier in January this year the Union home ministry had outlined appropriate conduct and protocols concerning Vande Mataram. The ministry had issued an order that all six stanzas of the official version must be rendered first whenever the National Song and the National Anthem are performed together. It said that the full six-stanza version was to be sung or played on key state occasions.These proposals became law in the just-concluded Monsoon session after Parliament amended the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, giving Vande Mataram equal legal standing to the National Anthem. The government is also midway through a year-long commemoration of Vande Mataram's 150th anniversary.The amended Act mandates Vande Mataram shall be honoured equally with ‘Jana-Gana-Mana’ and shall have equal status with it, and whoever intentionally prevents the singing of the Indian National Anthem or causes disturbance to any assembly engaged in such singing shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or both.
Could Congress have avoided this row
Clearly, given the BJP moves, the Congress would have been aware of the political fallout of its Vande Mataram decision. Minority appeasement has been one of the biggest weapons, which the BJP has used very effectively to attack and corner the Congress.In the last 12 years, we have seen the Congress suffer politically over allegations of minority appeasement. The Congress leadership has tried to fight back with a calculated push for soft Hindutva. Rahul Gandhi and other top Congress leaders have visited temples to counter BJP’s attacks on minority appeasement.In the 1980s, the Congress faced a Shah Bano moment, which is still used to target and corner the party over allegations of minority appeasement. The then Congress government led by Rajiv Gandhi enacted a law in Parliament to limit a Muslim husband's maintenance obligation to the three-month iddat period, neutralizing a Supreme Court maintenance order under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).Minorities, especially Muslims, for a very long time were part of Congress’s core vote bank and supported the party electorally. However, as the Congress lost political heft, the minorities gradually shifted to other regional parties. The same happened with other social groups like the SCs, STs and the OBCs. For the last many years, the Congress has been forced to align with the regional parties that weaned away its core voters. Now, as it tries to script its revival, it is trying to win back these communities into the party fold.We have seen Rahul Gandhi aggressively woo the SCs, STs and the OBCs by repeatedly taking up issues that impact them. The Congress leader’s sustained pitch for caste census was an open move to reach out to these core voters. But when it comes to wooing back the minority voters, the Congress perhaps wants to play it safe. And it’s not just the Muslim appeasement attack that the Congress wants to avoid, it perhaps also does not want to antagonize its ally in Uttar Pradesh - the Samajwadi Party.
Interestingly, Rahul and Akhilesh Yadav appeal to the same social support base and hence the alliance chemistry is always overshadowed by competing interests.It is in this context that one is left wondering: Has the Congress taken a calculated gamble?

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Chinese ship caught with banned shark fins in Pacific Ocean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:25:29 UTC
19:25:29 KST

Chinese ship caught with banned shark fins in Pacific Ocean in operation involving U.S. Coast Guard
Kiribati, a tiny Pacific neighbor to Hawaii that has grown ties with Beijing, detained a Chinese vessel this month for illegally harvesting shark fins, its maritime police told AFP.
The practice of cutting fins off live sharks and throwing the carcasses back into the sea is banned in much of the Pacific Ocean, but persists due to demand in East and Southeast Asia.
The Chinese ship was among four vessels detained in a surveillance crackdown by 11 Pacific island nations between Aug. 3 to Aug. 14, assisted by the U.S. Coast Guard in some areas and an Australian military aircraft. Kiribati, however, operates its own patrol boat.
The vessel was licensed to travel through Kiribati's waters but was detained by the maritime police after inspectors found shark fins on board, commander Tom Redfern told AFP.
"It was escorted back to Christmas Island for further investigation," he said, referring to a large atoll belonging to Kiribati and located south of Hawaii.
Kiribati has an exclusive economic zone spanning 1.4 million square miles of ocean, and has drawn interest from Chinese state companies since switching diplomatic ties from Taiwan in 2019.
It also hosts Chinese police, a decision the United States has said risks fueling regional tensions.
"A Kiribati Police maritime boarding officer, not under a shiprider agreement, boarded and inspected it, finding that the vessel was breaching its condition of license by keeping and retaining shark fins onboard," said Redfern.
Kiribati has recently strengthened cooperation with France, with French military personnel due to arrive next month on Christmas Island to rebuild local police stations.
The practice of removing shark fins is banned across the region.
The cruelty behind the shark fin trade is well-documented. Shark finning often involves slicing fins off live sharks and discarding the mutilated animals back into the ocean, where they die from blood loss, suffocation or predation.
"Hard to detect"
Andrew Chin, a fisheries researcher at Australia's James Cook University, said finning had led to "massive declines" in shark numbers, prompting stringent controls in the Pacific.
"Because it is now illegal, if people are doing it, it is going to be hidden and really hard to detect," he said.
Research on the DNA of thousands of shark fins sold in Hong Kong markets pointed to its origins in the region.
"We have seen evidence of illegal trade from the western and eastern sides of the Pacific," Demian Chapman, who conducted the research as director of the Sharks and Rays Conservation Research Program at Mote Marine Laboratory in Florida, said.
There have been other cases of Chinese vessels violating the finning ban, he told AFP.
Reduced demand in China for shark fin soup, including a ban on serving it at government functions, had contributed to a fall in the amount of fins being traded in Hong Kong, he added.
Last November, U.S. authorities assisted the Peruvian government in seizing an estimated 10,000 shark fins destined for China. The bust, at an industrial port outside of Lima, led to the arrest of three men tied to a transnational criminal network involved in illegal fishing and wildlife smuggling, officials said.
In 2020, wildlife inspectors at a port in Miami discovered 1,400 pounds of dried shark fins.

Fire at AGCC
- A fire broke out at the AGCC construction site, the plant’s press service said.

- To ensure safety and minimize potential damage, plant personnel are shutting down equipment that is currently undergoing commissioning.

- Air quality is being monitored at the site of the fire at the Amur Gas Chemical Complex, the plant’s press service said.
- The results will be published later on the company’s website and official social media accounts.
- A commission has been established to investigate the causes of the incident.

How to reset your child’s sleep schedule for back-to-school season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:23:02 UTC
19:23:02 KST

How to reset your child’s sleep schedule for back-to-school season
NEW YORK (AP) — After a summer of vacations and late nights, it’s time to set those back-to-school alarms.
A good night’s sleep helps students stay focused and attentive in class. Experts say it’s worth easing kids back into a routine with the start of a new school year.
“We don’t say ‘ get good sleep ’ just because,” said pediatrician Dr. Gabrina Dixon with Children’s National Hospital. “It really helps kids learn and it helps them function throughout the day.”
The amount of sleep kids need changes as they age. Preschoolers should get up to 13 hours of sleep. Tweens need between nine and 12 hours. Teenagers do best with eight to 10 hours of shut-eye.
Set an earlier bedtime
Early bedtimes can slip through the cracks over the summer as kids stay up for sleepovers, movie marathons and long plane flights. To get back on track, experts recommend setting earlier bedtimes a week or two before the first day of school or gradually going to bed 15 to 30 minutes earlier each night.
This article is part of AP’s Be Well coverage, focusing on wellness, fitness, diet and mental health. Read more Be Well.
Don’t serve a heavy meal before bed and avoid TV or screen time two hours before sleep. Instead, work on relaxing activities to slow down, like showering and reading a story.
“You’re trying to take the cognitive load off your mind,” said Dr. Nitun Verma, a spokesperson for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. “It would be like if you’re driving, you’re slowly letting go of the gas pedal.”
Parents can adjust their back-to-school plans based on what works best for their child. Nikkya Hargrove moves her twin daughters’ bedtimes up by 30 minutes the week before school starts.
Sometimes, her kids will negotiate for a few extra minutes to stay up and read. Hargrove said those conversations are important as her children get older and advocate for themselves. If they stay up too late and don’t have the best morning, Hargrove said that can be a learning experience too.
“If they’re groggy and they don’t like how they feel, then they know, ‘OK, I have to go to bed earlier,’” said Hargrove, an author and independent bookstore owner from Connecticut.
In the morning, soaking in some daylight by sitting at a window or going outside can help train the brain to power up, Verma said.
Squash back-to-school sleep anxiety
Sleep quality matters just as much as duration. First-day jitters can make it hard to fall asleep no matter how early the bedtime.
Dixon says parents can talk to their kids to find out what is making them anxious. Is it the first day at a new school? Is it a fear of making new friends? Then they might try a test run of stressful activities before school starts to make those tasks feel less scary — for example, by visiting the school or meeting classmates at an open house.
The weeks leading up to school can be jam-packed and it’s not always possible to prep a routine in advance. But kids will adjust eventually, so sleep experts say parents should do what they can. After all, their kids aren’t the only ones adjusting to a new routine.
“I always say, ‘Take a deep breath, it’ll be OK,’” Dixon said. “And just start that schedule.”

Hungary files a criminal complaint over $965M COVID-19 ventilator deal, citing possible fraud
BUDAPEST, Hungary (AP) — Hungary’s foreign ministry has filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors over what it says was possible fraud related to the previous government’s purchase of ventilators worth some $965 million during the COVID-19 pandemic, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said Tuesday.
Hungary’s previous government under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán purchased the roughly 17,000 ventilators from China in March and April 2020, drawing criticism at the time that it was buying far more units than could be realistically deployed and paying much more per unit than other European countries.
In a video posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Orbán, who is not related to the former prime minister, said the results of a ministry investigation into the purchase “raises suspicions of breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly substantial financial loss and other criminal offenses.”
She didn’t detail specific allegations, but noted that the investigation involved tens of thousands of documents — some of which had to be recovered using digital tools “after unsuccessful attempts to delete them” — and raised further questions “about the responsibility of the ministry’s former senior leadership.”
A statement released on the Hungarian government’s website on Tuesday pointed to other suspected irregularities related to the ventilator procurement, including that most of the units were purchased through intermediary companies that saw their revenues rise exponentially due to the transaction.
Some of the ventilators were defective, and a significant proportion of them was never deployed, the statement reads, adding that storage costs for the unused devices ran into the millions of dollars.
Hungary’s former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó cultivated close ties with China during his nearly 12 years in office, and oversaw the purchase of the ventilators as well as the procurement of 5 million doses of the China-produced Sinopharm COVID-19 vaccine.
Last month, Szijjártó resigned his seat in Parliament to take an executive position with Chinese automaker BYD, prompting accusations of a conflict of interest due to his role in facilitating substantial government subsidies given to the company while in office.
Hungary’s government later launched an investigation into large investments into Hungary made by BYD during Szijjártó’s tenure.

Putin issues decree opening door to state control of key sites after deep Ukrainian drone strikes

Putin issues decree opening door to state control of key sites after deep Ukrainian drone strikes
Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree allowing the government to temporarily take control of critical infrastructure if private owners fail to protect it from Ukrainian drone attacks or rebuild it after strikes, apparently the latest indication that Moscow is feeling the strain of war.
Russia is facing economic and political pressure due to months of escalating, deep and increasingly accurate Ukrainian strikes. Kyiv has used domestically developed long-range drones to target vital oil facilities, triggering fuel shortages that Putin publicly admitted, and major commercial hubs, embarrassing the Russian leadership.
Ukraine has also reeled from relentless Russian aerial attacks that have smashed its power grid ahead of winter and heavily damaged homes, as Russia’s invasion stretches into its fifth year.
The decree may pressure owners to undertake repairs
The Kremlin’s intentions with Putin’s decree, announced late Monday, are unclear. However, it applies to various sectors, including energy and fuel infrastructure, industrial, communications, transport and logistics facilities.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that “often business owners do not pay enough attention to taking measures to ensure safety, anti-drone safety.”
Given the drone threat against vital economic infrastructure, “we must take measures, we must ensure our own safety,” Peskov said.
Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in a statement Monday evening that the decree doesn’t imply nationalization of companies or a change of ownership — only “involvement of the state in the management of an enterprise to solve specific security problems.”
He added that “this mechanism doesn’t imply widespread use — targeted, carefully considered decisions will be made at the highest level.”
Russian political analyst Abbas Gallyamov said the measure might be a “tactical” step designed to make the owners of repeatedly damaged oil refineries undertake repairs that they might otherwise shy away from.
“Given the fact that the same refinery has already been hit three to five times, it’s safe to assume that the owners are now reluctant to invest in restoring what’s been destroyed,” he said on the Telegram messaging app.
“Why spend billions if they’re going to get hit again tomorrow?” asked Gallyamov, who once worked as a speechwriter for Putin.
The government is giving companies an ultimatum, he said: “If you don’t finance the restoration of the refineries, we’ll take them away from you.”
Russia suffers major economic challenges due to Ukrainian strikes
In the latest attacks, Ukraine’s General Staff said Tuesday its forces struck facilities at Russia’s Afipsky oil refinery in the Krasnodar region overnight, causing a fire. Krasnodar Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said a fire broke out at an oil refinery in the town of Afipsky.
A Ukrainian attack also damaged the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in southern Russia’s Rostov region overnight and halted operations, Rostov Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Tuesday. He didn’t provide any other details.
Russia faces fundamental economic challenges as the costly war drags on. The government has raised taxes and increased domestic borrowing to keep Russia’s budget deficit under control, and taking over major companies could potentially bring it windfall revenue.
At the same time, taking over damaged assets could bring another financial burden for authorities. The Kremlin may intend the measure as a way to pressure companies to shoulder more responsibility for air defense, as Russia’s vast territory is hard to protect comprehensively.
Russia has also introduced more help for its biggest online retailer, Wildberries, and businesses selling goods through it — the company and thousands of sellers working with it were hit hard by Ukrainian strikes on warehouses. The Finance Ministry proposed Monday extending deadlines for tax and insurance payments to give Wildberries and its sellers some financial breathing space.
On Saturday, Putin told Russian state television that in the wake of Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia, Moscow “must and will improve the air defense system and enhance its capabilities.”
“We need to streamline coordination between defense, law enforcement and civilian agencies at all levels, and to leverage the capabilities of state‑run enterprises and private businesses,” Putin said.
In May, with Ukraine’s deep strikes unsettling Moscow, Russian lawmakers approved a bill that allowed the country’s Central Bank, state-controlled Sberbank and some other financial services to fend off drone attacks by installing air defenses on their premises.
Russian news outlet RBC reported in May, citing anonymous sources in and close to the Defense Ministry, that a mechanism had been established for businesses to procure weapons and equipment to protect themselves from Ukrainian drone attacks, something Russian officials and lawmakers have said companies should do.

Government lays out housing plans but Burnham backtracks on social renting pledge
Good morning and welcome to the UK politics live blog.
The government has set out its plans to spend an initial £10bn on a mix of subsidised housing in England, with a target of 60% being social renting.
The funding, which comes from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme, is in line with the Starmer government’s policy and sees Andy Burnham backtrack on his proposal to rip up housing plans and boost social home building.
Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.
There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.
Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.
London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.
Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.
The Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnham has promised will be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.

Climate damage would obliterate any economic benefits of new North Sea fields, analysis shows
Damian Carrington
The climate damage caused by developing the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields under consideration by the UK government would destroy their economic benefits many times over, according to an analysis.
It estimates the economic damage caused by the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced would be between £119bn and £336bn in the coming decades, compared with the £28.7bn in value to the UK estimated by Adura, the fossil fuel company promoting the new fields.
The assessment applies peer-reviewed research on how rising temperatures harm economies to the production estimates for the fields from the company. The figures are likely to be underestimates, as they do not include losses from amplified extreme weather, sea level rise or climate deaths.
The analysis has been submitted to the Rosebank consultation and to an academic journal.
The decision on whether to approve Rosebank and Jackdaw has become highly controversial, with the oil industry, some energy leaders and rightwing political parties pushing for the go-ahead. Most centre and leftwing political parties, climate scientists and environmental campaigners are opposed.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, also faces a revolt from Labour MPs who oppose the plans, while the former energy secretary Ed Miliband once called the Rosebank proposal “climate vandalism”.

That’s exactly what we’re doing through this initial wave of funding.
