China’s J-16s face off against Egypt’s Rafales in combat drills as Iran war rumbles on
PLA pilots test strategic reach in 6,000km mission as Middle East conflict pushes Cairo and Beijing closer
Chinese fighter jets have conducted combat training with their Egyptian counterparts in a joint exercise following a major Chinese air force deployment to the Middle East.
The aircraft flew more than 6,000km (3,730 miles) over nine hours to reach Egypt, crossing four countries, according to a report by state broadcaster CCTV. However, it did not specify which four countries the PLA Air Force aircraft flew over, or whether their route approached Iran or any Persian Gulf nations.
“Through cross-border deployment and rapid loading and unloading operations, the exercise tested the air force’s capabilities in long-range force projection, rapid deployment and integrated operations,” CCTV reported.
During the flight, the J-16s conducted aerial refuelling from YU-20 tankers before landing at an airbase in Egypt on August 21, the report said.
The PLA Air Force then unloaded supplies, sorted equipment and coordinated briefings ready for training missions within a single day, according to the report.
“The joint exercises have provided a valuable platform for us pilots to improve our combat capabilities,” Ning Yiming, a pilot taking part in the drill, was quoted as saying.

Royal Navy urged to build Hybrid Navy operating system
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
11:00:08 BST
19:00:08 KST

A former Royal Navy commodore has warned that the Hybrid Navy will not succeed simply by buying autonomous ships and drones, arguing that communications, software, command systems and logistics must become the core of the programme.
The Royal Navy risks turning its Hybrid Navy concept into another collection of separately procured platforms unless it builds the digital, command and logistics architecture needed to connect them, according to a new analysis by a former senior naval officer, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Writing for the Royal United Services Institute, Commodore (Ret’d) Steve Prest argues that the emphasis on autonomous surface vessels, large uncrewed underwater vehicles and drones risks obscuring the more difficult task of creating the infrastructure that allows those systems to operate as an integrated fighting force. Prest, a RUSI Associate Fellow in Military Sciences, describes the Hybrid Navy as an ecosystem rather than a programme for replacing crewed warships with robotic equivalents.
He writes: “The temptation is to see Hybrid Navy as a programme to deliver autonomous ships. That would be a profound misunderstanding. Autonomous vessels are not the point; they are simply the most visible applications of a much bigger idea.”
The distinction matters because the Royal Navy’s emerging Hybrid Navy concept envisages crewed warships operating alongside increasing numbers of autonomous and remotely operated systems. Prest argues that simply procuring each new platform through separate programmes could reproduce the same organisational boundaries found in the existing Fleet, only with a different mix of hardware. Separate architectures, proprietary interfaces and isolated support arrangements could leave individual systems unable to generate the combined operational effect envisaged by the concept.
Prest writes: “There is a real danger that Hybrid Navy simply recreates the traditional acquisition model using different platforms.” He argues that replacing independently procured frigates, submarines and helicopters with independently procured surface drones, underwater vehicles and artificial intelligence would amount to a digital version of the existing fleet rather than a fundamentally different force.
At the centre of his proposal is what he describes as a maritime operating system. Rather than a single software package, this would encompass digital infrastructure, resilient communications, command and control, cloud services, cyber resilience, common data standards, artificial intelligence, software deployment, digital engineering and logistics. In this model, individual crewed and uncrewed platforms become nodes connected through a wider fighting architecture.
Prest argues that the Maritime Fighting Web, already identified as a central element of the Royal Navy’s future force, should form part of that architecture but requires greater clarity and resources. He writes that discussion about future ship classes risks becoming a distraction from what he describes as the “cognitive architecture” governing where decisions are made, what information is available and how weapons, sensors and autonomous systems interact.
He states: “Uncrewed, or even Autonomous, systems are not the operating system. They are applications running on it.” Prest argues that an autonomous vessel provides little additional combat power by itself, with its value instead depending on connectivity to communications networks, edge computing, artificial intelligence, mission data, logistics and command systems.
The commentary also proposes a practical test of whether the Royal Navy is developing that architecture quickly enough. Prest suggests demonstrating a disaggregated air-defence engagement in which a Sea Ceptor missile is fired by one ship against a target detected and tracked solely by the sensors of another platform, rather than by the firing ship itself.
He asks: “So, when is the first demonstration of, say, a Sea Ceptor missile engaging a target tracked only by an accompanying Type 45 destroyer and not from its ship’s own onboard sensors?” Prest argues that Britain should demonstrate such an engagement by the end of 2026, noting that it would test a fundamental assumption behind a distributed combat system without requiring an entirely new class of ship.

MADE: bush terminal by NYCEDC empowers creative ecosystem on brooklyn waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:07 UTC
19:00:07 KST

Along Brooklyn’s Sunset Park waterfront, MADE: Bush Terminal is home to a growing community of artisans, designers, and industrial pioneers shaping the future of New York City’s creative economy. To support these urban makers, New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC)revitalized the historic public building after decades of restricted access, creating productive workspaces designed to fuel local innovation alongside economic benchmarks – including a projected 165 permanent jobs and 2.6 billion USD in economic impact over 30 years. Designed by nARCHITECTS, the MADE (Manufacturers, Artisans, Designers, and Entrepreneurs) campus provides 140,000 square feet of manufacturing space and 30,000 square feet of public event programming. Public Records, a multifaceted music venue that originated in Gowanus, Brooklyn will program the ground floor as a music driven community space. The MADE campus serves as a collaborative incubator where local talent, craft-based enterprises, and technical innovators work side by side, cultivating shared knowledge, sustainable practices, and long-term economic resilience.
‘At MADE: Bush Terminal, NYCEDC continues to bring together design, manufacturing, and artistic partners to expand opportunity for all New Yorkers. By activating more than 66,000 square feet at the Brooklyn Army Terminal and MADE: Bush Terminal, we’re strengthening a thriving industrial ecosystem that supports manufacturers, mission‑driven companies, and the local community,’ said NYCEDC Interim President and CEO Jeanny Pak, ‘cementing Sunset Park’s role as a hub for innovation, entrepreneurship, and inclusive economic growth.’
NYCEDC REVITALIZES HISTORIC BUILDING FOR ECONOMIC GROWTH
Managed by NYCEDC, the project reflects a long-term strategy to modernize historic municipal spaces into drivers of inclusive design and growth. First established in the late 19th century as the largest multi-tenant industrial campus in the United States, Bush Terminal played a pivotal role in New York’s maritime history. Today, NYCEDC brings a new chapter to the waterfront site with advances in environmental stewardship, social equity, and active local engagement. Offering adaptable spaces for emerging enterprises, the initiativeensures that industrial investment directly fosters both job creation and community-centered development.
MADE: Bush Terminal anchors a new era of urban manufacturing on the Brooklyn waterfront
MADE: BUSH TERMINAL SCALES SUNSET PARK’S CREATIVE INDUSTRY
At MADE: Bush Terminal, a curated mix of craft-based and high-tech tenants is redefining contemporary fabrication on the Brooklyn waterfront. Lighting manufacturer Stickbulb expands its presence across campus to over 27,000 square feet in Buildings A and B, consolidating its production, design studio, and showroom into a unified circular design footprint. 3D-printing hub Makelab operates alongside design studios PELLE, Aripack, and MushLume. Together, these studios combine technical expertise with bio-based material exploration to push the boundaries of modern object design.
craft-based and high-tech studios redefine contemporary fabrication at MADE: Bush Terminal
This creative momentum extends across the broader Sunset Park ecosystem, where the neighboring Brooklyn Army Terminal (BAT) hosts audiovisual pioneer Audible Difference, clean-tech B-Corp EcoLogic Solutions, logistics provider GoLocker, and cinema technology leader Otto Nemenz. Complementing this industrial mix, NYCEDC launched the BATWorks climate innovation hub alongside a new cultural partnership with Public Service. With the transformation of 1,000-capacity space into a dynamic venue for live music and large-scale art installations, the project anchors MADE as a landmark model for civic design, material circularity, and creative industry.

Chinese dad’s chemotherapy note prompts food vendor’s US$15 donation, going viral
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

Chinese dad’s chemotherapy note prompts food vendor’s US$15 donation, goes viral
Father praises stranger’s compassion for bringing warmth to their darkest days
A street food vendor in central China received widespread acclaim after discreetly slipping 100 yuan (US$15) into a takeaway order for a family whose child was undergoing chemotherapy.
On August 17, Wang Xianhuang, an egg pancake vendor in Hefei, Anhui province, noticed a heartfelt note attached to a food delivery order that read, “For a child undergoing chemotherapy. Please do not include shredded kelp or lettuce. Make half of it non-spicy.”
The message resonated with Wang, prompting him to reflect on the challenges the child and family were facing.
After preparing the pancake, Wang added two complimentary cups of soy milk and tucked 100 yuan in cash inside the package.
The child’s father, surnamed Zhu, was profoundly moved and subsequently shared the story online. His four-year-old son, Haolin, had been diagnosed with leukaemia in February and was currently undergoing treatment.

====================================================================================================

Why AI Watermarks and Detectors Could Backfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Claude now watermarks AI-generated text to comply with European Union transparency rules. OpenAI and Google add invisible fingerprints to AI-generated images. And Substack is touting a feature that scans pieces for signs of AI. Will we finally be able to tell what’s real on the Internet? My take: not even close.
In fact, AI watermarks and detectors may leave us worse off by creating a false sense of confidence in content marked as genuine.
Watermarks and detectors are gaining traction as we lose our ability to trust our senses online. Look up the Will Smith eating spaghetti test, and you’ll see just how far AI has come. A 2023 AI-generated video shows the actor slurping spaghetti, face distorted, in a way that breaks physics. By 2025, AI was producing lifelike renditions. Deepfakes are so good that experts recommend families develop secret codewords to identify one another.
“But I know a fake when I see it,” someone might say.
Unfortunately, research consistently shows that you do not. This can feel especially hard to accept given the abundance of AI slop rocketing around the Internet. You may even start to think you can sniff out offending content. It might work, for a little bit. It almost never lasts. Any signal that becomes discernible is one a sophisticated actor will find ways to avoid.
We’ve seen this story before. During the earliest days of the Internet, visual polish at least told you something. Major institutions had the resources needed to produce well-designed websites. Janky-looking sites, on the other hand, screamed “scam!” Information experts directed Internet users to dwell on features such as design, broken links, and typos. But when the Internet changed, the advice didn’t.
A study I led, published in 2022, found that 96% of America’s leading colleges and universities offered outdated advice on how to evaluate online information—long after platforms like Wix, Squarespace, and Photoshop made it easier for bad actors to create fake but convincing-looking websites. Inexpensive software made slick graphics ubiquitous. Educators, however, continued to instruct Internet users to search for visual clues like a game of Where’s Waldo?
The most dangerous legacy of this aesthetic fixation is the inverse illusion: the cognitive tendency to believe that if the presence of a signal proves one thing, its absence proves the opposite. Yes, a site with misspellings that claims to show aliens still isn’t legit. But a beautiful site with a dot-org domain can also be harmful. In 2019, our research group found that nearly half of hate groups had dot-org domains. Bad actors know how to adopt the trappings of credibility.
The same is true with AI. Even if visible flaws sometimes linger, their absence doesn’t mean content is genuine. Yet, too often, experts offer surface-level clues to identifying AI-generated content. This is why in the lead-up to the 2024 elections, Stanford Professor Sam Wineburg and I warned about public officials who advised citizens to pay attention to lighting, strange shadows, or other visual cues to identify deepfakes, even after AI content stopped making these errors. Many 2026 guides to spotting AI content mislead readers with the same poor advice.
Which brings us to AI watermarks and detectors. These approaches, based on hidden signals in content, promise that while we can’t always spot the signs, their algorithms can.
I’m not a software engineer. Yet I was able to easily strip metadata from some AI-generated images just by screenshotting them. Anthropic confirms that file metadata can be “stripped through format conversion, re-saving, screenshots, or other means.” Watermarks like SynthID are stronger and can persist after screenshots. But I was able to use a free online tool to remove a SynthID watermark.
Google admits that the accuracy of detecting watermarked AI text is “greatly reduced” when users thoroughly rewrite what they generate, and that it “is not designed to directly stop motivated adversaries from causing harm.” More broadly, open-weight AI models that can run locally, outside platform terms and conditions, guarantee the spread of unmarked content.
Third-party detectors, too, have a spotty track record. I’ve regularly run AI-generated text through detectors that said it was human and vice versa. Many studies of text, image, and audio detectors find that they don’t work very consistently, and yet, their findings are used as the basis for public accusations. Every detector must confront an arms race with humanizer tools and other workarounds motivated actors find.
I would argue that the biggest problem for detectors and watermarks remains the inverse illusion. Just because content lacks a watermark doesn’t mean it wasn’t produced or edited with AI. As Anthropic notes: “lack of a detected mark doesn’t mean the content wasn’t AI-generated or processed.” Deferring judgment to AI detectors leaves us vulnerable to bad actors who know how to launder content and make it pass muster.
This is a confusing time. Many of us are, understandably, uncertain. In one recent pilot, our research group showed 117 students a confident chatbot answer about local history with hallucinated facts. Half said they weren’t sure if it was true. One student said AI is sometimes right and sometimes wrong and “you never know which is which.”
But just because we can’t trust our eyes or place full faith in detectors doesn’t mean we can’t trust anything. Rather than hunt for visual clues or outsource judgment to detectors and watermarks, we can turn to reputation and context. It’s easy to fake content. It’s much harder to fake a good reputation that’s validated by credible sources.
The next time you see unfamiliar content online, resist the urge to ask, “Does this look like AI?” or run the content through a detector. Instead, ask yourself, “Do I trust where this information is coming from?” Open a new tab and check if reputable people and organizations confirm what you’re seeing.
In an era of dwindling trust, we should not fork over ours to cheap signals or cheap software.

Summer Is Ending With a 'Blood Moon' Lunar Eclipse. Here's What To Know.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

It’s not often that 3.6 billion people—or 44.4% of the world’s population—look at the same thing at the same time. And it’s not often that something comes along that’s worth the attention of all those billions. But that will happen on the evening of Aug. 27 when much of the world will be able to witness a blood moon lunar eclipse, during which 96% of the face of the full moon will fall into Earth’s shadow, glowing a deep orange-red in the process.
Lunar eclipses occur during a full moon, when the Earth is positioned between the sun and the moon, blocking all or most of the solar light that otherwise bathes the lunar surface. On average, lunar eclipses occur two to three times per year, though total lunar eclipses, when the moon is entirely shadowed, make up only 29% of those events. The autumnal color the moon takes on is due to a trick of the Earth’s atmosphere. Not all of the sunlight that would otherwise be striking the moon during an eclipse is blocked by the Earth; some of it leaks around the periphery of the planet and manages to reach the moon. That light streams through the Earth’s atmosphere during its passage to the moon, and some of the wavelengths of visible light—particularly the blue—are absorbed and scattered. What’s left is principally the red spectrum which partially lights the moon. All total lunar eclipses result in blood moons.
In theory, a lunar eclipse ought to occur once a month. On every orbit around the Earth on its 27.3-day journey, after all, the moon will always pass through a point at which the planet sits between it and the sun. But the plane of the moon’s orbit around the Earth is tilted about five degrees compared to the Earth’s orbit around the sun. That means that on some passages behind the Earth the moon avoids the shadow, soaring above or ducking below the planet.
How long will the lunar eclipse last?
An eclipse of the moon plays out slowly. The one that will begin on the evening of Aug. 27 and continue into the early hours of Aug. 28 will last a total of five hours and 38 minutes. Even the most dedicated eclipse chaser, however, may not be able to take it all in. Depending on where in the world an observer is—and this eclipse will be visible in Europe, Africa, North and South America, and western Asia—the moon may set before the eclipse is done or rise after it’s already begun. That will be the case in the Americas, where observers will see an eclipsed moon come up in the skies. Finding a flat area with few buildings and a clean sight line may be necessary to witness the eclipse, since in many places the moon will be low in the sky, close to the horizon. In the U.S., the eclipse will begin at 9:23 p.m. ET on Aug. 27, and end at 3:01 ET the next day.
There are three phases of any lunar eclipse—the penumbral, partial, and total or maximum. The penumbral phase occurs first, when the moon moves into the faint, outer reaches of the Earth’s umbra, or shadow. The partial phase comes next, when the true, darker shadow of the Earth begins to cover the lunar disk. The total or maximum phase is when only a small portion—or none at all—of the moon remains unshadowed. For the upcoming eclipse, the penumbral phase will take one hour and ten minutes, the partial phase one hour and 39 minutes, and the maximum phase, when the moon will be 96% obscured, will also take one hour and 39 minutes. That maximum shadow will occur at 12:12 a.m. ET. The eclipse will then return to the partial and penumbral phases before the moon soars on and leaves the Earth’s shadow behind.
What is an 'eclipse season'?
This eclipse occurs in a busy time for the skies. On Aug. 12, just over two weeks before the lunar eclipse is set to occur, there was a total eclipse of the sun, visible in Spain, Portugal, Iceland, Greenland, and Siberia. There is actually such a thing as an eclipse season, a month-long stretch occurring twice a year—in the summer and winter—when the moon passes the point in its five-degree orbit that the Earth, moon, and sun align in a way to make both types of eclipses possible.
If you fancy eclipses, you’re well advised to take this one in while you can. The next total lunar eclipse will not be until Dec. 31, 2027 to Jan. 1, 2028. New Years Eve fireworks will be going off that night, but they will be nothing compared to the sky show the Earth, the sun, and the moon will serve up.

Border Wall Construction Threatens 6,000 Years of History on Private Lands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Outrage has exploded over border infrastructure that recently began tearing up pristine desert landscapes in Big Bend National Park. But there’s a quieter battle taking place on private lands in Texas, where the US border wall is set to cut across some of North America's richest archaeological sites, digging up ancient indigenous artifacts and fracturing millennia-old rock art in its path.
The US Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection awarded billions of dollars in contracts this year toward the construction of a wall and other barriers in West Texas along a remote 500-plus-mile (800-plus-kilometer) riverfront expanse of the US-Mexico border that includes Big Bend National Park and other idyllic parklands.
Bipartisan backlash against border wall construction in the national park was swift, ultimately prompting DHS to scuttle plans for a 30-foot steel bollard wall, instead replacing it with miles of riverside vehicle barriers and 200-plus miles of road construction. Bulldozers began clearing along the Rio Grande corridor near Santa Elena Canyon on August 6.
Construction has since been paused in the park in response to lawsuits. But the agency is still planning to construct the wall, as well as a web of road construction, over mountains and across canyons outside the national park. That includes private property that ranchers and other landowners say have archeological sites worth protecting, too. And they’re concerned that construction of the wall will bifurcate their own land and damage archeological sites, many of which have yet to be fully studied.
Archeologist Bryon Schroeder has been digging on rancher Jeff Fort’s property for two years. Schroeder runs Sul Ross University’s Center for Big Bend Studies, a research program dedicated to studying the cultural, historical, and archeological legacy of the region. He removes 4 inches (10 centimeters) of sediment at a time, and his meticulous digs have uncovered pottery and melted adobe slick building material from as early as the year AD 800. He’s found turquoise, too, and marine shells, both signs of trade outside the region. Evidence shows the site is related to Paquimé, an UNESCO World Heritage site that’s 200 miles away in Mexico.
Schroeder’s dig site, Canta Recio, is directly in the path of the proposed wall. Some of it is set to be bulldozed over. If the wall is built, other parts of the site will also become effectively inaccessible.
Schroeder likens Canta Recio to how Egyptians set up shop along the Nile, surmising the site was settled four or five times between 800 and 1400 by groups who were likely drawn to fertile land afforded by routine floods. Of course, those floods also mean that groups were eventually forced to move on when the Rio Grande overtopped its banks, only for another group to eventually settle the area once the silt firmed up. A settlement, a flood, an exit, on repeat.
“There's some bigger, cooler sites up the river that are just insane,” Schroeder said. “They have so much pottery, they have Mesoamerican copper bells, they have turquoise. They have all sorts of crazy stuff.”
The paradox facing Schroeder and other archeologists: They can't fully measure what's at risk because many of the archeological sites exist on private ranches and have never been studied.
That means construction may erase history before anyone gets to record it. A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told WIRED that the agency is conducting environmental and cultural reviews to minimize impacts and balance operational needs with responsible land stewardship.
But previous studies haven’t stopped historically important sites from being sentenced to destruction. A 30-foot bollard wall is set to go right through the Polvo site, in Redford, Texas, which is home to a prehistoric village complete with burial ground dating back to the 1300s. The same site also has evidence of a Spanish mission that was built in the 1600s. Eagle Nest Canyon in Langtry, one of the most significant and intensively studied archeological sites in all of Texas, is also slated to see some form of barrier erected through it. That site includes the southernmost bison jump site in the US, where Native Americans hunted the animals en masse by funneling them over a cliff.
Patrick Zuberbueler, a rancher 350 miles downriver in Comstock, Texas, population 268, spent his youth picnicking in the shadows of 6,000-year-old rock art, with some displays up to 50 feet tall and hundreds of feet wide, across his family’s property. The government took some of that land by eminent domain in the 1960s and 1970s, forming the Amistad Reservoir and Seminole Canyon State Park, but he and his family still hold onto thousands of acres.
As a child, Zuberbueler would catch minnows in a stream running through Painted Shelter, a limestone rock shelter on his family’s property. To him, it was “a place we’d go picnicking.” To archeologist and rock art expert Carolyn Boyd, it’s “one of the most important archeological sites in the region.”
Painted Shelter has three distinct styles of rock art, painted between 6,000 and 1,000 years ago. Rock artworks encode stories and cosmologies, and are “libraries of human knowledge,” says Boyd, a research professor at Texas State University in San Marcos who founded Shumla Archaeological Research and Education Center in 1998.
Painted Shelter is also right in the path of border construction.
“A vehicle barrier going in just immediately above it will destroy the stream, and it will potentially destroy the paintings themselves,” says Boyd, one of the nation’s leading scholars on rock art.
Vibration from construction could potentially cause the limestone to spall, or sheet off, she says, leaving the rocky canvas in tatters. She knows of 12 other rock art sites across the region that are also at risk from construction, while another 79 will become inaccessible.
The region around the Zuberbueler ranch, known as the Lower Pecos Canyonlands Archeological District, was designated as a National Historic Landmark on January 13, 2021, under the first Trump administration. Federal law dictates that agencies “to the maximum extent possible undertake such planning and actions as may be necessary to minimize harm” to National Historic Landmarks. But with the National Historic Preservation Act one of dozens of laws waived by the Department of Homeland Security in its pursuit of a border wall, those requirements to minimize harm are off the table.
For Zuberbueler, pushing back against the border barrier isn’t just about the archaeology his land holds. It’s about the legacy of his great-grandfather, who started working the land in 1898.
“The ranch continues to shrink and shrink and shrink, and you can't effectively ranch something that way,” Zuberbueler says. “They're hurting our livelihood as producers.”
Boyd, who has dedicated four decades to unearthing the history behind the region’s rock art, says she feels like she’s living a nightmare. “Maybe it’s wishful thinking,” she says, but she hopes she can get the government to understand the significance of the region’s archeology and revise its plans to rely on technology to patrol the area rather than physical infrastructure.
But time is seemingly running short to make that case. Several miles of steel bollards lay in piles at staging areas, and several temporary workforce housing “man camps” have cropped up on newly cleared land across the region. Locals say wall contractors have already bulldozed private property before they were legally allowed to, damaging irrigation systems and clearing vegetation. But some locals aren’t ready to give up. And there are signs of resistance to development on private lands elsewhere, including suits filed earlier this month by residents in San Ygnacio, which sits about 275 miles further south of the Big Bend region.
“It's almost unfathomable to even put it into context, the different ways that this can be detrimental to us,” Zuberbueler said about the border construction. “We're not going to go down without a fight.”

Defense Forces strike electronic warfare systems and warehouses, damage enemy MiG-29 — General Staff
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
13:00:00 EEST
19:00:00 KST

Defense Forces strike electronic warfare systems and warehouses, damage enemy MiG-29 — General Staff
Kyiv • UNN

Details
"On August 24 and during the night of August 25, 2026, units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck a number of military targets belonging to the Russian aggressor," the statement said.
"Thus, in Luhansk, the specialized Peresvet-M electronic warfare system was struck. A Starlink satellite communications suppression station was also struck in Myrne (temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea). In addition, an enemy fuel, lubricants and ammunition depot was struck in Berdiansk, Zaporizhzhia region," the General Staff reported.
As noted by the General Staff, "among other targets, warehouses containing material and technical supplies of an occupier unit were struck in Prymorsk, Zaporizhzhia region."
"Based on the analysis of the data, damage to a MiG-29 fighter jet at the ‘Millerovo’ airfield in Russia’s Rostov region on August 24, 2026, was confirmed," the General Staff stated.
The extent of the damage is being clarified.

Iran-linked Swiss oil trader hit by US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:59:21 UTC
18:59:21 KST

Iran-linked Swiss oil trader hit by US sanctions
The Trump administration has extended sanctions against the sprawling network of Iranian oil trader Hossein Shamkhani, targeting his Wellbred group of commodities businesses as part of a wide-ranging set of measures intended to isolate Iran.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control has sanctioned Singapore-based Wellbred Capital, United Arab Emirates-based Wellbred Trading FZCO and Switzerland-based Wellbred Trading, according to a notice on Monday. It also named a French cooking oil refinery described as being owned by Wellbred, La Nivernaise de Raffinage SAS.
+ Iran war: Switzerland expects bumper tax from oil traders
“Shamkhani built Wellbred as a company outside the network’s Iranian business, though Shamkhani is ultimately responsible for Wellbred’s operation,” the Treasury said in a statement.
Washington has already sanctioned Shamkhani, the son of late senior Iranian security official Ali Shamkhani, and other companies in his network.
The Singapore-based Wellbred entity did not immediately respond to calls and emails requesting comment. The UAE and Swiss-based companies also did not immediately respond to queries outside normal business hours.
Washington unveiled sanctions against dozens of entities on Monday, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying the US was focusing on five of Iran’s “most vital lifelines,” including digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Bessent also threatened to sanction a major financial institution over Iran ties by the end of this week but didn’t name the target.

Kremlin rebukes Finland's Stubb over support for long-range Ukrainian strikes

EU posts $25.4B trade deficit in Q2, 1st time since 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:58:59 UTC
18:58:59 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The EU recorded a trade deficit of €21.8 billion ($25.4 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, as non-EU goods imports exceeded exports, official data showed on Tuesday.
 
According to Eurostat, goods imports from non-EU countries reached €701.8 billion, while exports stood at €680 billion during the April-June period.
 
This marks the bloc's first trade deficit since the second quarter of 2023, ending a period of positive trade balances.
 
The trade deficit was driven primarily by an expanding energy deficit, which grew to €101.1 billion in the second quarter from €71.3 billion in the previous quarter.
 
Deficits also widened in raw materials, reaching €9.4 billion, and in other manufactured goods, which rose to €9.1 billion.
 
Meanwhile, trade surpluses declined in key sectors, as machinery and vehicle surpluses fell to €23.2 billion, and other goods dropped to €9.1 billion.
Conversely, chemical surpluses expanded to €54.0 billion, while food and drink surpluses grew to €11.5 billion.
 
Quarter-on-quarter, EU exports increased 5.4% or €34.9 billion, while imports surged 9.9% or €63.4 billion.
The growth halted a continuous decline in trade since mid-2025 that was previously driven by global tariff tensions.

MANILA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Two Philippine surgeons performed the country's first telesurgery on Tuesday in China's Shanghai by operating a surgical robot on a 53-year-old Filipino patient in Quezon City, the Philippines, according to local media reports.
The procedure was carried out at the Urology Center of the Philippines, using high-speed internet and robotic technology for real-time coordination between Shanghai and Manila. The surgeons operated from Shanghai, with a local team on standby at the Quezon City site, according to GMA News.
The surgery marked a new step in China-Philippines medical cooperation, following previous collaborations in liver transplants, physician training, and cloud-based medical platforms.
The Philippines, an archipelago with unevenly distributed medical resources, could benefit from remote surgery as a new option for patients in remote areas. ■

South Australia announces H5N1 bird flu vaccination program for captive species
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
17:58:11 CST
18:58:11 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Authorities in South Australia (SA) on Tuesday said they will vaccinate about 100 captive birds against the H5N1 strain of avian influenza amid a growing outbreak in the state.
Clare Scriven, SA's minister for primary industries and regional development, and state Environment Minister Emily Bourke told reporters that a vaccination program has been approved for populations of 30 species at the Cleland Wildlife Park in southeast Adelaide.
They said that critically endangered orange-bellied parrots and regent honeyeaters are among the species that will be vaccinated at the park.
"Vaccinating wildlife is challenging because the bird flu vaccine requires multiple doses, making it difficult to catch the same bird twice; however, Cleland Wildlife Park provides an environment where successful vaccination of captive birds is achievable," Bourke said.
The SA Department of Primary Industries and Regions on Tuesday reported 10 new suspected H5N1 events and confirmed that a long-nosed fur seal that was found dead at an island conservation park off the state's coast returned a positive result for the strain.
It marks the second confirmed case of the highly pathogenic strain in a mammal in Australia, after the first was reported on Sunday in a long-nosed fur seal found in mainland SA.
According to the latest data from the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, as of Monday there had been 318 confirmed positive events of H5N1 bird flu in Australian wildlife, 194 of which have been in SA.
Speaking alongside Scriven and Bourke on Tuesday, federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said Australia has around 12,000 vials of the vaccine available.
The federal government announced earlier in August that vulnerable species in captivity would be prioritized for vaccination. ■

In Kramatorsk, 12 people injured after eight Russian strikes, including infant
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:57:09 EEST
18:57:09 KST

In Kramatorsk, 12 people injured after eight Russian strikes, including infant
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces attacked Kramatorsk eight times with aerial bombs. Twelve civilians were injured, including a two-month-old girl in serious condition.
12 people were injured as a result of today's Russian strikes on Kramatorsk in Donetsk region, including a two-month-old infant, Donetsk Regional Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin and the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office said on Tuesday, UNN reports.
Details
According to the Prosecutor's Office, on August 25, between 10:33 and 10:40, the Russian army attacked Kramatorsk. "This morning, the Russians attacked the city eight times. According to preliminary information, they used aerial bombs," Filashkin added.
According to the Prosecutor's Office, residential areas came under enemy fire. Some of the weapons struck apartment buildings.
"Numerous high-rise buildings and an infrastructure facility were damaged," the head of the Regional Military Administration said.
As of now, at least 12 civilians are known to have been injured, including a two-month-old girl. The child is in serious condition
"The number of injured has risen to 12," Filashkin confirmed the data as of 12:50.
All those affected are receiving medical assistance, it was reported.

From "poor, corrupt Ukraine" to EU candidate: how Italy won over Germany and opened the EU’s door to Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
12:56:00 EEST
18:56:00 KST

From "poor, corrupt Ukraine" to EU candidate: how Italy won over Germany and opened the EU’s door to Kyiv
Pier Francesco Zazo was one of the few ambassadors of EU member states who was in Kyiv on 24 February 2022. At the time he had headed Italy’s diplomatic mission in Ukraine for more than a year, and he remained in the position until 2024.
The Italian ambassador did not have a particularly high profile during his time in Ukraine, although everyone involved in supporting Ukraine and its path towards EU membership was aware of his personal role in backing the country and its European integration.
Now Zazo, who will soon turn 67, has left the diplomatic and public service.
"Now I am a free man, and I am happy to speak openly about what I know and what I think," he admitted during his interview with the editor of European Pravda.
We took advantage of Zazo’s visit to Kyiv to hear his candid recollections of how Ukraine has been perceived by its partners, how attitudes changed after the full-scale war began, how the negotiations over EU candidate status were conducted, and what we can expect going forward. And this isn’t just about Italy.
"There are Italians with a pro-Russian attitude, and I can't convince them with arguments"
You’ve heard the news about Iryna Mudra. How do people in Europe perceive the news that high-level Ukrainian politicians are suspected of such serious crimes?
It definitely doesn't help Ukraine. Being pro-Ukrainian, I always try to explain the positive side of these cases: I tell people that this proves Ukraine is really fighting against corruption; that the anti-corruption bodies work well; that it’s a process which is ongoing and needs time.
But still, this is a weak point.
People who sympathise more with Russia use this as a strong argument: "This proves that the Italian government shouldn’t give money to a corrupt Ukraine."
But it’s not a disaster. I see many articles explaining the positive side – that Ukraine is moving in the right direction. The mere fact that you’re able to investigate corruption at the highest level is definitely a good sign. And one more positive aspect which seems important is that Ukrainians are ready to go out into the streets and protest. That would never happen in an autocratic country like Russia.
Therefore you can see it in a positive way and in a negative way.
Do these explanations work in Italy?
It depends who you talk to.
Italian society is very polarised.
If you talk to pro-European Italians, they appreciate your fight for freedom and the rule of law. Also, those who have some knowledge about Ukraine and the war tend to recognise that Ukraine’s transition to democratic rules is happening.
Also, in my experience, these explanations work well with those who are neutral towards Ukraine, who don’t have any prejudice. I can tell you that because I often talk to this type of person. They want to understand; they listen to me very carefully, knowing that I have previous experience both in Ukraine and in Russia.
But there are also Italians with a pro-Russian attitude, and I'm not able to convince them with arguments. There are quite a few people in Italy who have never been to Ukraine, but they have a position based on the clear Russian narrative.
They would tell me that everything was staged in Bucha. And if I tell them that I have been there personally, that I’ve spoken with the mothers of people who were killed, that I saw a lot as an ambassador, they don't trust me. I see no way to convince them.
Fortunately, this type of person is a minority.
So Ukraine has to work more with the people who are in between – and they are ready to listen.
"Italians were really caught by surprise that Ukrainians resisted"
What does Ukraine mean to people in Italy today? And what did it mean to them a few years ago? I imagine that 10-15 years ago, the main things people in Italy associated with Ukraine were [the footballer] Andriy Shevchenko, perhaps Chernobyl, and the idea that Ukraine was somewhere near Moscow.
Yes, that's very true. This perception was formed under strong influence from Russia.
Since 1990, Ukraine had been perceived as a poor, corrupt country with a strong presence of oligarchic powers, plus Chernobyl and environmental disasters. The image was completely negative, and it persisted not just until 2014, but until the outbreak of the full-scale war in 2022.
One of the few positive aspects about Ukraine was the Ukrainian diaspora, which was respected in Italy, but it was not a very influential one. Many Ukrainians worked [as carers] for elderly people, and they never created problems with the justice system. Here comes a very important point, which may surprise you today, but in Italy Ukrainians were perceived as a community with a very weak national identity.
The community did not fight that stereotype, partly because Ukrainians abroad are quite individualistic.
This was also partially a Russian narrative, as Russia worked hard to convince Italians and Europeans that all the former Soviet Union countries basically have a Russian identity and sooner or later they will return to Great Mother Russia.
That created an incredibly simplified image of Ukraine, even among my colleagues.
Do you mean that even within the Foreign Ministry, some diplomats saw Ukraine as essentially part of Russia’s sphere?
Yes. Even in 2021, when I came here as an ambassador, there were very strong narratives against Ukraine. For instance, many people in Rome believed that Ukraine was suppressing Russian-speaking people, that people in South-Eastern Ukraine were being discriminated against because they spoke Russian.
The first thing I did on arriving in Ukraine was to go to Kharkiv and Odesa and start writing reports to my capital explaining that that wasn’t true: that many people speak Russian, but they feel Ukrainian.
Of course not every diplomat had that wrong image of Ukraine, but many did.
Russia really worked hard in the field of disinformation – it’s where they are strong. Also with all this narrative of "there's no Ukraine", "Ukraine is an artificial state", "they're just part of Great Mother Russia".
Therefore, the Italians were really caught by surprise not just by the fact that the war had started, but even more by the fact that Ukrainians resisted.
Everyone in Italy was convinced that in two or three days everything would be over. Even my colleagues thought so.
What other myths or misconceptions about Ukraine were widespread in Italy?
I would stress the underestimation of the economic potential of Ukraine.
For me, it was always clear that Ukraine has huge potential, but in Italy, it was never known. People were usually surprised if I said that Ukraine was the second most important republic in former Soviet Europe. No one knew before 2022 that you had a very strong defence industry, space industry. No one had heard about your success in digitalisation.
For the majority of people, everything good was related to Russia.
Everything bad could be Ukrainian.
Andriy Shevchenko played for AC Milan. Did Italians see him as Ukrainian, or simply as a talented footballer from the former Soviet Union?
Yes, and this contributed very positively, though it was never enough compared to the negatives.
By the way, I was among the first Italians who knew that Shevchenko was going to play in Italy. At the time, I was working here in Kyiv as a consul, and I issued him the visa to move to Milan. I remember it well – it was 1999.
I love football, and I used to watch the games of Dynamo Kyiv here. I knew that he was a great player.
I called some of my friends in Milan and said, "Look, you know who is moving to your team?" and my friends answered: "What? Ukraine? Do they play football?"
After a few months, they called me back saying: "Yeah, he's a great player!"
"Until 23 February, nobody in Rome believed there would be an invasion"
What changed in Italy’s perception of Ukraine after 2022?
As I said, your resilience was a huge surprise, and the attitude also changed completely. Ukrainians were admired.
Let me give you one example that demonstrates this change. Before 2022, there were no books about Ukrainian history available in Italy. There was only The Gates of Europe by Serhii Plokhy. Now there are many books about Ukraine available. Italians have discovered that there is a Ukrainian nation and a Ukrainian national identity.
What changed?
The Russian invasion came as a huge shock. Italian foreign policy changed immediately, in 24 hours. I always say that paradoxically, my work [as an ambassador] became easier after the invasion.
Italian business and public opinion quickly turned to being pro-Ukrainian. To some degree, it was sympathy for the victims (even if many did not believe Ukraine would manage to survive). It has slowly decreased. After four and a half years of war, people still support Ukraine politically, but they would rather go out into the streets to protest for Gaza, not for Ukraine.
But the political position has completely changed.
How did that change happen? Given that Russian narratives were quite influential, including within parts of the government and the Foreign Ministry, and that Italy had traditionally been relatively close to Russia, how did it become such a strong supporter of Ukraine? Was Mario Draghi instrumental in that shift?
Absolutely yes, but not only him.
I would say that first of all, it was Italian public opinion. People didn't even understand the difference between Ukraine and Russia, they used to have strong cultural links with Russia, and the invasion came as a shock to Italian public opinion.
In Italy, nobody expected full-scale Russian aggression.
I can tell you that until 23 February, nobody in Rome believed there would be an invasion. Nobody! I was here in Kyiv and I was sure that Russia would attack, but nobody even wanted to talk to me.
Up until 24 February, Italy perceived all the developments as: okay, we are G7 members, so we participate in joint sanctions and don’t block them, but we are not very enthusiastic supporters.
On the morning of 24 February, everything changed immediately.
I went to the embassy and everyone called me – the foreign minister, the prime minister. And the reaction was immediate, even if they were caught by surprise (although later I discovered that Mario Draghi had also expected the war to start). The Italian government immediately adopted sanctions, immediately confirmed support for Ukraine – political, economic, humanitarian.
Prime Minister Draghi played a very important role in the joint efforts to freeze Russian sovereign funds. You know, he is a former governor of the European Central Bank, and he knew the correct way to immobilise them.
Later I had a chance to talk to him about the events of those days, and he told me how he talked to Biden and agreed that.
Also, he told me about his contact with Putin [on 1 February 2022].
As an economist, he had the impression that Russia was preparing for the war, as they had started accumulating reserves. His conversation with Putin confirmed that feeling.
But even so, Italy did not believe that Russia would actually invade Ukraine. Why was that?
One of the reasons was that our foreign minister, Luigi Di Maio, paid a visit to Kyiv in mid-February, right before the invasion, and two days later to Moscow, where he was told by Lavrov that nothing would happen.
There was also a wishful desire not to believe in this scenario, so as not to jeopardise the strong economic relationship between Italy and Russia.
But thank God, later Italy completely changed its mind. And then we got the Meloni government, which cemented the role of Italy as a very responsible member of NATO, the EU and the G7 in supporting Ukraine – even if now, after four years of war, a certain fatigue has emerged.
"It wasn’t clear what Scholz would say until the joint press conference"
How did Italy become one of the key countries advocating for Ukraine to receive EU candidate status?
It started even in 2021, when our foreign minister, Luigi Di Maio, visited Kyiv and during that visit quickly agreed – to my surprise – to publicly support Ukraine’s European aspirations. He accepted much more positive wording than Italy had ever accepted: we accept Ukraine’s aspiration to join the EU, provided of course that you carry out the reforms.
But the person who really played the fundamental role was Draghi.
He was the most convinced supporter of Ukraine, and he played a decisive role in the decision to grant Ukraine candidate status in June 2022.
I was there, I accompanied him on the visit to Kyiv that he made with Macron and Scholz, and I saw that with my own eyes. There was a goal to convince Chancellor Olaf Scholz, and it started even before they arrived in Kyiv – on the train.
I was told that wine was involved. What happened?
Yes, that’s true. By the way, I just met your former foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba, and we were discussing whether it was French or Italian wine.
But wine was there, and it contributed a lot.
Still, during the visit to Kyiv, Scholz remained very cautious, and there was no clarity about what he would say up until the joint press conference. Draghi was saying that we have to support Ukraine, Macron was also in favour, although he was more interested in pushing his own initiative, the European Political Community.
And it was only during the press conference that Scholz finally declared: "Okay, we accept Ukraine as a candidate." He confirmed that only at the press conference, although he was probably preparing to accept it.
The role that Draghi played was immense – of course, with Macron’s support. By the way, there was also the Romanian president, Klaus Iohannis, but the key talks were only for three leaders.
Why was Draghi so convinced that Ukraine belongs in the EU?
I also asked him this question.
My impression is that Draghi was outraged by the aggression.
He felt betrayed by Russia.
When it happened, he took a very immediate decision: Russia had crossed a red line, and although the economic links were very strong, they had to be cut.
He told me that at the beginning, he was very worried about the economic consequences, but Italy was very quick in decreasing its economic dependence. Within a few months, Draghi and Di Maio paid visits to Azerbaijan, to Algeria, and Italy was much faster than Germany in getting rid of Russian gas and oil.
Earlier, you said that Russian propaganda had portrayed Ukraine as a poor and corrupt country. How then did Italy end up supporting EU membership for Ukraine?
Draghi did not buy that narrative, of course. Talk about a "poor, corrupt country" works with ordinary people. Not with those in the government.
Draghi was removed in July 2022, and then came Meloni.
"We don't want to have the same experience we had with Orbán"
Let me also ask you about Giorgia Meloni. In 2022, many Ukrainians were wary of her. She leads a right-wing party, so her strong pro-Ukrainian position came as something of a surprise. Why did she take such a clear stance in support of Ukraine?
First of all, Meloni is not a fascist, as some opponents depict her.
Yes, Fratelli d’Italia is a right-wing party, but not that right-wing. And yes, in 2022, she was absolutely not pro-European, although now she's becoming pro-European because of Trump. The way Trump is treating her is shifting her position more and more towards the EU.
Meloni’s party is a nationalist party; she personally believes in nationalism. And that’s why she respects countries that fight for their homeland. That’s a very important aspect of why she supports Ukraine.
And secondly, she used to be very pro-American and pro-NATO. The fact that Biden took a pro-Ukrainian approach was very important in forming her pro-Ukrainian stance. Even if now her relations with the US are changing, I’m confident that
Meloni will remain pro-Ukrainian.
Personally speaking now as a free citizen, I like her pro-Ukrainian approach, and I think for Ukrainians it's good that she is the leader of Italy. What I don't like, and where I disagree with her, is that she's still quite against changing the decision-making mechanism within the EU. She's in favour of the unanimity rule.
I believe in enhanced cooperation in Europe, or multiple speeds, like we have with the euro and with Schengen.
This is also in the interest of Ukraine.
Ukraine needs a strong Europe. We don't want to have the same experience as we had with Orbán again – if every country has a veto, it's very dangerous.
But also the European Union needs a strong Ukraine. Therefore, Ukraine must join the European Union.
Will Italy continue to support Ukraine?
I’m confident about Italian support for Ukraine in the political or humanitarian field. The way towards EU membership is also not really an issue for Italians.
The problem is military support. According to the latest polls, the majority of Italians are against military aid. Next year we have elections in Italy.
Also, within the coalition, two parties, the majority – Meloni’s party and Forza Italia – are pro-European and pro-Ukrainian, but the third party, Lega, is more loudly opposing military aid to Ukraine.
Let me put it bluntly: they are pro-Russian.
Yes. Lega even has an agreement with United Russia. They have received Russian money in the past.
Therefore Meloni, although she is still pro-Ukrainian, has to be very cautious. Even though she still supports Ukraine militarily, she doesn’t speak a lot about it.
You have to keep in mind that Italians are very pacifist people. It has always been in our DNA because of Christianity and the Vatican. It's very difficult to talk to pacifists, I tell you.
We also have a problem with the opposition, which is looking for a way to get more votes.
The third most popular party in Italy is the Five Star Movement led by former prime minister [Giuseppe] Conte. His position is: we condemn Putin, but we have to talk to Putin. The second most popular party, the Democratic Party, is divided on Ukraine. There is a minority which is strongly pro-Ukrainian, but the leader of the party, Elly Schlein, is different.
Therefore, we have to see the outcome of the next elections.
The situation could be dangerous. Russia will likely invest in its disinformation campaign, aiming to support the "sovereigntist" populist parties, whether they are left– or right-wing.
"Italy is perceived by Russia as a weak link"
Do you believe the EU will be brave enough to reach a consensus on membership for Ukraine?
It depends upon the outcome of the political elections. Next year there will be elections in Italy, in France, in Spain and in Poland.
These elections come at a time when Europeans are under attack both by Russia and by Trump.
People need to understand that it’s time to change, including our approach to Ukraine. It’s now or never, otherwise we are condemned to a steady decline.
Europe has shown its ability to surprise everyone.
Who would have expected Europe to increase its support for Ukraine to an extent that it is able to completely replace the US after it suspended financial aid? Who expected the EU to provide military assistance in the numbers we see now, including through the €90 billion support package?
Europe is doing a lot to reinforce the European pillar of NATO.
We’ve started accession negotiations with Ukraine. I’m sure it would be a mistake if Ukraine does not join the EU now. Of course the negotiations have to be finalised and reforms in Ukraine are needed, but it’s quite possible to do it in three years.
It also depends on when the war ends.
Absolutely. Also because of Article 42 in the EU Treaty about joint defence – nobody will dare to attack Ukraine if it automatically triggers Article 42.
To join the EU, you have to respect the Copenhagen criteria, where the main point is democracy. There should be elections, but it's impossible to hold democratic elections now.
You also have to prepare adequately for membership.
I want to stress that I’m very much convinced that Ukraine will join the EU because it's in the interest of Europe, even in terms of defence. Of course there will be obstacles, mainly from Eastern member states, but studies show there are much more advantages to Ukraine’s accession than disadvantages.
Will Italy support NATO membership for Ukraine? Given what you said about Italy being more cautious when it comes to defence and security issues, would that be a difficult position for Rome?
Italy is more cautious on military support, but NATO membership is not a very sensitive issue. Italy will support what the big countries decide.
You referred to Russian propaganda. How is Russia currently working to undermine Ukraine in Italy?
They are using all the weapons of disinformation in Italy.
Italy is perceived by Russia as a weak link.
For example, even Telegram is quite widely used here, as well as TikTok. Fake news, the spread of official Russian statements, interference in Italy’s internal affairs – all of this works. They are very strong in corruption. Just recently, two former agents of the Italian intelligence service were arrested because they gave confidential material to Russia.
I'm sure, but I can't prove it, that there are journalists and opinion leaders paid by Russia.
Unfortunately, Italy is not ready to accept how big the threat represented by Russia is.
We don't have a legislative framework to act against those who disseminate disinformation and fake news. We don't have a national agency coordinating the fight against it – some other European countries do have one.
Italian public TV shows and media have a lot of pro-Russian views. There's no proper fact-checking.
But I still hope we will avoid a U-turn in our policy. If you put together the votes for the different parties, you will see that the majority of Italians are pro-Ukrainian. I don’t see a risk of a pro-Russian majority emerging after the elections.
And again: Meloni is still in the lead, and she will not change her pro-Ukrainian stance after the elections. She is becoming more and more pro-European.
Sergiy Sydorenko,
Editor, European Pravda

The IRGC has been designated by the US as a Foreign Terrorist Organization since 2019. Washington has repeatedly accused the force and its branches of supporting armed groups and conducting operations that threaten US personnel and infrastructure.

Hong Kong power firms to raise fuel charges from September amid geopolitical tensions
CLP Power and HK Electric announce higher fuel-related charges, while offering rebates and subsidies to ease the burden on households
Hong Kong’s two electricity suppliers will raise fuel-related charges from next month, citing geopolitical tensions and volatility in international energy markets.
As electricity costs rise, CLP Power and HK Electric have introduced rebate and relief schemes as grass-roots households face higher air-conditioning expenses after a summer with an unusually large number of very hot days.
HK Electric, which supplies electricity mainly to Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Tuesday that its fuel clause charge would rise to 60.7 Hong Kong cents (7.74 US cents) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September.
The charge will increase by 3.4 cents, or 5.9 per cent, from August, marking the fourth consecutive monthly increase since May.
Together with the basic tariff, the average net tariff will rise to 188.6 cents per unit in September, an increase of 1.8 per cent from August.
“International energy prices remain volatile, with spot prices for liquefied natural gas having more than doubled compared with levels before the geopolitical developments earlier this year and still rising,” HK Electric said in a statement.

Ship disabled by attack in Strait of Hormuz and other news from around the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:53:01 UTC

Ship disabled by attack in Strait of Hormuz and other news from around the Middle East
An oil tanker was hit with a projectile off the coast of Oman in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a report Tuesday that highlighted the ongoing dangers for shipping companies attempting to use the waterway while Iran holds it in firm control.
The attack came as a high-level delegation from Pakistan, which has been a main mediator between the United States and Iran, was wrapping up meetings in Tehran with the goal of bringing a negotiated end to the nearly six-month old war.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Monday. Full coverage can be found here.
Oil tanker hit and disabled off the eastern coast of Oman
The oil tanker was hit Monday night a few miles off the east coast of Oman, according to a report Tuesday from the British military’s United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization.
The unknown projectile hit the engine of the ship and disabled it, but all crew have been reported safe, the UKMTO said.
There were no immediate reports of any environmental impact from the attack, but oil spills from other ships damaged during the war have caused growing concerns about ecological damage.
About a fifth of the world’s traded oil was shipped through the Strait of Hormuz freely before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Iran now has a stranglehold on the shipping traffic through the strait and periodically fires at vessels attempting to transit, though there was no immediate claim for Monday’s attack.
The U.S. is also operating a blockade of Iranian ports and has fired on vessels.
Pakistani officials say ‘highly positive’ talks held with Iran
A delegation from Pakistan led by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir departed Tehran on Tuesday after talks with Iran’s president and other senior officials on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving stalled negotiations to end the Iran-U.S. conflict, the Pakistani military said.
Pakistan has sought to mediate a resolution between Iran and the U.S., maintaining contacts with officials in both countries and urging them to resolve their differences.
Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who accompanied Munir, said their meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had been “very positive and productive,” focused on eventually bringing about an end to the conflict.
“Significant progress was made, and the meeting concluded on a highly positive note,” Naqvi said in a post on X. He added, “We remain hopeful that this momentum will help pave the way for further progress and lasting peace in the region.”
Discussions also included reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the military said.
Iran and Oman, which is on the opposite side of the strait from Iran, are currently finalizing their own proposal for managing the waterway, but it remains unclear whether it would be a plan acceptable to the U.S.
Oman’s foreign minister was to meet with Iranian authorities Tuesday.
No answers a year after Israeli soldiers kill 22 Palestinians including journalists and rescuers
Tuesday marked one year since Israeli soldiers killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and rescue workers, in a double strike on a hospital in Gaza that provoked global outrage. No one has been held accountable.
Israeli officials said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof of Nasser Hospital. Among those killed were Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for The Associated Press and other news organizations.
Despite repeated requests by the AP, the army has not provided details about the investigation or a timeline for when it could be completed. Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution.
China warns about US sanctions threat disrupting Iran cooperation
China’s Foreign Ministry says it is closely following plans announced by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to expand sanctions to entities and individuals linked to Iran, including some based in China.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said China-Iran cooperation “should not be disrupted or undermined,” noting that it had been conducted in accordance with international law.
China is one of Iran’s biggest trading partners and purchases the majority of its total oil exports.
The Treasury Department on Monday said it was imposing sanctions on nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, including several based in China.
But Bessent stopped short of imposing secondary sanctions on countries that trade with Iran, which Bessent said was because he wanted countries to have an opportunity to shift away from Iran before it was too late.
He did not name any countries that could face sanctions, saying “they know who they are.”
Lin said unilateral sanctions “lack a basis in international law” and added that economic warfare would only “further exacerbate tensions.”

U.S. Air Force C-17 lands in Moscow, no reason given
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:52:28 UTC
18:52:28 KST

- A U.S. Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga, Latvia, to Vnukovo International Airport near Moscow on August 25.
- Neither the U.S. Air Force nor the Department of War has publicly confirmed the flight's purpose or destination.
A U.S. Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from Riga, Latvia, to Vnukovo International Airport near Moscow on the morning of August 25, according to flight tracking data reported by Flightradar24.
The flight, carrying the callsign REACH4555, landed in Russia at approximately 10:04 a.m. Moscow time, according to Russian outlet RBK, which cited Flightradar24 data.
The aircraft, tail number 07-7181, departed Riga at roughly 8:50 a.m. Moscow time. Flightradar24 posted images of the flight’s tracked path showing it crossing Latvia and Lithuania before continuing into Russian territory and landing at Vnukovo.
Flight tracking accounts on X initially questioned whether the aircraft had actually entered Russian airspace, noting that some position data appeared inconsistent with typical automated tracking. One account, Coffe Report, said the aircraft’s position was later confirmed through an ACARS initialization message and that Flightradar24 showed the full approach and landing at Vnukovo.
Neither the U.S. Air Force nor the Department of War has issued a public statement confirming the flight’s purpose or destination. Coffe Report, citing unnamed sources on X, described the flight as filed under a “SECDEF support code,” a designation that would indicate the mission was tied to Department of War leadership travel or logistics support, though this claim has not been independently confirmed.
Flight history data reviewed by Brit Brief showed the aircraft’s recent routing began in the United States on August 22, when it departed Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst in Wrightstown, New Jersey, and landed at Joint Base Charleston in South Carolina. The following day, the aircraft flew from Charleston to Joint Base Andrews in Camp Springs, Maryland, before continuing to Riga.
Vnukovo International Airport, the third-busiest airport in Russia, has periodically served as a landing point for diplomatic and military flights during the war between Russia and Ukraine, though direct U.S. military flights into Russian territory have been rare since the war began in 2022.
The flight’s arrival was widely noted on social media given the current state of U.S.-Russia military relations, though no context has been publicly confirmed for the visit. The C-17 is a heavy-lift transport aircraft used by the Air Force for cargo, troop movement and, at times, VIP or diplomatic support missions.
What prompted the flight, who was aboard, and how long the aircraft remained at Vnukovo have not been disclosed by U.S. or Russian officials.

Yorkshireman believed to be first Briton to die fighting for Russia against Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:51:23 UTC
18:51:23 KST

A man from Yorkshire is believed to be the first British citizen to die fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
Bradley Townsend, a 33-year-old fisher from Barnsley, left Britain in April to join up with Russian separatists in eastern Donbas to aid in their invasion of Ukraine, despite having no previous combat experience or familiar ties to eastern Europe. Alongside 49-year-old Ben Stimson and 39-year-old Aiden Minnis, Townsend was granted Russian citizenship for joining the country’s military campaign.
He is believed to have been killed by a remote-controlled first-person-view drone near Lyman, a city in Donetsk, on 10 June. He appeared in videos posted to social media by pro-Russian accounts, including one seemingly owned by Stimson, who was jailed in the UK in 2015 prior to Russia’s full scale invasion for travelling to join pro-Russian troops to fight in the region.
Although Townsend’s death was only widely reported on Monday, unconfirmed reports that he had been killed began circulating in June. One pro-Russian report, seen by LBC, described Townsend as a “warrior in a holy war” who had “sacrificed his life for the cause”.
Back in his native Yorkshire, his death was met with sadness and frustration. One former friend posted that Townsend, who was understood to have had struggled with mental health and addiction, was a “normal guy” who had been “indoctrinated” by people who “saw his vulnerability as an opportunity to recruit him into their twisted cause”, while another said that he had been “brainwashed” by his fellow British defectors.
In videos taken after he had joined up with Russian forces, Townsend could be seen describing himself as a “normal working-class lad from Yorkshire” and laughing with Stimson and Minnis as the trio drank and played cards. He had also posted that the Donbas miners had donated to miners in Yorkshire during strikes in the 1980s, before he was born, and he intended to “repay that favour”.
In a post after his death, Minnis described Townsend as “our beloved comrade-in-arms” who went “into the storm and fell on the battlefield” while comparing Ukrainians to Nazis, a common analogy used in Russian propaganda.
In the same post, Minnis said that Townsend “sacrificed his life for our cause. His service was brief but he blazed the brightest star”.
Townsend, who reportedly told his family he was travelling to Romania when he left Britain in April, also defended his decision to go to Russia on social media, while acknowledging he would be “persecuted” if he ever went home.
In a post he wrote: “I came with the idea that I probably wouldn’t be able to go home. I’d definitely get persecuted if I went back. I’m not here for a suicide mission, but I understand that’s what can happen. This was my own decision, I wasn’t pushed into anything.”
Tom Tugendhat, the former Conservative MP and security minister who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, expressed his sympathies to Townsend’s family but described his actions as “unbelievably stupid” and “extremely misguided”, adding: “No question about it, it’s criminal because you’re engaging in an army that is committing the most barbarous war crimes that the world has seen in decades.”
The Foreign Office is supporting Townsend’s family.

Expert Insights: A couple of tips for students new to Copenhagen, and a couple of obstacles that we locals might be able to help the newcomers overcome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

About the author: David Zepernick is Director for Member Engagement and Communication of Medicon Valley Alliance. Photo: Ida Wang.
Indian Summer in Copenhagen can be wonderful, and once again, thousands of young students who have arrived to study for a semester or two in Copenhagen will experience our city, perhaps for the first time.
University of Copenhagen is attracting roughly 5,500 international students annually, and Copenhagen Business School is welcoming around 2,400 new and exchange international students each year. On top of that, we also have DTU (The Technical University of Denmark and the ITU (IT University of Copenhagen). Since this week, I have had the pleasure of inviting a young German ITU student to rent a room in my apartment. I will do my utmost to make sure he feels welcome and enjoys his stay.
Most of them probably had Copenhagen as a top priority. Apart from the renowned institutions mentioned above, part of the reason is that Copenhagen ranks as the top Nordic capital and one of the world’s most liveable and attractive cities. There are, however, a couple of obstacles, which we “natives” might be able to help the newcomers overcome.
Housing is expensive and hard to find. Even for young Danish people, prices for housing have skyrocketed. Then imagine if you arrive from Portugal or Poland. Do you have a room to spare, which you might consider renting out for six months or a year? Maybe it would be an interesting personal experience for you as well?
Transport is expensive too, unless you own a bike! For foreign students, the bike is the key to mobility. But new bikes are often too expensive for a short stay, and most students are, consequently, looking used bikes, which they can buy cheaply and sell again when they leave.
If you have an old bike, which you are not really using, now is the time to sell it. Don´t worry, if the price is right, they will find your ad on www.dba.dk.  
Sightseeing is always better with a local guide. If you happen to meet the newly arrived students, why not invite them for a bit of informal sightseeing? I happen to have a Tivoli Gold card myself, which means that I can invite my new tenant and three of his friends to visit Tivoli free of charge.
The idea that you can actually swim in the harbor is now taken for granted, but for foreigners it is still somewhat exotic. They might find the water a bit cold, but with a little luck there will still be some Indian Summer Days in early September to enjoy this rather unique opportunity.
Then there is the Freetown Christiania. Perhaps it is still a somewhat controversial place to visit, but it is very Danish indeed, you can visit for free, and I believe it still ranks at least in the top 5 among things to see in Copenhagen. Why not invite one of the new foreign students for a free afternoon to remember, within walking distance of the city center?
To be quite honest, we Danes are not considered particularly hospitable compared to most other cultures. But culture is not set in stone. Culture is dynamic, created by people, and constantly shaped by new ideas, daily actions, and changing needs. With just a few friendly micro-actions, I believe we can change that image for the better.
