A year after Israeli strikes killed journalists at a hospital, no one has been held accountable
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — It’s been a year since Israeli soldiers killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and rescue workers, in a double strike on a hospital in Gaza. No one has been held accountable.
Israeli officials said the target was a suspected Hamas camera on the roof of Nasser Hospital. Among those killed were Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri and Mariam Dagga, a visual journalist who worked for The Associated Press and other news organizations.
Despite repeated requests by AP, the army hasn’t provided details about the investigation or a timeline for when it could be completed. Rights groups say Israel rarely holds troops accountable for killing Palestinians, pointing to long investigations that rarely lead to prosecution.
As global outrage over the Aug. 25, 2025, strikes grew, the Israeli military said that in addition to taking out the camera, six of those killed were linked to Hamas, without providing evidence.
But an Israeli soldier, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution, now says the military could find no evidence linking the camera, which belonged to al-Masri, to Hamas. The soldier, who was privy to discussions surrounding the military’s response, said none of the six was the intended target of the strikes.
AP sent detailed questions to the military about the allegations, as well as other questions about the strikes. The military didn’t address the questions but said the incident is being examined and findings will be transferred to the Military Advocate General’s Corps to reach a verdict on whether to open a criminal investigation. It didn’t provide a timeline.
AP reported at the time that one of the six Israel said was linked to Hamas wasn’t on the hospital’s list of casualties and two others were medical or emergency personnel. That, along with the soldier’s account, raises serious questions about Israel’s rationale for the strikes.
Why did troops fail to identify the cameraman as al-Masri, even though journalists were known to film at the hospital? Why did they strike a second time, causing most of the deaths and raising accusations of a “double tap” attack on first responders, which would be a war crime?
AP and Reuters released a statement Tuesday calling again for Israel to provide a full explanation of the strikes. The news organizations also called on Israel to give journalists access to Gaza to support colleagues who have been covering the war from the beginning.
“A year later, we remain devastated by their deaths and are still searching for answers from the Israeli authorities about what happened that day,” the statement read.
Nasser Hospital was a vital location for journalists
News agencies like Reuters and AP supplied live video footage to newsrooms around the world from the hospital, one of the few functioning in Gaza at the time. AP repeatedly informed the army that its journalists were there.
The first strike killed al-Masri and another person. As other journalists, including Dagga, and rescue workers rushed up an external staircase to help the wounded and document what happened, the military struck again, killing 20 people. Based on footage and multiple eyewitnesses, none was armed. In all, Israel struck the hospital four times using high-explosive tank shells.
Israeli officials afterward said Hamas was using the camera to observe nearby troops. They alleged “suspicious behavior” around the camera, but the only example they gave was that a towel draped over the camera and the person filming appeared to be an effort at concealment.
Al-Masri routinely covered equipment with a white cloth to protect it from the sun and dust, a common practice among journalists in Gaza and other hot climates.
Last week, the army announced criminal investigations into two other high-profile attacks by its troops in Gaza — the 2024 killing of 5-year-old Hind Rajab and her family, and the 2025 killing of 15 paramedics. It cleared troops in three other attacks that killed workers from international aid groups.
Soldier details an attempt at damage control
The soldier was connected to AP through Breaking the Silence, a group founded over two decades ago by Israeli veterans that collects testimony from soldiers and is critical of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territories.
The soldier said after high-profile strikes that kill civilians without clear military purpose, army officials search for militant links among those killed.
Breaking the Silence said its testimonies show there is a “retroactive incrimination process” in which Palestinians who are killed are automatically counted as militants, even when unarmed.
Retroactive incrimination is used as a “near automatic justification for every bullet, shell or missile fired, and as a tool used to avoid carrying out real investigations,” Nadav Weiman, the group’s executive director, said.
AP independently confirmed some details of the soldier’s account, which is consistent with the military’s public response. Breaking the Silence said it corroborated the account with its own sources.
The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals throughout the war, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters, though it’s provided evidence for only some of its claims.
Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. Earlier this year, Doctors Without Borders suspended some operations at Nasser Hospital for several months after patients and staff reported seeing armed, masked men roaming parts of the building.
Tank shells were fired after a drone failed
The soldier, and a former military official with knowledge of the situation, said a high-ranking army official initially approved use of a precision weapon to take down the camera but an attempt by drone failed for unknown reasons. The former official spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to talk to the media.
The division commander then approved an alternative method, said the soldier, without saying what the method was. It’s unclear who made the decision to fire tank rounds, which can cause more damage than drone strikes.
Oded Ailam, former head of the counterterrorism division in Israel’s Mossad spy service, said while commanders on the ground have a degree of freedom, they don’t have a “blank check.”
“If the change is significant, particularly where it may affect the risk to civilians, it must remain within the authority, rules and intent of the original order, or require renewed approval,” he said.
Israeli troops have killed over 200 journalists in the war
Israeli troops have killed 207 Palestinian reporters in Gaza since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack ignited the war, according to the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists. Israel has barred foreign journalists from entering Gaza, giving Palestinian journalists a critical role.
Sara Qudah, CPJ’s Middle East and North Africa regional director, said Israel has a responsibility to conduct a prompt and transparent investigation. “When journalists can be killed without credible accountability, it becomes harder and more dangerous for the press to document conflicts and for the public to know what is happening,” she said.
The lack of answers has been agonizing for families.
Ezz al-Din al-Masri said he doesn’t understand why his brother, Hussam, was killed. “Unfortunately, we found that the blood of journalists in Gaza is cheap … as if the rules protecting journalists do not apply to them,” he said.
Dagga, 33, had just taken her last photos before rushing up the stairs. Whenever her father, Riyad Abu Dagga, visits her grave, he carries her phone and camera with him — she always had them with her. He visits her apartment near Nasser Hospital and cries.
“Had any of the daughters of the soldiers been killed unjustly, they would not have stayed silent,” he said of the Israelis. “They would want to know why.”

AP reporter Wafaa Shurafa in Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army on Monday defended its Northern Combined Training Center against allegations of possible collusion in a waste dumping scandal, saying the military facility was a victim of the scheme.
The controversy began after the Taoyuan City Department of Environmental Protection discovered during an inspection in February that a local company had transported waste stored at its facility to the Northern Combined Training Center for use as road backfill, per Liberty Times. The training center had contracted Hung Ping Construction to improve roads at the facility by replacing red earth with Class B5 recycled aggregate made from bricks or concrete chunks.
Prosecutors said Hung Ping Construction owner Chen Hsin-hung (陳信宏) signed false contracts with multiple companies to make it appear that recycled aggregate was being used for the roadwork instead of waste. During an excavation at the site in April, investigators found that the material used as backfill contained concrete chunks, polystyrene, wires, iron, plastics, rubber tubing, and other waste, per PTS.
Prosecutors ordered the training center, Hung Ping Construction, and five other companies involved in the case to submit plans to remove the waste buried at the training ground. Chen and eight other suspects, along with six companies, were indicted in connection with the case.
KMT Legislator Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) questioned how roughly 100,000 cubic meters of waste, equivalent to about 39 Olympic-size swimming pools, could have been buried at the facility without being detected, per UDN. She said the operation was unlikely to have gone unnoticed, given the perimeter checks, construction supervision, and inspections of the materials used.
Ma also challenged the military’s assertion that the contaminated backfill does not affect training safety, urging the Army to release the results of load-bearing and other tests conducted on the roads. She called on prosecutors to investigate the flow of more than NT$1.3 billion (US$40.8 million) in alleged illicit gains attributed to Chen and his associates and determine whether any military personnel were involved.
The Army said the training center remained a victim of the scheme and that an investigation found no evidence it had conspired with the contractors, per CNA. However, the Army acknowledged shortcomings in the center’s oversight and said it had established an internal team to investigate administrative failures.

Taiwan’s private-sector green procurement grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:22:28 UTC
16:22:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Green procurement reported by private companies and organizations in Taiwan topped NT$100 billion (US$3.1 billion) last year for the first time, CTEE reported.
The Ministry of Environment said Tuesday that the total reached NT$100.6 billion, up about 35% from 2024. The initiative encourages businesses and organizations to purchase and report environmentally friendly products and services, with the goal of expanding green business opportunities and promoting sustainable consumption, according to Phoenix Tours.
Among different industries, large traditional manufacturing companies remained major contributors. Large non-manufacturing companies, meanwhile, recorded the strongest growth, with their purchases rising from NT$9.85 billion in 2024 to NT$19 billion last year, an increase of 92.94%.
Smaller businesses are also playing a growing role in greener supply chains. Green procurement reported by small and medium-sized non-manufacturing companies more than doubled last year, rising 113% from the previous year.
Participation is expanding beyond businesses to educational and medical institutions. Green purchases reported in the category covering these and other organizations increased 68% last year.
The initiative recognizes organizations with strong records. Among last year’s award recipients, 74 companies received awards for the third consecutive year, while 83 won for the first time.
Taiwan has set a target of NT$160 billion in combined green procurement by the public and private sectors by 2030. The ministry said the practice has evolved beyond purchasing decisions, giving businesses a way to encourage lower-carbon changes across their supply chains while supporting Taiwan’s goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.
The ministry said it will expand the types of purchases eligible for reporting, including products with environmental certifications, resource-circulation products, and other environmentally friendly products. It also plans to include newer models such as leasing instead of purchasing.

What to know about Trump's tariffs on Canada and the escalating trade war

What to know about Trump's Canada tariffs and the escalating trade war
Canada plans to respond to US President Donald Trump's new tariffs on Tuesday, as the once close neighbouring allies spiral into a trade war. Ottawa and Washington failed to reach a deal on Friday to avert new 50 percent US tariffs on select Canadian goods after weeks of talks.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday after US President Donald Trump told Canadian leaders on Monday to “fall in line” or face consequences “far worse” than existing tariffs and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney accused Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.
After trade negotiations crumbled at the eleventh hour, Trump's 50 percent tariffs on scores of Canadian imports kicked in over the weekend.
The new levies, which took effect Saturday, are set to impact about 5 percent of Canada's annual exports to the US – or $20 billion in goods ranging from hockey sticks to agricultural products. Carney quickly promised that his government would roll out retaliatory measures “dollar for dollar” starting September 8.
Additional threats have piled up in the meantime. Ontario Premier Doug Ford told The Associated Press on Monday that “everything is on the table," noting his province would be ready to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the US if the trade war worsens. Meanwhile, Trump suggested his administration could also increase taxes on Canadian automobiles next year.
The US and Canada once held one of the world's most durable trade alliances, but the latest escalation plunges the North American neighbours deeper into a rupture that has kept both sides of the border on edge throughout Trump's second term in office. Steeper tariffs raise costs for businesses – and almost always trickle down to households in the form of higher prices.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Here's what we know.
The 50 percent tariffs from the US are set to affect $20 billion of Canadian goods.
Canada sends the vast majority of its goods exports to the US (72 percent last year), and the Trump administration says the new taxes will be levied on products ranging from hockey sticks to wine and cement. The list is long. According to documents published by the White House, other goods subject to the tax include honey, seeds and agricultural products – as well as select makeup, perfumes, clothing, jewellery, furniture, cameras, fabric and more.
The 50 percent levy also applies to some products that were previously protected under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), a trade pact from Trump's first term. This marks a shift from past levies – and further underlines questions around the future of the USMCA overall.
Trump reinstated a long-dormant Great Depression-era law: Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.
When the US and world economies were in collapse nearly a century ago, Congress passed the 1930 law as part of broader Smoot-Hawley legislation (named after its congressional sponsors). But Section 338 – which authorises the president to slap import taxes of up to 50 percent on imports from countries that have discriminated against US businesses – has never been used specifically to raise tariffs until now.
No investigation is required to justify the levies. Nor is there any limit on how long they can stay in place. Since there's no precedent however, the latest tariffs may also see legal challenge.
Trump has claimed that Canada unfairly discriminates against US exports of automobiles, alcohol and dairy products. The president expressed anger over Canada's retaliation against his own tariffs in 2025 – noting how Canadian imports of American alcohol and cars started to fall last spring.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
On Saturday, Carney quickly promised to match the new levies “dollar for dollar” – later announcing that those countermeasures would begin September 8. He noted Canada would target US steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
In the meantime, provincial leaders like Ford have reiterated Canadians' willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to US pressure.
Trump "underestimates Canada. We’re all in,” Ford said Monday. Beyond potentially cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario, he also called for Canada to consider using oil and potash as leverage.
Meanwhile, Trump made new threats on social media. He threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel to 50 percent starting January 1, 2027. Like other countries, Canada currently faces a broader 25 percent tariff on autos. A 50 percent sectoral tariff on most steel imports is already in effect.
“WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!” Trump wrote Monday.
Read more‘We don’t need Canada’: Trump threatens to double auto tariffs after trade talks collapse
Carney on Monday said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would “gradually dismantle” Canadian production. He also questioned what Trump’s latest move would mean for workers in US states who depend on Canadian demand.
The prime minister added that Canada remained willing to negotiate, but only if the US approached the talks as a partnership between sovereign countries. He said “an attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept.”
Tariffs are taxes paid by importers or businesses that buy goods from abroad. Their impact typically trickles down to consumers through higher prices – and, as seen over the last year, they can also create uncertainty for workers across affected sectors.
“Nearly all industries and professions are likely to see downstream effects from this spiraling trade dispute,” Augustine Lo, of law firm Dorsey & Whitney, which advises clients on international trade, said Saturday.
The 50 percent tariffs come on top of previously imposed levies, including a 10 percent rate that Trump slapped on Canada just last month – ostensibly for failing to do enough to prevent imports produced by forced labour and separate sectoral levies globally.
The growing trade war underscores Trump’s willingness to risk breaking established alliances. And Canada’s reluctance to accept a deal may reflect recent experience.
Read moreTrump says Canada wants 'benefits of being a State, without being one' as trade war deepens
Trump has threatened tariffs in response to everything from a TV ad criticising his trade policies (later pulled by Ontario's government) to Canadian wildfires that blackened skies across North America.
Steeper tariffs have already contributed to higher inflation, but have appeared to level off in recent months, according to researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis – most notably after the Supreme Court struck down some of Trump's most sweeping levies in February.
Still, the weekend's escalation with Canada marks the latest instance of Trump turning to other laws to impose tariffs. And Washington’s ongoing war with Iran has driven prices even higher. With the cost of living at the center of many voters' minds in a midterm election year, political ramifications could mount for the Republican president in the coming months.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

US Treasury’s Scott Bessent ‘will lose’ battle with bond markets, former mentor warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:14:06 UTC
16:14:06 KST

Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm the bond markets and push down America’s cost of borrowing have attracted a rebuke from the US Treasury secretary’s former mentor.
The billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, who worked with Bessent at George Soros’s fund management firm in the 1990s, has warned that his former pupil is courting danger by trying to suppress US bond yields.
Druckenmiller, writing in the Wall Street Journal, argued that the US should “let the bond market speak”, rather than expand its bond purchases in an effort to push up prices, and lower borrowing costs.
“Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The only variable is how much they spend before conceding,” he wrote.
Druckenmiller argued that Washington should heed the rise in borrowing costs – measured by bond yields – and take steps to cut the budget deficit, rather than interfering in the market to push yields down again.
“The long-term Treasury yield is the most important price in the world. It is also the only fiscal disciplinarian the US has left. Neither party will run on entitlement reform. Both have spent the past decade expanding commitments while ignoring arithmetic,” he wrote.
Druckenmiller’s intervention comes after Bessent decided to at least double the maximum size of the Treasury’s buyback operations, from $2bn (£1.5bn) to $4bn. That move briefly led to a drop in US long-term bond yields, but this quickly reversed.
“The market’s verdict was swift and correct: This wasn’t liquidity management, it was price management – and a mistake far larger than $4bn suggests,” Druckenmiller said.
Bond yields fall when prices rise, and vice versa.
Yesterday, CNBC reported that Bessent could increase his bond-buying firepower by conducting purchases using the Treasury’s near-$1tn General Account, a government fund held at the Federal Reserve.
Last week the US national debt hit $40tn, and rising, and the annual deficit is expected to hit $2tn this year.
Addressing this primary deficit is the “only thing that durably lowers long-term yields”, Druckenmiller wrote in the WSJ.
“The reward is enormous: A credible fiscal package would do more for the long end of the curve than a buyback program 1,000 times this size,” he said.
Bessent’s bond market intervention is a signal that “Washington is increasingly uncomfortable with soaring long-term borrowing costs,” said Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG.
Bessent’s attempts to battle the financial markets are ironic, as he worked alongside Soros when he beat the Bank of England and forced the pound to crash out of the European exchange rate mechanism in 1992.
That drama, which became known as Black Wednesday, showed how hard it is for a government to defend a currency when investors believe it is overvalued.
But despite that experience, Bessent took part in a joint operation with Japan to prop up the yen earlier this month – seemingly to prevent Tokyo selling US bonds to fund yen purchases.
“The irony of the guy working for Soros and Druckenmiller who broke the Bank of England back in 1992 pretending that you can do FX intervention alone, and lastingly defend a currency, is just amazing,” Adam Posen, the president of the Peterson Institute and an expert on the Japanese economy, told the Financial Times earlier this month.
Rising geopolitical tensions have pushed bond yields higher, as the failure of the US-Iran peace talks lifted the oil price – which threatens to drive inflation higher.
The collapse of US-Canada trade talks last weekend has also put foreign policy back in the spotlight, weakening the Canadian dollar. A North American trade war could hurt US growth, creating more fiscal pressure.

The minister emphasises that he is doing everything in his power to make this possible. “I have already deployed 77 additional officers and am looking into whether that number can be increased further. You must realise, however, that police officers need specific experience in this area. We cannot simply send the first person who comes along.”
Meanwhile, Mayor Spinette of Sint Gillis is demanding that the Brussels region is able to count on exactly the same level of support and funding as the police in Antwerp. “Even though I have just reinforced the Federal Judicial Police in Brussels more than in Antwerp!” Quintin retorted to that criticism.
Shared responsibility
Minister Quintin emphasises the importance of better cooperation. He points to shared responsibility. “I am providing extra personnel and resources, but I do not decide how they are deployed on the ground.”
As an example, he cites his investment of 1 million euros in new CCTV cameras around Brussels-South. “If it then takes two years to install those cameras because it isn’t prioritised locally, there’s nothing I can do.”
Police chief De Landsheer had previously emphasised the fact that the police cannot win this war on drugs on their own. Quintin agrees and advocates a broad, multi-faceted approach. “I am the Minister for Public Order and am trying to secure funding, but drugs are just as much a public health issue. So, let’s all sit down together and discuss this,” he concludes.
Quintin is visiting police headquarters in Anderlecht today, one of the Brussels municipalities plagued by the recent violence.

Lawmakers question U.S. Navy’s handling of Iran deployment strain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:11:09 UTC
16:11:09 KST

- Senate Democrats are calling for an Armed Services Committee hearing on extended U.S. Navy deployments tied to operations against Iran.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea more than 250 days, and the USS Gerald R. Ford suffered a fire and plumbing failures during its own extended deployment.
A group of Senate Armed Services Committee Democrats is asking Chairman Roger Wicker to hold a public hearing on extended deployments tied to U.S. military operations against Iran, according to a letter released August 24 by Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).
The letter cites conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which left San Diego on November 21 and has remained at sea for more than 250 days without a scheduled return date. The carrier’s roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines went more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a modern-day record for a U.S. Navy carrier.
Military Times reported August 11 that multiple sailors aboard the Lincoln had attempted to go overboard during the deployment, based on accounts from family members. CNN separately confirmed with U.S. officials that a sailor went overboard on August 3 and was recovered within an hour by a search-and-rescue helicopter, treated aboard ship and transferred for further care. A second overboard incident involving the same strike group occurred last spring, according to a sailor aboard the Lincoln and two U.S. officials who spoke to CNN.
Family members confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at a town hall in San Diego, with one spouse describing a message from her husband saying he hoped he would not wake up the next morning, according to Military Times and Stars and Stripes reporting cited in the letter.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has disputed the Military Times account, calling it “completely misrepresented.” The Navy has said no service members aboard the Lincoln have died and that the August 3 sailor was quickly and safely recovered.
The senators’ letter also points to the USS Gerald R. Ford, which suffered a laundry-room fire on March 12 that took more than 30 hours to extinguish, injured two sailors and damaged roughly 100 sleeping berths. The Navy initially described the fire as contained and said the ship remained fully operational. Later footage obtained by CNN showed more extensive damage, including burned bunks and exposed wiring in crew living spaces.
The Ford left frontline operations and sailed to Souda Bay, Crete, for repairs, then stopped in Split, Croatia, before returning to sea on April 2. The ship had also experienced recurring failures in its roughly 650-toilet vacuum waste system throughout the deployment. The carrier ultimately spent about 11 months at sea, exceeding the Navy’s typical seven-month deployment target, before returning to Norfolk in May for scheduled maintenance.
Both carriers were redirected from other missions to support Iran operations. The Lincoln had been headed for a routine Indo-Pacific patrol before its diversion to the Middle East in January. The Ford was pulled from a planned deployment to Europe, sent briefly to the Caribbean in connection with operations against Venezuela, and then routed to the Middle East.
“The toll this unauthorized, disastrous war is taking on our troops is unconscionable,” the senators wrote, characterizing the military campaign against Iran as illegal and citing what they described as a pattern of inadequate planning for extended deployments.
The senators asked the Armed Services Committee to examine morale conditions, financial strain on military families, and the Department of War’s plan for ending the extended deployments. They also requested that the department detail how it plans to sustain troops in the region if the campaign continues.
The USS George Washington has since been ordered to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official cited by CNN. As of the senators’ letter, no public timeline had been given for the Lincoln’s return to San Diego, and Chairman Wicker had not publicly responded to the hearing request.

Chinese factory workers accidentally caught on camera glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:10:39 UTC
16:10:39 KST

Camera glasses contain footage that appears to have been accidentally filmed inside Chinese factory
Factory workers who helped make a Chinese-brand of camera glasses appear to have been unknowingly filmed by the devices in accidental videos.
7.30 bought a pair of budget glasses made by Shenzhen-based company Oho Sunshine online and found footage already on the device, which appears to be from inside the factory.
The collection of four short videos, dated last year, shows a number of workers sitting at their desks inspecting the glasses, while listening to jaunty electronic music.
One video clearly identifies a worker lifting a pair and shaking them vigorously.
Another three videos, up to 10 minutes long and dated this year, show only black with atmospheric audio, suggesting the glasses were activated while inside a case or box.
The shoot button on the side of the frames is sensitive and easily switched on.
7.30 approached Oho Sunshine, with questions about the apparent privacy breach but received no response.
Oho Sunshine was founded in 2009 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen in Guandong province, north of Hong Kong, as a smart wearable technologies manufacturer, according to the company's website.
The accidental leak perhaps proves not even the workers who make camera glasses are safe from being filmed and provides a rare insight into the globalised production chain.
Rise of camera glasses
Camera glasses are enjoying a surge in popularity as cheap brands flood the market. Oho is just one of numerous companies manufacturing similar devices.
They look like ordinary glasses and allow you to record video and audio, largely without people knowing.
While some models have a built-in light to indicate filming, there are now services that remove the indicator cheaply.
The glasses can play music and make calls, with more high-tech versions allowing users to live-stream or swipe through messages on a display in the lenses.
Meta's fashionable Ray-Ban smart glasses can cost up to $700 a pair, but basic versions can be bought online for as little as $40.
Kmart Australia's $89 Anko brand of camera glasses recently sold out, prompting an online petition to stop their sale amid concerns about privacy and their use by male content creators recording women without their knowledge and uploading the videos to potentially millions of followers.
While filming in public places is generally legal, the devices have raised new concerns around privacy.
Filmed without consent on 'rizz cam'
Beth Knight, 18, found herself the subject of lurid commentary from online users after a man filmed her with camera glasses and uploaded it to social media without her knowledge.
At the time of the incident late last year, she was 17 and by herself at London's busy Waterloo station.
"I'd missed my train, so I had 40 minutes to wait in the station," Ms Knight told 7.30.
"Then pretty much immediately a man approached me and opened with, 'I've seen you, I found you attractive,' and I immediately shut him down and I said I had a boyfriend."
She discovered that their conversation had been turned into content after she heard about other cases.
"I started looking up buzzwords. I was looking up "picking up girls", "Meta glasses", "Waterloo", all of those into the TikTok search bar and that's when I found his page."
She saw a video of her interaction titled, "POV: You approach her instead of walking by".
"It was framed as a successful pick-up, like a win, when I know in the moment I was incredibly uncomfortable … because it was a strange man refusing to accept my soft hint of a no," she said.
"He had very much framed it as, 'Look, I've picked her up, I got her Instagram, I've won here,' and over the top of the video he was instructing men watching that when girls say they have a boyfriend they're lying."
Ms Knight was not lying and thought the man would get the message and leave.
The man is a content creator who touts himself as a pick-up artist and advertises male coaching on his social media account.
Digital extremism researcher Milica Stilinovic, from Sydney University, said such content was known as "rizz cam" — rizz being slang for charisma — when women are sometimes filmed without their consent.
"I would find it horrendous to be treated that way and then subjected to a global audience," she told 7.30.
Ms Stilinovic led a study that reviewed more than 350 Instagram videos filmed with camera glasses.
"Pick-up artists are adjacent to the manosphere, or part of the manosphere, and they have a dual purpose to exist," she said.
"One is to build the self-confidence of men, supposedly through the subjugation of women, and the second part is to sell male coaching, which is basically like a multi-level marketing scheme.
"Some of the worst examples included underage girls. Some of [the filmers] approached women who were inebriated. Some of them approached women who were semi-nude at beaches."
Ms Knight said her experience left her feeling angry.
"It's weird to watch it back," she said.
"But the anger definitely came from the fact that it was spun so heavily to look good on his part.
"I went home and sobbed to my parents."
She said she asked the content creator to take the video down, but he blocked her.
7.30 has contacted the creator for comment, but he did not respond.
Is it legal?
According to Australia's Privacy Commissioner, Carly Kind, the use of camera glasses in public is largely legal, with laws varying across states.
"Wearing smart glasses in public to capture images of things that happen in public is generally not illegal under Australian law," Ms Kind told 7.30.
"[But] when you are in a private premises or a private space, and that might include a private home, a vehicle, or potentially a semi-private space like a gym or a workplace, for example, then you're likely going to run up against laws that do prohibit the use of surveillance devices."
In Victoria, where filming inside a private business is generally allowed, one content creator known as "The Latte Bloke" uses camera glasses to review coffee around Melbourne.
He is not a pick-up artist, but his videos feature staff and customers.
One 19-year-old cafe worker said she did not consent to being filmed while serving him.
Her aunt, Tara Venn, told 7.30 her niece was upset after seeing herself in a video online.
She was new in the job.
"It was a bit affronting [for her]," Ms Venn said.
She said content creators should consider the ethics of filming someone.
"Common sense says you are polite and you ask if you are going to invade a person's privacy by filming them without them knowing,"
"I just want people to think and to actually use good manners and decency."
The content creator declined to be interviewed but told 7.30:
"Latte Bloke is all about filming the latte experience and having a bit of fun reviewing the coffee. The focus has never been on the staff or customers, and I'd never intentionally want to make anyone feel uncomfortable."
Potential real-world consequences
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has asked Australia's Privacy Commissioner to make recommendations about camera glasses in Australia.
Ms Kind says she was already worried about them.
"If you think about their use in workplaces, there's a high likelihood that corporate espionage could be permitted through these kinds of glasses without proper control,"
"I think the theft of personal information through the use of the glasses is also a potential offence that we could see spiralling out here, and [there are] obviously real risks around vulnerable groups, women and children."
In New South Wales it is illegal to create or share sexually explicit videos or audio of someone without their consent.
Last year, new federal privacy laws made serious invasions of privacy an offence; however, the commissioner told 7.30 there was a high bar to prove it was intentional and caused harm.
In the UK, some pubs and restaurants have reportedly banned the devices, while in Germany, rights advocacy group HateAid has lodged a complaint to German prosecutors against Meta and other companies, claiming such devices breach the country's covert recording laws.
Ms Stilinovic wants camera glasses temporarily banned in Australia.
"I would suggest that we stop the rollout of smart glasses until regulation and policymakers have caught up to keep societies safe,"

Majority of South Koreans view US 'unfavorably,' 1st time in over 20 years: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:04:30 UTC
16:04:30 KST

Aamir Latif
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
For the first time in over two decades, a majority of South Koreans have an unfavorable opinion of the US, a survey showed.
Some 55% of the participants expressed an unfavorable opinion of the US, up from 39% last year, according to the survey conducted by the Washington-based Pew Research Center.
The survey, released Monday, revealed that 18% of respondents had a "very unfavorable view," up from 9% in 2025.
Fewer than half of South Koreans, 45%, have a favorable view of the US, marking a 16-point drop from 61% last year, and a 35-point drop from 2018, the second year of US President Donald Trump’s first term, when it stood at 80%.
The US has some 39,000 soldiers deployed in South Korea under a defense treaty with Seoul, according to Trump, who recently ordered the Pentagon to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea.
In response, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reiterated his push for military independence from Washington.
Around six in 10 South Korean adults, 57%, consider the US a reliable partner. That’s down from 83% in 2022, during the Joe Biden administration.
There has also been a decrease in the share of South Koreans who think the US takes into account the interests of countries like their own when making international policy decisions. This year, 21% of South Koreans think the US does this a great deal or a fair amount. That’s down from 38% in 2023.
The share of South Koreans who say that Washington contributes a great deal or a fair amount to peace and stability around the world has also fallen, from 74% in 2023 to 47% this year.
Only 14% approve of Trump's handling of tariffs. Earlier this year, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on South Korean goods to 25% if the country’s legislature did not approve a proposed trade deal.
The South Korean parliament later approved the deal.
Around three-quarters of South Koreans disapprove of the way Trump is dealing with Iran. That includes nearly half, 47%, who strongly disapprove.
Despite viewing Washington less favorably this year, South Koreans still overwhelmingly name the US as their country’s most important ally. This share has decreased slightly since last year, 84% compared to 89%.

Uganda's Gaza 'stabilisation force' plan sparks debate in Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:04:24 UTC
16:04:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Uganda's participation in Gaza 'stabilisation force' sparks debate in Africa
Uganda's parliament approved the deployment of army troops to the" International Stabilisation Force" in the Gaza Strip at the beginning of August as part of US President Donald Trump's plan. The move marks the first official declaration by an African country of its readiness to participate in Gaza.
The approval came on 6 August after Ugandan Defence Minister Kiria Kiwanuka told lawmakers that Trump had asked President Yoweri Museveni in July for Uganda to contribute to the proposed international force in Gaza.
After the Ugandan parliament's approval, a Ugandan soldier in military uniform posted a video on social media in which he appeared alongside the words, "Gaza, we are coming", indicating that the idea of a military deployment had begun circulating within Uganda's military and media circles.
The Ugandan government has not yet specified the number of troops it may deploy to the territory or when they would be sent.
Israel's public broadcaster reported last Monday, 17 August, that senior officers from Uganda and Burundi had arrived at the US command headquarters in Kiryat Gat in the occupied Palestinian territories as part of advanced talks with the two countries to send hundreds of soldiers to the territory as part of the multinational stabilisation force.
The broadcaster also said last Thursday, 20 August, that Morocco had been chosen to train members of the force.
Ugandan forces in the Gaza stabilisation force has sparked debate inside the Ugandan parliament, with opposition lawmakers calling for more information about the nature of the mission, the number of troops, its funding, and the guarantees provided to soldiers and their families.
The opposition also warned of the security and political risks associated with sending troops to a devastated territory and under highly complex field conditions.
Uganda has extensive experience in peacekeeping operations, particularly in Africa, where its forces participate in missions in Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The defence minister cited this experience to justify the Ugandan army's ability to participate in a new international mission.
Without African backing
The decision has also raised questions about Kampala's approval of it and whether it has broad African backing or bypasses African consensus by being taken without Uganda consulting its partners in the African Union.
The African Union has consistently supported the Palestinian cause in principle and calls for the implementation of a two-state solution.
However, Israel has built relations with several African countries over decades, viewing the continent as an arena of Arab-Israeli competition.
In 2021, the union accepted Israel as an "observer member", a move that prompted Palestinian and Arab protests and was later revoked.
Uganda's relations with Israel, meanwhile, have continued to grow.
The Ugandan judge Julia Sebutinde, vice-president of the International Court of Justice, has attracted attention after she was described as believing that "God relies on her to stand with Israel". Sebutinde opposed the six rulings imposed by the court in 2024 to protect Palestinians and stop the genocide in Gaza.
Ugandan military leadership also recently said that any attempts to "destroy" Israel, amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, could prompt Uganda to intervene in support of the occupying state.
Uganda is also one of the largest importers of military technology and spyware from the occupying state.
In this context, Sudanese writer and researcher Abbas Saleh, who is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, told The New Arab that Uganda's potential participation in the proposed international force for the Gaza Strip reflects a renewed predicament facing the African Union.
Decisions and positions adopted by the continental organisation often appear non-binding on member states, which may adopt unilateral policies that conflict with the union's collective positions.
"Despite the clear positions adopted by the African Union on the Palestinian cause, its rejection of Israeli violations and its repeated calls for an end to the war and the protection of civilians, the involvement of some member states in international security arrangements linked to Gaza could weaken the unity of the African position and expose the organisation's limited ability to turn its political positions into practical commitments by its members," he pointed out.
According to Saleh, Uganda is among the countries whose name has for years been associated with a broad security and military role in Africa, as well as close relations with Western powers, particularly in the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa.
He explained that this role "has given it a prominent position in several regional security issues but has at times made its foreign policy a subject of debate over the extent to which its decisions are independent of the calculations of international powers".
"The Ugandan move is significant beyond the participation of a single country, as it could set a precedent encouraging other countries that had been hesitant or reluctant to join the proposed international force, particularly if they are provided with appropriate political and security guarantees or international incentives," Saleh opined.
He stressed that participation in a military mission inside Gaza carries significant risks, given the complexities of the security and political situation, continuing disagreements over the future of the territory and governance and security arrangements, and the sensitivity surrounding the presence of foreign forces in the Palestinian territories.
"Uganda's move places the African Union before a difficult test: how can the organisation maintain a unified African position on the Palestinian cause while each member state has broad scope to make its foreign and security decisions independently?" he added. "The union's ability to deal with these contradictions could be an important indicator of the effectiveness of its political positions, not only towards Palestine, but also towards international crises affecting the continent and the interests of its countries."
Contradictions, differences
Meanwhile, researcher on Sahel and Sahara affairs Mohamed Torshin told The New Arab that the participation of Ugandan forces in the peace process in Gaza clearly reflects the scale of contradictions within the African Union and its limited ability to impose or implement decisions taken collectively, whether at the level of the AU Commission, the Peace and Security Council or the General Assembly.
Although African Union decisions and collective positions are supposed to form a common political framework for member states, the Ugandan position, along with other previous cases, reveals clear differences in the positions of African countries towards several sensitive regional and international issues.
In many cases, these differences push some countries or regional blocs to adopt policies and approaches that conflict with the union's collective position.
According to Torshin, the repercussions are not limited to a particular issue but extend to the effectiveness of African decision-making in general.
When a member state, in his view, adopts a position that clearly contradicts the union's collective position, this weakens the organisation's ability to present itself as a unified political actor and limits its ability to exercise diplomatic influence on issues requiring a coherent continental position.
In this context, Torshin noted that the repetition of such cases could widen the gap between decisions issued by African Union institutions and the policies pursued by some member states at the national level.
"This would gradually weaken the ability of the AU Commission and its political bodies to turn collective positions and decisions into effective and binding policies, making African decision-making more vulnerable to fragmentation and differences between countries and regional blocs," he added.
Torshin pointed out that the lack of protocol and political coordination between different African countries, ministries and institutions, and the absence of unified positions and decisions on common issues, could create space for international parties with interests and programmes in Africa to deal with countries individually and implement their policies and projects according to their own interests, away from the collective frameworks and decisions of the African Union.
He argued that "as this divergence and the multiplicity of positions within the continental organisation continue, international powers may find themselves with greater room to manoeuvre and negotiate with African countries bilaterally, gradually weakening the union's ability to formulate and defend a unified African agenda".
"In the long term, the continuation of this fragmentation could affect the future of African integration, making the implementation of continental policies and projects more closely tied to the interests of countries and external partners, and less subject to the collective vision that the union is supposed to represent," Torshin warned.

OnlyFans owner Radvin̦skiy received $700 million in dividends before his death - FT

Unknown Publisher

OnlyFans owner Radvin̦skiy received $700 million in dividends before his death - FT
Kyiv • UNN
OnlyFans revenue grew to $1.6 billion, while profit rose to $715 million. Owner Leonid Radvin̦skiy received more than $700 million in dividends.
OnlyFans paid more than $700 million in dividends to its owner before his death earlier this year, according to the annual accounts of the British streaming platform, which will be filed in the UK this week, the Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
"The results of Fenix International, which owns the British streaming platform used by sex-industry workers, show that revenue rose by one-tenth to $1.6 billion in the year to November 2025, while pretax profit increased by 5 percent to $715 million. The highly productive business has just 47 employees," the publication writes.
Most of the profit in the 2025 accounts reportedly "went in the form of dividends to its owner, Ukrainian-American entrepreneur Leonid Radvinsky, who died of cancer in the spring." His death preceded the sale of a 16 percent stake in the business to San Francisco-based private investment firm Architect Capital in April for $535 million, giving the company a valuation of $3.2 billion.
According to the company's accounts, "Radvinsky was paid $535 million in dividends in the 2025 financial year, compared with $497 million the year before. However, according to the accounts, a further $174 million was paid in several installments after the end of the financial year."
Some Wall Street advisers considered the sale valuation low for such a profitable company, which was attributed to investors' reluctance to participate in the business, the publication notes.
In 2025, the total number of creator accounts on OnlyFans grew by 9 percent to 5 million, while the number of fan accounts worldwide increased by 16 percent to 437 million.
Of the 5 million creator accounts, 2.5 million were classified as "active" because they were used during the financial year ending November 30, 2025, while there were 132 million active fan accounts.
Last year, creators were paid approximately $6.2 billion after OnlyFans took its 20 percent share of their revenue. The total amount paid to creators now stands at $30 billion since the platform was founded in 2016.
The site also hosts other creators, such as actors, musicians and sports stars, who seek to earn money directly from fans, often in exchange for accepting requests for certain types of content.
The reports, which will be filed with the UK corporate registry Companies House this week, confirm that the group is now controlled by a family trust headed by Kateryna Chudnovska, Radvinsky's widow.
OnlyFans is marking its tenth anniversary, having been founded in 2016 by British entrepreneur Tim Stokely and his father Guy, and then sold to Radvinsky in 2018. It remains based in the UK.
OnlyFans Chief Executive Officer Keily Blair said: "In the 10 years since the platform launched in 2016, OnlyFans has paid more than $30 billion to creators worldwide, including more than $1 million to over 5,000 creators. As a British business, we have also made a significant contribution to the UK economy, paying more than £600 million in corporate taxes from 2016 to the present."
The group's largest market is the US, where it generated $965 million in revenue in the latest financial year. The UK and Europe contributed $347 million, while the rest of the world contributed $241 million.

Speaking in Kyiv after a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Burnham went on: “I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion. Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
If it did take place, it would be Burnham’s first visit to the US since taking office, and could potentially provide an opportunity for a face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump.
Dozens of world leaders gather annually for the general assembly. This year’s meeting takes place from 22-28 September, which could be logistically tricky for Burnham given Labour’s annual conference begins in Liverpool on 27 September.
Attending would give Burnham the opportunity to meet a number of other world leaders at once, even if bilateral talks tend to be brief amid the frenetic schedule of the gathering.
Burnham’s policy background is predominantly domestic, and since entering No 10 he has had to rapidly develop a foreign policy – thus far very similar to that of Keir Starmer – and get to know world leaders.
In Kyiv on Monday, for his first official overseas trip since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham laid a wreath for Ukraine’s Independence Day, joining a number of other European leaders, including the European council president, António Costa.
He also used the trip to announce that the UK government would allow the European defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components of the Anglo-French Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles to help Ukraine build its own version.
During his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said there would be “no change in the UK’s steadfast support” for Kyiv.
He also urged Ukraine’s allies to send more Patriot missiles to Kyiv as Ukraine struggles under continued Russian bombardment, and co-chaired his first coalition of the willing meeting, where he said the group was doing “everything we can” to “dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”.
Zelenskyy has pleaded for more US-made interceptor missiles in recent months as Kyiv’s stocks have diminished. Supplies of Patriots have been diverted to the Middle East since the outbreak of the US’s war against Iran, with Ukraine receiving significantly fewer missiles this year than in previous years.
During the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said he felt “really confident” the weaponry problem was fixable, but added: “There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with. It’s probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation.”
Russia has sought to capitalise on the shortage by increasing its ballistic missile strikes, killing at least 23 people and wounding more than 100 in the past three days.
Russia has threatened unspecified potential retaliation against the UK for what Moscow says is increased involvement in the conflict.

- Poland received 28 K2 tanks, the first delivery from an August 2025 contract with Hyundai Rotem, assigning them to the 16th Mechanized Division.
- Future batches under the contract will include the K2PL variant, with 61 of 64 units to be assembled in Poland using domestic components.
Poland has received its first batch of tanks from a second, $6.5 billion contract with South Korea’s Hyundai Rotem, Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Tuesday.
Twenty-eight K2 tanks arrived in Poland and will go to the 16th Mechanized Division, he said.
The contract was signed August 1, 2025, and covers 180 additional tanks. It follows an earlier deal for 180 K2GF tanks that Poland completed receiving in November 2025.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the tanks delivered in this batch are standard K2 models, and that future shipments under the same contract will include the K2PL variant, a Polish-modified version built in part from domestically produced components. The second contract calls for 116 K2GF tanks between 2026 and 2027, followed by 64 K2PL tanks between 2028 and 2030. Of those K2PL tanks, 61 are set to be assembled in Poland at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice, which belongs to the state-owned defense group PGZ.
The K2 Black Panther is a South Korean third-generation main battle tank armed with a 120 mm smoothbore gun and an autoloader. It also carries a 7.62 mm machine gun and a 12.7 mm heavy machine gun.
Kosiniak-Kamysz described the delivery as a step that expands Poland’s domestic production capacity and strengthens the country’s defense posture, tying the arrival of the K2PL variant to the broader technology-transfer terms of the contract.
The 16th Pomeranian Mechanized Division, based in northeastern Poland, has been the primary recipient of K2 tanks under the earlier contract, which equipped the 20th Bartoszyce Mechanized Brigade, the 9th Braniewo Armored Cavalry Brigade and the 15th Giżycko Mechanized Brigade. Six additional tanks from that contract went to the Land Forces Training Center in Poznań.
The second contract, worth roughly $6.5 billion, also includes 81 support vehicles based on the K2 chassis: 25 combat engineering vehicles, 25 armored bridge layers and 31 armored recovery vehicles, along with ammunition, a logistics and training package, and technology transfer. Brigadier General Artur Kuptel, head of Poland’s Armament Agency, signed the agreement on the Polish side at the Bumar-Łabędy facility, with Hyundai Rotem CEO Lee Yong-Bae signing for the South Korean company.
Poland’s tank purchases from South Korea are part of a broader rearmament effort that has included M1A2 SEPv3 Abrams tanks from the United States and continued operation of Leopard 2 tanks acquired from Germany. Poland had roughly 117 M1A2 SEPv3 tanks delivered as of early 2026. Officials have said Poland aims to field around 900 tanks across the three platforms by 2030, which would make it one of the largest tank fleets in Europe.

The war on ‘loudcasting’ phones can be won, but it will take some very British nudging | Dan Hancox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:00:51 UTC
16:00:51 KST

‘Interesting cities can’t be quiet”, runs one of grime DJ and music industry thinker Elijah’s epigrams – and in its essential spirit, he is right. Silent, tidy, prim cities should be treated with suspicion. Any such atmosphere denotes that something has gone wrong at a macro level: either you’ve wound up in an authoritarian regime or, worse, Switzerland.
But not all urban sounds are created equal, and some are more unwelcome than others. Take the tide of (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube) reels crashing on the shores of our collective attention on public transport, thanks to the astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK to surf the slopwave without headphones.
These rotters are accompanied by people taking their phone or video calls out loud on speakerphone. In the early days of mobile phones it was a widely agreed social truism that the white-collar worker unselfconsciously bellowing “I’m on the train!” into their BlackBerry was a grade-A public nuisance, plausibly worthy of throwing in the stocks. Well, at least then we were only being subjected to one end of the conversation.
The spread of 5G across the country is making such unsolicited noise more possible and more common: “loudcasting”, the BBC called it in a recent in-depth look at the phenomenon. A public backlash is suddenly mounting. Never one to miss an opportunity for free press coverage, last week Wetherspoons boss Tim Martin banned it from his pubs.
It’s funny how social pressure points like this fade in and out of public view, as the technology that touches our lives evolves: 19 years ago, the same practice was christened “sodcasting” by Pascal Wyse in this newspaper – at that point there were no reels, no AI drivel, no streaming video calls, no such thing as an Instagram influencer, nor Instagram either. The moral panic back then was about tinny MP3s being played aloud from much more basic mobile phones – and the purported juvenile delinquency that had surely led to such a crisis.
I probably annoyed a lot of Guardian readers that year, writing more than 2,000 words in defence of sodcasting: more precisely, in defence of teenagers playing music on their phones on the bus, the train or otherwise in public. There was something qualitatively different about that iteration, I would argue. It was a necessary claiming of public space by people who are often bullied out of it: adults-in-training, still working out how to exist in the outside world as independent beings, still learning to navigate their own social lives, and (an underrated asset, this) learning to enjoy music together, as a group activity. For the rest of us, this form of sodcasting amounted to an occasional, brief and usually joyful burst of alfresco music – and we could all do with hearing Crazy Cousinz and Giggs more often anyway.
The 2010 furore about sodcasting followed a decade of punching down by Britain’s power-wielding adults against its most marginalised young people – the “chavs” and “hoodies” against whom New Labour and the tabloids collectively went to war, driven by the reactionary moralism of what was risibly called “the respect agenda”. A time of asbos, public spaces protection orders and curfews for young people.
Interestingly – and admittedly anecdotally; this stuff isn’t easy to measure – sodcasting 1.0 seemed to disappear as a phenomenon after a year or two. New social behaviours that emerge in response to new popular technologies tend to do so: things settle down as a new consensus on how we should all use them is slowly reached, and reached collectively.
Let’s hope that happens again, because what we are all hearing on buses and trains thanks to sodcasting 2.0 is measurably more antisocial and individualistic: for one thing, 2010’s groups of teen sodcasters weren’t changing songs every 10 seconds. For another – warning, more anecdotal analysis incoming – these days it always seems to be full-grown adults rather than teenagers taking calls on speakerphone or watching reels with no headphones. It is maddening behaviour to anyone who has experienced it: like being on a bus or a train with someone who is flicking TV channels, constantly.
So, as Lenin once asked of matters of similarly grave importance: what is to be done? Last year, the Lib Dems proposed a £1,000 fine for sodcasting – an amusingly illiberal policy to make one of their centrepieces. For what it’s worth, I don’t think a fine is very useful, realistic or enforceable – though, God bless the ironclad French state, for it managed to find a way to do exactly that, fining a man €200 (£170) for taking a call on loudspeaker on a station platform.
The truth is that we have more sane and effective options for shaping public behaviour in the form of nudge messaging. Transport for London has a strong history of this, via adverts on its trains, tubes and buses. In 2008, its Considerate Travel campaign seemed to help quieten down the mobile phone DJs and its current Act Like a Friend and Travel Kind campaigns aim to address hate crime, misogynistic creeps and encourage others to help passengers who may be unwell. Sodcasting 2.0 pisses me off no end, too, but I think people can change with a little nudging.
Stefan Stern made an excellent case in these pages recently that we should all remove our headphones – and turn off the content altogether – to hear and more fully participate in the noisy, messy city around us. Hopefully we can achieve this via social consensus, gentle persuasion, and without the soundtrack of someone broadcasting AI monkey videos. And if all else fails, well, sod it: let’s nudge the culprits into the stocks.
- 
  Dan Hancox is a writer and editor covering music, politics and cities. His latest book is Multitudes: How Crowds Made the Modern World

Speeding for online glory: the internet subculture where young men drive dangerously for likes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:00:51 UTC
16:00:51 KST

The hashtags tell the story of the potentially lethal social media subculture where young men film themselves hurtling at illegal speeds down busy roads: #speedhunters, #needforspeed, #racing.
The fast-driving internet trend on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube is fed by footage shot from a driver’s perspective of cars going “#fullsend” – the jargon for roaring down dual carriageways – and “#gapping” or “#swimming”, as in weaving dangerously through packed traffic. The posts attract thousands, sometimes millions of views and have been described by Andy Burnham on Monday as “truly reprehensible”.
The prime minister spoke out after seven deaths on Saturday, including two police officers and five young men aged 17 to 23, when the young men drove the wrong way down the A66 in Teesside after a police chase. It has been reported one of the young men killed in the car previously posted fast-driving clips. Cleveland police said there was currently “no evidence that filming of the activities on Friday night and Saturday morning was for the purposes of TikTok”.
Last week a similar incident shocked Ireland when five teenagers – some of whom had previously posted videos of reckless driving – were killed when their car travelling in the wrong direction on the M9 crashed into another vehicle. The Irish police said: “In some cases it is being done for social media likes.”
Several factors are behind this trend, experts say. Young men have long been sensation seekers with a tendency to push whatever limits adults impose, according to Sonia Livingstone, professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics and an expert in social media harms.
Social media now extends the momentary thrill of speed with the promise of clout and glory as the drivers’ exploits spread through the internet. It is a case, Livingstone said, of “putting their foot down in the offline world knowing it wins them points in the online world”. If views rise high enough, there is also the prospect of cash rewards from some of the social media companies.
“There is a lot of research on how the online world of fame and visibility is increasingly significant for boys and young men in a context in which they don’t have a lot of other ways of affirmation,” said Livingstone, who called the incidents absolutely horrifying.
“We might ask how else boys and young men get a moment of affirmation,” she said. “Many young people are feeling depressed and hopeless about the future. It doesn’t offer them opportunities to shine and a path where they can see their future.”
The reach of the most popular accounts can be huge. Joseph Ondrak, director at Peryton Intelligence, a company that monitors harmful online subcultures, identified a user called Squeeze Benz with more than a million followers on TikTok and Instagram and another called wheres981 with 457,000 YouTube followers. Their clips “show some incredibly dangerous driving” and have been “key in popularising the squeezing/swimming/gapping trend”, said Ondrak. He said infamy and subcultural influence appeared to be greater driving forces than monetisation.
“Both of these accounts and others like them also have an army of ‘clippers’ taking key moments from streams and longer videos and editing them for short-form and compilation consumption for higher engagement and reach,” Ondrak said.
The government reaction has been to demand the big tech platforms remove posts of dangerous driving. A spokesperson said Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, is seeking assurances from the tech companies and from the online communications regulator Ofcom “that this content is being proactively sought and removed in line with their legal obligations and that accounts that post this type of activity are shut down immediately”.
Ofcom last month launched a separate investigation into TikTok amid concerns about children being exposed to harmful content. Dangerous driving is not mentioned among the categories of illegal content listed in the 2023 Online Safety Act which focuses on issues such as child sexual abuse, terrorism, suicide and self-harm. However, it could be considered harmful to children under the category of content promoting dangerous challenges. If so, the law requires platforms to protect children – but not anyone 18 or over – from seeing it.
TikTok said it removes videos and accounts that break its rules including content that glorifies violence, or promotes crimes that could harm people, that depicts activities likely to be imitated and that could cause significant physical harm, including risky driving. Yet clips of dangerous driving were not hard to find on Monday.
One TikTok user, CrazyGappers, showed a driver hurtling down the M25 towards Dartford in a clip titled “Serious driving #driving #gapped #racing”. Another shows a driver accelerating to high speeds along unlit lanes with the caption “nothing can top full sending your car on your favourite b roads” #fullsends #backroads”. On Instagram Ukdriverz has a clip titled “200mph on UK roads” with the caption “entertainment purposes only” while on YouTube, 2.5 million people have watched a clip of a Honda being driven at breakneck speed through a council estate and then down a narrow country road.
Instagram’s owner, Meta, said it prohibits people from promoting, advocating for or encouraging participation in high-risk viral challenges, including the trend of dangerous driving against incoming traffic. After the Guardian highlighted it, Google, which runs YouTube, removed the channel showing the speeding Honda.
“We don’t allow content featuring harmful or dangerous activities that risk serious physical harm on YouTube,” a spokesperson said. “As such, we quickly removed the flagged videos, and terminated the associated channel.”
