====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: U.S. consumers crave affordable Chinese EVs amid soaring car prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:36:00 CST
15:36:00 KST

by Julia Pierrepont III
LOS ANGELES, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- As American automakers increasingly focus on higher-priced, more profitable vehicles, a growing number of ordinary Americans are calling for highly cost-effective imports from China to fill the void.
"I'm an auto mechanic," Juan Vega, a local Angeleno, told Xinhua in a recent interview. "And Chinese cars give great value for the price compared to American cars. In America, we say it's all about market competition, so why can't I buy an affordable Chinese car if I want one?"
That sentiment is becoming increasingly common because cars made in China by companies such as BYD and Geely can cost as little as the equivalent of 10,000 to 20,000 U.S. dollars but are effectively shut out of the U.S. passenger-car market by tariffs and other restrictions. Meanwhile, average new-vehicle transaction prices in the country have risen to around 49,000 dollars to 50,000 dollars in recent years. Typical monthly payments have remained high, as elevated interest rates, insurance premiums and repair costs have added to the burden.
Despite facing steep tariffs, Waymo, which operates public commercial robotaxi services in several U.S. metropolitan areas, has imported over 3,200 Chinese-built Zeekr electric minivans into the United States since 2024. But for millions of ordinary Americans, the new-car market is becoming less a marketplace than a gated community.
Detroit's product strategy has shifted decisively toward trucks, SUVs and premium models because those vehicles offer higher profit margins. Ford has largely abandoned traditional sedans in the U.S. market, while General Motors and Stellantis have leaned heavily on pickups, large SUVs and higher-priced configurations, leaving many U.S. consumers with fewer affordable options.
Sam Fiorani, vice president of Global Vehicle Forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, has argued that Chinese automakers have succeeded in producing reasonably priced small and midsize cars that appeal to consumers.
"The ride, the handling, the comfort and the luxury tech were off the charts," said car enthusiast Ken Wheeler, 39, who had test-driven a Chinese vehicle at a Consumer Electronics Show (CES) event. "And the price -- I'm sold!"
With U.S. car costs so high, Edmunds, a car-shopping research firm, said in a recent survey that 73 percent of U.S. consumers had delayed buying a vehicle because of high prices. "Affordability concerns among American car shoppers aren't going away anytime soon," it concluded.
"U.S. car prices are killing us," said R. Clark, 39, a Californian native and restaurant worker with modest wages and a family of three. "I gotta put off buying a new one again this year, even though my current one is in for repairs half the time."
For workers who need reliable transportation to get to jobs, schools, medical care and childcare, the loss of affordable cars can have consequences far beyond household budgets.
But affordable cars from China remain effectively off-limits to American consumers, largely because of steep tariffs and other trade and security restrictions.
The result, consumer advocates and some industry analysts say, is a policy collision: Washington says it is protecting American jobs and national security, while many households are left struggling with higher car bills and fewer affordable transportation options.
Chinese automakers have built small electric cars that sell overseas at prices well below many U.S. options and have received praise for their efficiency, technology and value. Even so, the tariff barrier makes direct competition in the U.S. market impossible, forestalling market testing. The problem has deepened since the United States imposed steep tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
Chinese automakers have increasingly turned to international celebrities to promote their brands. Leonardo DiCaprio became a brand ambassador for BYD's new-energy vehicles in China in 2016, while Daniel Craig has more recently appeared in advertising for BYD's premium brand, Denza.
Views from the automotive community shed light on the issue.
Clint Simone, senior features editor at Edmunds, told Reuters that he had driven several Chinese vehicles at CES earlier this year and was struck by their value proposition. "The technology they offer for those lower price tags was astounding," Simone said.
Ben Nelmes, chief executive of New Automotive, told CBS News earlier this year, "China is miles ahead of the rest of the world."
"If China is willing to make a good car I can actually afford and Detroit won't, then bring it on," a family man who called himself Clark told Xinhua. "The government should either help guys like us by pressuring American carmakers to step up with rides in our price range -- or get out of the way and let China do it."
But despite stepping away from the low-priced sedan market, Detroit automakers and their allies warn that a wave of low-cost Chinese vehicles could damage U.S. factories, suppliers and dealerships.
"They used that tired old argument against Japanese cars in the 1970s, and Detroit didn't go under then, did it?" Vega told Xinhua.
Critics said those older arguments may protect shareholders, executives and lobbyists at the expense of ordinary American consumers. They argued the policy has created a protective wall around companies that increasingly prefer to sell fewer, more expensive vehicles rather than competing aggressively for budget-conscious buyers.
Policy discussions in Washington frequently focus on industrial strategy, geopolitical rivalry and the profits of major manufacturers. Policymakers can overlook how deeply transportation affordability affects ordinary Americans. A rule that looks prudent from a national security briefing can be punitive to a worker who cannot afford the vehicles left on the lot. ■

The official said the encounter with the Chinese vessel was essentially a communications test conducted when the ships met in international waters, according to Liberty Times. The US responded to both developments, warning against Chinese actions that undermine peace and stability and urging other countries not to amplify Beijing’s destabilizing narratives. ====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Japan's rice market swings from shortage fears to oversupply woes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
14:35:43 CST
15:35:43 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- Sushi, rice balls, curry rice and eel rice - rice is an indispensable part of Japanese people's daily diet. Yet over the past year or so, rice prices in Japan have gone on a roller-coaster ride: prices surged from the summer of 2024, at one point triggering a nationwide "rice shortage," only to fall rapidly since the beginning of this year as inventories grew and newly harvested rice entered the market. Farmers in some producing areas are now even facing the prospect of selling rice at a loss.
Analysts believe that the dramatic shift from consumers being unable to afford rice to producers struggling to sell it reflects an imbalance between supply and demand in Japan's rice market. If prices continue to decline, farmers' willingness to grow rice could be undermined, further weakening the country's agricultural production base.
VOLATILE RICE PRICES
Rice prices in Japan began rising sharply in the summer of 2024, with supermarkets in many areas imposing purchase limits or running out of supplies. The Japanese government released several rounds of reserve rice in an effort to stabilize prices, but the measures had limited effect.
In 2025, prices of rice-related products rose 67.5 percent, the largest increase since comparable records began in 1971. The average retail price for a 5-kilogram bag of rice in Japan reached a record peak of 4,416 yen (about 27.7 U.S. dollars) at the end of last year.
Prices have gradually declined this year. According to the latest data from Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, the average retail price for a 5-kilogram bag of rice stood at 3,191 yen during the week of Aug. 10-16.
The arrival of newly harvested rice is putting further downward pressure on prices. Advance payments made by the National Federation of Agricultural Cooperative Associations (ZEN-NOH) to farmers are regarded as an important benchmark for new rice prices. Recent figures from major producing regions indicate substantial reductions in advance payments, suggesting that prices for the new crop could fall further.
According to Japanese media reports, Niigata Prefecture, Japan's largest rice-producing region, has set the advance payment for ordinary Koshihikari rice produced in 2026 at 18,500 yen per 60 kilograms, down 38 percent from the previous year. Hokkaido Prefecture has set the advance payment for its main rice varieties at 17,000 yen per 60 kilograms, a decline of 41 percent.
Some supermarkets have already begun selling rice harvested in 2026, but an unusual phenomenon has emerged: newly harvested rice is in some cases cheaper than older rice. Naoya Matsudaira, assistant professor at the School of Agriculture, Utsunomiya University, said this price inversion between new and old rice could persist.
PERSISTENT IMBALANCE
Whether rice prices are soaring or plunging, the fundamental problem is an imbalance between supply and demand.
In reviewing the "rice shortage" in its 2025 agricultural white paper, the agriculture ministry acknowledged that the government had underestimated rice demand and consequently failed to arrange sufficient planting acreage. High temperatures and other factors also reduced yields and quality, tightening supply. Earthquake warnings and other developments prompted consumers to stockpile rice, further widening the supply gap. Delays in the government's assessment of market conditions and in releasing reserve rice also prolonged the shortage.
Japan's rice market is now facing the opposite imbalance: supply has expanded significantly while demand has weakened.
"Supply and demand are currently out of balance to the worst extent," said Sadao Yamamoto, president of major rice wholesaler ZEN-NOH Pearl Rice.
On the supply side, rice inventories have surged. According to agriculture ministry statistics, private-sector rice inventories stood at 2.43 million tons at the end of June, up 57 percent year on year and the highest level on record. The figure is well above the 1.8 million to 2 million tons generally considered an appropriate level.
The rapid increase in inventories reflects several factors, including expanded planting after the government raised its expectations for rice demand, as well as the release of reserve rice and increased rice imports.
On the demand side, the previous surge in prices appears to have changed consumer behavior.
Masaaki Yamaguchi, a senior analyst at Nomura Securities, said that as rice prices soared, rice consumption in Japan declined again last year. Statistics from an organization supporting stable rice supplies show that Japan's per-capita monthly rice consumption was 4.435 kilograms in fiscal 2025, a 6.1 percent year-on-year decrease and the lowest level in seven years.
Some analysts believe that as rice became more expensive, an increasing number of Japanese households switched to noodles and bread, which are cheaper alternatives.
An editorial in the Tokyo Shimbun noted that although rice prices have fallen, they remain substantially higher than before the "rice shortage," meaning many consumers may still consider rice expensive.
FOOD SECURITY CONCERNS
Falling rice prices have eased the burden on consumers, but they have created new pressure on producers and distributors. Japanese media and experts warn that prolonged low prices could drive some farmers out of agriculture, potentially affecting the country's food security.
Japanese farmers have little reason to celebrate this year's good rice harvest. Production costs have continued to rise, with prices of agricultural chemicals, fertilizers and other inputs pushed higher amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Ryoji Ito, an assistant professor at Niigata University, said that in Niigata, farmers could face a situation in which "the more they produce, the more they lose" unless they can sell 60 kilograms of rice for between 20,000 and 24,000 yen.
Yoichi Takahashi, a rice farmer in Niigata, said he had calculated his business costs when purchasing agricultural machinery on the assumption that rice would sell for about 24,000 yen per 60 kilograms. With prices now falling, his income could decline by around 10 million yen.
Rice wholesalers are also under pressure. A rice warehouse in Chiba Prefecture is almost full, with about 300 tons of rice from last year still in storage even as the new crop is about to enter the market. To make room for new supplies, low-price competition and clearance sales have already emerged.
Japan's agricultural sector has long faced challenges including high production costs, low efficiency and a shrinking workforce. The large number of small-scale farms and fragmented farmland makes it difficult for farmers to reduce costs and improve efficiency.
The number of agricultural operators in Japan has also continued to decline. In 2025, there were only 836,000, down 60 percent from 2005. Kimio Inagaki, a research fellow at Mitsubishi Research Institute, estimates that the figure could fall to just 200,000 by 2050.
"If rice prices fall to a level that no longer allows farmers to continue growing rice, Japan's rice production could gradually decline," said Yoshito Shinno, president of the Central Union of Agricultural Cooperatives. ■

It is possible that many more people have fallen ill. “The figures are always an underestimate. Not everyone becomes seriously ill from salmonella. People in good health will, at most, experience some flu-like symptoms; they do not always go to the doctor for this and tend to recover quickly. Young children, the elderly and pregnant women can become more seriously ill.”
4 codes to look out for
The eggs were withdrawn from sale on 10 August, but people may still have some at home. “Eggs have a shelf life of 4 weeks after they are laid. The eggs currently on sale in shops are safe. If you bought eggs before 10 August, it’s best to check the codes on them again. There are four codes involved. They can be found on our website. It’s best not to eat those eggs anymore.”
Which are the codes of the affected eggs?
2-BE-1073-01
2-BE-1073-02

2-BE-1073-04
You can return eggs with these codes to the shop where you bought them.

The new study used the BakhtarRadar subsurface radar system to identify layers and anomalies deep beneath the Durupınar Formation.
An international team studying the Durupınar Formation near Mount Ağrı claim that the ship-shaped structure may not simply be a rock but could be the remains of Noah’s Ark.
Located 29 kilometers south of Mount Ağrı, Türkiye’s highest mountain at 5,137 meters, the ship-shaped Durupınar Formation has long divided opinion. Many scientists, however, argue that the Durupınar Formation is a geological structure created by natural processes. The debate has now drawn the attention of Iranian-born scientist Dr. Khosrow Bakhtar, an expert in geomechanics, electromagnetism and subsurface radar technologies.
According to the Daily Mail, a team led by Bakhtar has said that the Durupınar Formation could contain remains of Noah’s Ark.
The study reportedly used a specialized imaging system known as BakhtarRadar, developed through research associated with the U.S. Air Force, to examine areas deeper underground than previous surveys.
The team said it detected strong subsurface anomalies and distinct layers within the 157-meter-long formation, challenging the view that it is a single homogeneous rock mass.
“My team and I are evaluating the subsurface data. With the capabilities of BakhtarRadar, we will distinguish petrified, man-made timber from natural bedrock formations,” Bakhtar said.
The new study led by Bakhtar reportedly used the BakhtarRadar subsurface radar system to identify layers and anomalies deep beneath the Durupınar Formation.
The electromagnetic technology can produce three-dimensional images of underground structures without physically excavating the site, and the team said it had obtained significant digital data from the Durupınar area.
Jones, who has been working for years to prove that the Durupınar Formation is Noah’s Ark, said the “ultimate goal is to enter the ship,” adding that permission from Türkiye would be required to do so.
According to the biblical account, Noah, his family and animals of every kind survived a great flood aboard the ark around 4,300 years ago.

e-DNA to probe missing remains in Türkiye’s northwest

Researchers will conduct environmental DNA testing at an 86,000-year-old cave in the northwestern province of Çanakkale this September, aiming to solve the mystery of why no organic remains have been found despite the discovery of 40,000 stone tools.
The İnkaya Cave, nestled in the Bahadırlı village of the local Çan district, yielded zero organic materials during previous excavations. Ankara University Professor İsmail Özer from the Faculty of Language, History and Geography’s Anthropology Department and Paleoanthropology Section called the situation an anomaly.
“We are doing e-DNA, environmental DNA analysis in the field for the first time this year to identify the bacteria consuming the organic material,” he said. Experts from the university’s genetic evolution laboratory will collect soil samples to determine the region’s paleoecological structure.
The analysis could reveal surrounding vegetation, animal remains and the exact human species utilizing the cave. This data promises to shed light on Paleolithic period migrations between Anatolia and the Balkans.
Özer discovered the site during the 2016 Muğla and Çanakkale Provinces Surface Survey. An international team subsequently carried out periodic excavations from 2017 to 2020 under the Troy Museum Directorate. The site gained presidential decree status in 2021.
A coalition of state and private entities supports the ongoing 2026 works. These include the Culture and Tourism Ministry, the Cultural Heritage and Museums General Directorate, the Ankara University Rectorate, the Çanakkale Governorate, Truva Bakır Maden İşletmeleri A.Ş. and T-Design Mühendislik Şirketi.
Environmental DNA analysis allows scientists to detect genetic material left behind by organisms in soil without physical fossils. This technique helps archaeologists identify microscopic biological footprints in ancient sediments.

The government is considering making annual dope tests mandatory for every pilot, instead of the current requirement covering 10% of the pilot network.
NEW DELHI: The aviation ministry is considering mandating dope tests for all pilots at least once a year, civil aviation minister Ram Mohan Naidu Kinjarapu said on Tuesday.The current rules require dope testing of 10 per cent of the overall pilot network, but the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) is examining whether testing can be expanded to cover every pilot at a random time during the year.
“There are multiple ways of approaching this dope test. Right now, the rule says 10% across the overall pilot network. DGCA is engaging, and one of the opinions from our side is that everyone has to go through it in the year at a random time,” Naidu told reporters.
The minister added the government would need to balance aviation safety with the operational impact of implementing 100 per cent testing.“We have to see how all the stakeholders are going to respond to this because one is the safety aspect of it, and the second thing is the operational impact, which also has to be taken into consideration,” he said.Meanwhile, addressing the recent Delhi-Phuket flight incident, Naidu said the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) is investigating the incident and a preliminary report is expected soon.The minister said the flight data recorder and the aircraft are intact and in the possession of the investigating agency, which would help in the probe.“AAIB is presently taking up the investigation. Because everything is intact, the flight data recorder and everything is intact, and the plane is also in their possession, I believe that we can expect a preliminary report very early from now,” he said.
Naidu also said the DGCA is holding consultations with stakeholders on existing regulations concerning substance use and ways to strengthen the policy.“More importantly, in terms of substance use and everything, DGCA is also having stakeholder consultations right now on what the regulation says today and how we ensure there is a strict policy around this in the future as well. So, this consultation is going on right now,” he said.The AAIB is examining the circumstances surrounding the incident, while the DGCA consultations are focused on reviewing existing regulations and strengthening safeguards related to substance use in aviation.The development comes after Air India flight AI2379, operating from Phuket to Delhi on August 4, experienced a sudden 300-foot altitude drop over Odisha, leaving 20 passengers and four cabin crew members injured.
The Airbus A320, bearing registration VT-EXO, subsequently stabilised and landed safely in Delhi. The aircraft was carrying 137 passengers, including three infants, and eight crew members, comprising two pilots and six cabin crew.A purported post-flight maintenance report has also revealed a series of technical warnings involving the aircraft’s hydraulic systems, flight controls and autopilot during the journey.The report lists repeated low-pressure alerts across the green, blue and yellow hydraulic systems, along with low fluid levels in the yellow and blue reservoirs. Autopilot disconnections were also recorded twice.

The 'extraordinarily expensive' project reshaping a state — and drawing political battlelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:33:35 UTC
15:33:35 KST

In brief
- Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says changes to the Suburban Rail Loop will mean it is "built under budget".
- There has been division over the infrastructure project's costs, with the state Opposition vowing to review it if elected.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has announced $2 billion in cuts to the state's largest infrastructure project, the Suburban Rail Loop (SRL), saying: "I respect your money."
His comments underline the controversy over the 90km underground rapid transit project, which will link Melbourne's middle suburbs and allow passengers to travel across the city without passing through the CBD.
The state government says the mega-project will reshape Melbourne into a multi-nodal city, bringing services and jobs closer to where people live, building more homes, and creating more jobs.
But its enormous cost, disputed economic benefits and lengthy construction timeline have also made it one of Australia's most controversial infrastructure projects.
Liam Davies, a lecturer in sustainability and urban planning at RMIT University, said the SRL was a step towards transforming Melbourne's city-centric public transport system into an interconnected network.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Melbourne's greatest challenge is that it has become an extraordinarily large city, physically," he told SBS News.
"We can't just adopt the transport strategy for a denser, more compact city like London. We need to do something of our own, and the SRL is an attempt to do that in a Melburnian context."
With Labor and the Coalition deeply divided on the SRL, the project's future could be decided when Victorians head to the polls in November.
Why is the project so controversial?
The SRL will connect Melbourne's middle suburbs from Cheltenham in the south-east to Werribee in the west via Melbourne Airport through a 90km underground rail line.
The project is split into three stages. The first section — SRL East — is under construction, running from Cheltenham to Box Hill via six new underground stations. The first trains are expected by 2035.
Critics argue the mega-project's business case doesn't stack up, and the multi-billion-dollar price tag is a financial liability for Victoria, which has the second-highest debt per capita of any state or territory, behind the Northern Territory.
More than $33 billion has already been invested in SRL East, according to the premier.
A Parliamentary Budget Office analysis puts the price tag for building the East and North sections at $96.4 billion, though there is currently no fully costed estimate for the entire project, which includes the final stage, SRL West.
An evaluation last year by Infrastructure Australia — an advisory body to the federal government — found the SRL's business case was insufficiently detailed and relied on future stages to justify its benefits.
It also urged the Victorian government to develop "exit strategies" should the project be unable to be completed.
Allegations of corruption and unlawful conduct in state-funded projects, which recently led to a royal commission into the construction industry being called, have also heightened public concerns about the SRL.
Davies said there are questions about which other infrastructure projects will miss out on investment because of the SRL.
"This is still an extraordinarily expensive project," he said.
"Is this the only project that we build over the next 35 to 50 years, or do we build other projects at the same time?
"If it's the only project that we build, I don't think it's the best allocation of resources."
Are there alternatives?
Carroll, who replaced Jacinta Allan as premier last month, has clearly recognised that many Victorians are unhappy with the eye-watering cost.
On Tuesday, he announced $2 billion in savings, with underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley no longer to be built, instead replaced by surface transfers.
Among other changes, a second station entrance will not be built at Clayton, and pedestrian bridges in Burwood and Cheltenham have also been axed.
"I respect your money," Carroll said in a statement.
"The SRL will be built on time. Today's changes mean it will be built under budget."
Davies said construction of SRL East was well advanced, with tunnel boring machines in place to begin excavating twin 26km tunnels.
"The reality is that that project is so far along; it will continue," he said.
But it's the project's latter stages which have scope for change.
Davies said better rail services and upgrades to the northern and western suburb lines, including electrification of the entire track, would fulfil many of the policy ambitions of SRL West at a fraction of the time and cost.
"We have an exploding population in our northern and western suburbs, and the infrastructure is not keeping up at all," he said.
He said there could also be alternatives to the SRL North, such as elevated rail, light rail, or a rapid bus transit system with dedicated bus lanes.
"There are challenges to each of those options; each of them has trade-offs," he said.
"All of them would be cheaper options than what we currently have, which is tens of billions of dollars in tunnelling."
Where do the parties stand?
The project's future could hinge on the outcome of the state's November election.
Labor has committed to seeing the SRL through, arguing it's essential infrastructure for a growing Melbourne.
The state Opposition has previously called for the project to be scrapped, arguing that it's too costly and the funds should be redirected to other, higher-priority transport projects, such as a long-sought-after airport line.
In 2024, Liberal MLC Evan Mulholland described the SRL as a "vanity project" that was "robbing the next generation of getting the infrastructure that they deserve".
But the Coalition's position has evolved over time, with Opposition leader Jess Wilson now promising to pause and review the project if elected.
Whatever the outcome, the project will remain a defining political issue for years to come.
"Transport projects are big and expensive, and they almost always have controversy," Davies said.
"It's almost impossible to build something that everyone is going to be absolutely happy with. Maybe this is just another example of that."

Millions of Teslas recalled in China over door handle safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:30:27 UTC
15:30:27 KST

People work on the Tesla Model Y production line at the Tesla Gigafactory assembly plant during a media organized tour, in Shanghai, China (AP Photo)
Tesla is recalling nearly three million cars in China with interior door handles that could hamper a person's ability to exit their vehicle in an emergency, Beijing's national market watchdog said.
Eight Chinese carmakers also filed recalls over similar safety risks, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced on Aug. 21.
Some recalls were effective immediately, while others began over the weekend and on Aug. 24.
Tesla's recall involves 2.9 million domestically-made units of its Model 3 and Model Y electric cars and begins on September 25.
The U.S. carmaker — which operates a huge factory in Shanghai — is also recalling around 46,000 imported units of its Model 3, Model X and Model S cars, the SAMR announcement said.
The recalled cars have inner emergency mechanical handles "similar in color to the interior, making them difficult to identify and operate" in emergencies, the watchdog said.
In Tesla's Model 3, for example, passengers must reach into a compartment inside the door pocket and find a release cable to manually open the rear door, according to the company's website.
"In extreme situations such as severe collisions causing the vehicle's low-voltage system to fail, (the handles) may affect passengers' ability to quickly open car doors for escape and rescue operations outside the vehicle," SAMR said.
SAMR said Tesla was separately recalling 2.7 million domestically-made Model 3 and Model Y EVs over issues with monitoring systems while a driver is using steering assist functions.
It was not clear whether some Teslas were counted in both recalls.
Chinese EV makers including Xiaomi, XPeng, Geely, Chery and Leapmotor are also recalling cars with handles that blend in with their interior.
Xiaomi began recalling around 390,000 units of its 2024 SU7 series on Aug. 21, and XPeng started recalling nearly 265,000 cars on Aug. 22.
Beijing-based BAIC BluePark, a subsidiary of state-owned automaker BAIC, on Aug. 22 began recalling around 46,000 Arcfox Kaola EVs over a "lack of dedicated text prompts" near the emergency mechanism on its right rear sliding door.
Beginning on Aug. 24, Geely is recalling around 92,000 cars from its luxury brand Zeekr.
Companies offered to attach warning labels near the handles for free, and some said they would remotely upgrade software involving lowering windows after a crash.
Safety concerns have risen in China recently over sleek car designs that are prone to losing operability in the event of a crash.
The mass recalls are in line with China's plan to ban hidden door handles on cars from January 1, 2027, local media reports said.
Those rules, announced in February by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, will require door handles to have both interior and exterior mechanical releases.
Electronic door handles were introduced with Tesla's 2012 launch of the Model S, later becoming popular with Chinese EV brands prioritising high-tech features.
Folding into the body of the car, such door handles provide a slight boost to efficiency by reducing drag while the vehicle is in motion.

Donald Judd’s Artillery Sheds in Texas to Undergo Major Restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

The Chinati Foundation has announced plans to restore the Artillery Sheds in Marfa, Texas, the former military buildings adapted by artist Donald Judd to house his 100 untitled works in mill aluminum, created between 1982 and 1986. Led by architect Troy Schaum of Schaum Architects, the multi-year preservation project is being developed with the Getty Conservation Institute and will address the historic buildings' envelope, accessibility, environmental performance, and landscape while preserving Judd's site-specific installation. The project follows the Artillery Sheds' inclusion in the National Register of Historic Places in 2025 as part of the expanded Donald Judd Historic District.
Located on the grounds of the former Fort D.A. Russell at the northeastern edge of the Chihuahuan Desert, the Artillery Sheds were constructed in 1939 by the US Army Corps of Engineers for large-scale mechanical work. Judd began adapting the two structures in 1980, replacing their garage doors with quartered glass windows of his own design and adding curved Quonset hut-style roofs that doubled the buildings' exterior height. He finalized the placement of the 100 aluminum works in 1986, the year the Chinati Foundation was established.
The restoration will repair the roofs, gutters, and facades and introduce more than 10,000 square feet of energy-efficient glass to provide additional protection for the artworks from Marfa's extreme weather conditions. The project will also improve accessibility through updated paths and access points and introduce rainwater harvesting systems to support native grasses and the surrounding Chihuahuan Desert landscape.
Related Article
Stefano Boeri Architetti Converts Former Rome Transit Depot Into Multifunctional Civic Space
The project team is working to limit interventions that could alter the relationship between Judd's works and their architectural setting. "The real ingenuity of the restoration is maintaining Donald Judd's vision and editing around the edges," said Troy Schaum, describing an approach that incorporates low-energy mechanical systems and other discreet interventions into the existing buildings.
As part of the restoration, Judd's 100 aluminum works will be moved for the first time since their installation in the 1980s. The works will undergo extensive documentation and material analysis before being reinstalled after construction. Chinati's conservation team, led by Head of Conservation Bogna Skwara, is working with Alfred Lippincott, co-owner of Lippincott's LLC and one of the original fabricators of the works, as well as the Getty Conservation Institute.
The restoration forms part of Chinati's Art as Intended capital campaign, to support collection stewardship, infrastructure improvements, visitor experience, and long-term financial sustainability. The 39th annual Chinati Weekend, taking place October 9–11, 2026, will be among the final opportunities to view the Artillery Sheds and Judd's installation before construction begins. The buildings will remain closed to visitors throughout the multi-year restoration, while other permanent installations across the Chinati site will continue to be accessible.

In Turin, MVRDV and Balance Architettura have unveiled their proposal to renovate the 1959 Civic Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art (GAM), introducing flexible exhibition systems and publicly accessible storage while restoring the museum's connection to the city. Meanwhile, Stefano Boeri Architetti will transform Rome's former Depositi delle Vittorie transport depot into a mixed-use complex combining cultural, educational, commercial, and leisure spaces with new public areas and landscaping.

Putin adviser raises attacks on British drone factories
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:25:18 BST
15:25:18 KST

An adviser to President Putin has said British factories producing drones for Ukraine could be attacked by what he called unknown sources, as part of a possible Russian response to UK military support for Kyiv, in an interview with BBC Newsnight.
Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian deputy foreign minister who advises the Kremlin, was speaking to Adam Fleming on the programme on Monday. Asked what a semi-military response might involve, he said: “For example, something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine, etc, etc.”
Pressed on whether he meant British factories in Britain being attacked militarily by Russia, he said: “They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources.”
Fedorov said pressure was building on Putin to act against the United Kingdom, telling the programme: “There’s a very serious political and public pressure on President Putin today, to undertake certain measures against UK, because he is considering UK as part of the war in Ukraine, and assistance from the UK is considered as a direct involvement of UK in this war.”
Asked where that pressure came from, he said: “It’s coming from the public opinion polls, it’s coming from journalists, from mass media, it is coming from military. And UK, of course, as considered in the context of Ukraine, is evil Number 1.”
He said Putin had described current developments as the opening of Pandora’s box, and that there had been a very negative reaction in the Kremlin.
On what form a response might take, Fedorov told the programme: “In the coming future we will face a new stage of escalation, in the Ukrainian conflict, and sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK.”
He said the options under discussion included a technical reaction, possibly a hacker attack from an unofficial source, along with political steps, and that he could not entirely exclude something semi-military.
Asked whether he personally would be content with such an attack, he said he would not, adding: “The problem is that we are now facing, in front of the danger, that Ukrainian conflict will be beyond Ukrainian borders. And remembering that UK is a member of NATO, and UK is a nuclear state, the risk is, of course, much higher than it was before, even a couple of months ago.”
Challenged on how such an attack could be justified under international law, he said: “Frankly speaking, who cares today about international law?” He said many in Russian society believed the president had waited too long to answer the UK.
On cyber targets, he said a hacker attack would be directed at a specific enterprise or system rather than broadly, and confirmed when asked that this would mean something governmental, security or military related, “especially to production of the drones or some components for Storm Shadow missiles.”
Fedorov linked the Kremlin’s assessment directly to the transfer of missile blueprints, saying the step meant that from Moscow’s point of view Britain was much more involved, and that a system capable of producing missiles, whether Storm Shadow or a Ukrainian modification, would be considerably more effective than what came before.
He described Moscow as considering the actions of the British Prime Minister as direct military involvement in the conflict.
On the domestic picture, Fedorov acknowledged that fuel queues and Ukrainian strikes on warehouses, including those belonging to the online retailers Wildberries and Ozon, were having an effect, but said he could not say public opinion had changed seriously. He noted that parliamentary elections are due on the 18th or 20th of September and that the war is regarded as a consolidating factor for them.
Put to him that anti-war parties had been blocked from standing, he confirmed that Yabloko had been kicked out of the race.
Fedorov holds no current government office, and his remarks carry no official standing. Figures of his kind are used periodically to place a position in the public domain without the Kremlin owning it, and the construction he uses, attacks carried out not by Russia but by unknown sources, is the same formula applied to the sabotage of undersea cables, arson at warehouses across Europe and parcel bombs placed on cargo aircraft.
British defence manufacturing sites have been treated as a protective security concern for some time. MI5 has warned repeatedly about Russian sabotage plots on British soil, and several prosecutions have followed attacks on premises linked to Ukraine, including an arson at a warehouse in Leyton in east London in 2024 for which men were convicted under the National Security Act.
The interview was broadcast on BBC Newsnight on 24 August.

UK, EU missions in Dhaka stress Rohingya right to return to Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:21:59 UTC
15:21:59 KST

Sm Najmus Sakib
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
On the ninth anniversary of the mass exodus of Rohingya to Bangladesh, 16 diplomatic missions, including those of the UK, Australia, Canada, and the EU, in Dhaka on Tuesday recalled the Rohingya's right to return to their home country, Myanmar.
Bangladesh has been sheltering about 1.2 million persecuted Rohingya on the southeastern Cox’s Bazar coast after they fled a brutal Myanmar military crackdown and started crossing the border on Aug. 25, 2017.
However, nine years after the mass exodus, conflict is escalating across Rakhine and humanitarian needs are rising, according to the foreign missions’ joint statement.
“Deepening insecurity, airstrikes on civilian infrastructure and the Myanmar authorities’ blockades on aid and trade are worsening the humanitarian crisis,” the statement said, marking Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day, observed on Aug. 25.
This instability is driving further displacement into Bangladesh, and across the region, leading to tragic loss of life through dangerous sea crossings, it said, adding that these conditions do not currently allow for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable repatriation.
They said conditions for Rohingya return will require a strategic, coordinated, and long-term approach to address the root causes of displacement, build trust between communities, and support greater peace and stability in Myanmar.
They also said they will continue to work with Bangladesh to find pathways toward building the conditions for repatriation.
“As this crisis enters its tenth year, we must ensure that the Rohingya people are not forgotten. We will continue to amplify the voices of Rohingya communities, pursue justice and accountability, and work with Bangladesh and international partners to sustain global support,” the statement added.

Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:10:49 UTC
15:10:49 KST

Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
A newly-formed committee has signed a preliminary agreement, but divided state institutions and legal voids threaten its execution.
Libyan negotiators have agreed to an initial election pact aimed at ending years of political divisions within the country.
The agreement covers electoral laws and the restructuring of the national elections commission, moving the process toward a highly complex and delicate implementation phase, experts and officials told Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Can US, Middle Eastern powers unite Libya 15 years after Gaddafi overthrow?
- list 2 of 4One geography, two states: Saudi Arabia’s security approach to Sudan
- list 3 of 4Libya rivals test a new path towards unity, 15 years after Gadaffi downfall
- list 4 of 4Libya’s brain drain, 15 years after Tripoli fell
Since 2014, Libya has been divided between two bitterly opposed administrations that separately control the east and west of the country, with repeated United Nations-led efforts to end the crisis.
Current negotiations have been conducted by a committee consisting of four representatives from the House of Representatives, based in eastern Libya, and four representatives from the High Council of State, linked to the internationally-recognised Government of National Unity in Tripoli.
The United Nations-backed ‘4+4 committee’ signed the initial draft in Tunis on August 20, with the challenge now in getting other parties in Libya on board.
Legal expert Al-Mahdi Kashbour told Al Jazeera that there appears to be a gap between the powers of the parties that signed the agreement and the institutions with the authority to implement it.
Libya political analyst Elias Al-Barouni stressed that the pact does not make any concrete plans for the country’s elections. Even if legal hurdles are cleared, the problem then shifts to who governs Libya in the interim, he added.
This could be the most difficult test yet for the peace process, as the transitional authority would control state resources and have to navigate a highly sensitive security environment.
Key Libyan legislative bodies and politicians have strong reservations about the negotiations. Among them is Nuh al-Malati, a member of the High Council of State, an advisory body for the Government of National Unity.
“The council has not yet received an official copy of the agreement that was reached… these changes do not enjoy consensus within the council,” he told Al Jazeera.
Al-Malati claimed that the Government of National Unity-linked members of the ‘4+4’ do not represent the official position of the council.
Mohamed al-Menfi, the leader of the Tripoli-based presidential council, also criticised the ambiguity surrounding the basis of the talks.
“The success of any consensus is linked to the clarity of its basis, its jurisdictions, and its applicability, especially when it comes to sovereign institutions like the elections commission,” al-Menfi wrote on X.
There appears to be equal scepticism about the arrangement from members of the eastern authority.
Khalifa al-Daghari, a member of the House of Representatives, told Al Jazeera that lawmakers in this grouping did not participate in choosing negotiating team members.
“[They] followed the details of the committee’s meetings and the course of its talks through the media and official statements, without receiving any direct briefing on what took place in them or their outcomes,” he added.
He also claimed there was “secrecy over its proceedings”, and that the House of Representatives “cannot therefore determine its position on the agreement before officially reviewing its text and outcomes”.
Still, United Nations spokesman Mohammad al-Asadi told Al Jazeera that the pact was an “important step and a conclusion to the negotiations on all points under discussion”.
Amid criticism over the alleged secrecy of the negotiations, al-Asadi said the document will be made publicly available after the final signing.

China’s new traffic safety law set to clarify liability for fully automated cars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:03:45 UTC
15:03:45 KST

China’s new traffic safety law set to clarify liability for fully automated cars
Lawmakers are set to establish clear liability standards for self-driving cars, a move that could open the floodgates for next-gen vehicles
Beijing could soon hold carmakers legally responsible for traffic violations when autonomous driving systems are in use, marking an important step towards clearing regulatory hurdles to wider commercialisation.
“The definitions of autonomous vehicles and driver-assistance functions would be clarified in the amendments,” Xinhua reported, without revealing when the revised law would enter into force.
Self-driving systems switched off during a journey would remain subject to existing rules and laws, according to Xinhua, while analysts noted that carmakers could be held accountable for accidents and traffic rule violations when such systems were activated in a vehicle legally recognised as autonomous.
“As they are required to shoulder the responsibilities for the cars’ operations on the roads, automotive companies will also be allowed to build and sell cars of this kind to attract consumers,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst based in Shanghai.
“When the amended law is promulgated, dozens of new autonomous models will hit the streets.”

Last November, Lloyds Bank informed me, in my role as treasurer of my parish church, that the church account was to be closed and that I should open a new business account instead. This can only be done online, but a fault with their system prevented me – and local branch staff – from doing so.
At the branch staff’s suggestion, I opened the new account with a different bank in early March. Since then, I’ve been trying in vain to get Lloyds to transfer the balance from the closed account.
I’ve been repeatedly told to visit my local branch and repeatedly told that the money would arrive within weeks. At one point I was told that the bank had lost my identity verification documents and so had put the case at the bottom of the pile.
We are owed nearly £5,500, which, for a congregation of 10 in a village of 60 houses, is a significant sum. We have had to borrow from parishioners to pay for essential repairs and to settle the electricity bill.
CI, Yorkshire
The apparent indifference of Lloyds is outrageous. As was its energy spurt when it realised public exposure was pending.
As soon as I questioned its inertia, it winged off a mea culpa acknowledging poor and inconsistent communications and offering £400 in goodwill, plus £96 in lost interest.
What the letter from the executive complaints manager did not mention was the still-missing funds.
So back I had to go to Lloyds, and off went another letter from the bank apologising for the omission.
The money was transferred more than four months after the account was closed.
A Lloyds spokesperson said: “We’re sorry the customer had such a difficult experience. We should have handled things better.”

Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.
“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, wrote last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming.
As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Studies, media outlets and website owners alike are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.
Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”
We want to hear from you. Do you think Google’s infusion of AI has made its search engine better or worse?

Australia’s music charts ban AI-made songs amid backlash over Madonna cover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:00:38 UTC
15:00:38 KST

Australia’s music charts ban AI-made songs amid backlash over Madonna cover
Tracks that use AI in a ‘supporting role’ will still be eligible for inclusion in the official charts.
Australia’s official music charts have banned tracks mostly created by artificial intelligence (AI) following a backlash over a cover of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” that relied heavily on the burgeoning technology.
“Wholly AI-generated” music will be excluded from the charts under the changes, while tracks that use AI in a “supporting role” will still be eligible, the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said on Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
- list 2 of 4US plans to revoke business, tourism visas of 200,000 asylum seekers
- list 3 of 4Brutal gang attack on strategic Haiti hillside leaves at least 30 dead
- list 4 of 4Man killed in world’s largest annual bullfighting event in Mexico
AI-generated music will also not be considered for recognition at the annual ARIA Music Awards under the new rules, which are set to take effect on Friday.
ARIA said it would rely on a labelling system introduced by music industry groups last month to distinguish AI-generated tracks from those that use AI to complement human creativity.
Under the labelling rules announced by a coalition of organisations including the Recording Industry Association of America, tracks may be labelled “AI-Generated” or “AI-Assisted” depending on the level of human involvement in the writing and recording process.
Tracks are classed as “AI-Generated” if AI was used to create the “entirety or the primary portion of the creative elements of the recording” and “AI-Assisted” if the technology was used only for “some expressive elements”.
ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said while the music charts should evolve to reflect the legitimate use of AI, they should not recognise music generated “wholesale” by technology that relies on other artists’ work.
“These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is – to say the least – a rapidly developing space,” Herd said in a statement.
ARIA, whose members include major music labels such as Sony Music Entertainment Australia and Universal Music Australia, publishes more than two dozen weekly music charts in Australia, including the top 50 singles and top 50 albums.
The industry association’s decision comes after a Brisbane-based DJ’s chart-topping cover of Madonna’s 1989 hit Like a Prayer attracted a backlash over its use of AI-generated vocals and drums.
Josh Fawaz last month belatedly acknowledged using AI on the track after music fans and producers raised suspicions that it was not produced by a human.
The cover has racked up more than 48.5 million listens on music streaming platform Spotify and currently ranks number one on the ARIA Top 20 Australian Dance Singles Chart.
Fawaz, who has defended the use of AI as a “tool” in his music, described ARIA’s new rules as a “great move”.
“I understand that AI in music isn’t for everyone and that’s fine. Good to see Aussie artists killing it globally!!” Fawaz wrote in a social media post responding to the announcement.
Oliver Bown, an associate professor at the University of New South Wales who researches the relationship between technology and art, said the impact of AI on creative industries such as music demands urgent attention.
“Many large commercial AI music generation companies have assumed they can scrape training data without permission, and so are potentially predatory on artists,” Bown told Al Jazeera.
“I believe people can do great artistic work using AI respectfully, but there is also a predatory phenomenon whereby you can just go fishing for plays and profits,” he added.
“Many organisations have developed rules about AI use and an increasing number see the need to ban full-AI works. I think this is the right thing to do.”
Ivan Zavada, a senior lecturer in composition and music technology at the University of Sydney, said the changes have been widely viewed as a “necessary step” to protect “genuine human musical creativity and performance”.
“More work needs to be done on the legal and intellectual property fronts to enable more trust and clarity in these tools,” Zavada told Al Jazeera.
“AI will be an essential part of standard music production in the very near future. We are living a very exciting yet concerning transition period in the digital and electronic arts.”

Omega Just Released a Mini Moonwatch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

I have skinny wrists. So skinny, in fact, that during the craze from the late 1990s to early 2010s, when watch cases started to tip over 48 mm, it became hard to find pieces that suited those of us not blessed (or cursed) with Schwarzenegger-sized forearms. Thankfully, watch case sizes have calmed down considerably since then, and now it's easy to find smaller models, particularly around that 38- to 40-mm Goldilocks zone.
This brings us neatly to Omega's latest collection of Speedmasters, all of which come in that ideal 38-mm size. The seven references in new color variations have been tweaked to improve the existing 38-mm Speedy collection. The most notable improvement? The oval subdials have been banished in favor of proper rounded versions seen on the Moonwatch. The bezels have also been overhauled in Moonwatch style and are now thicker with the essential Dot-Over-Ninety.
Across the new collection, two self-winding movements power the pieces. The Caliber 3330 powers the six references with date functions, including a $11,700 “cappuccino” style version with an ivory-color main dial, contrasting brown PVD-coated subdials, a stainless steel case, and an 18K Sedna gold bezel.
It's the seventh Black Dial reference with no date that's the pick of the bunch, however, powered by the Caliber 3332. Omega positions the $6,500 watch as much more “closely aligned with the signature look of the Moonwatch,” which it certainly is, compared to the existing black 38-mm model with a date window and inferior bezel design.
The reduced sizing, clean, uncluttered black matte-finish varnished dial, Moonwatch-style five-link bracelet, and much-improved black aluminum bezel bring to mind the classic Speedmaster Reduced from the late 1980s. A friend of mine has a Reduced, and I have coveted it for years as, when I see it, it always looks the perfect size on the wrist.
Launched in 1988, the Speedmaster Reduced had an ideal 38.5-mm case size, rather than the 38 mm in this new model. Other subtle differences include the crown position on the Reduced, which is lower and visibly offset from the pushers, and the bezel doesn't have the Dot-Over-Ninety, either.
The biggest giveaway that this is not a faithful reissue of the Reduced is that the subdials are in different positions. On the Reduced, the layout was running seconds at 3, 12-hour totalizer at 6, and 30-minute totalizer at 9. On this 38 mm, it's reversed, with the 30-minute totalizer at 3, and running seconds at 9, just as on the larger Moonwatch.
So perhaps it's best to think of this enticingly sized new 38-mm black Speedy as a “mini Moonwatch,” as it shares more design cues with the iconic Speedmaster, even if its diminutive dimensions conjure up memories of the Reduced models from the ’80s. Either way, the 38-mm’s price makes it the cheapest black-dial “Moonwatch” Speedmaster now available, which is most welcome—and it's a rare thing indeed to be rewarded for having skinny wrists.

Attacks by illegal Israeli settlers across the occupied West Bank surged 63 percent from January through July compared with the same period last year, a Palestinian government agency said on Monday.
The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said it recorded 4,113 attacks during the seven-month period, up from 2,524 a year earlier, an increase of 1,589 incidents.
The commission said the surge coincided with the expansion of illegal settlement outposts, particularly pastoral ones, as well as the arming of illegal Israeli settlers and the incorporation of some into security formations.
It also cited Israeli military protection and declining accountability as factors behind the rise.
The agency said weak international deterrence and accountability had helped turn attacks by illegal Israeli settlers from isolated incidents into an organised tool to impose new realities on the ground and push Palestinian communities towards displacement.
On Saturday, the commission said the occupied West Bank had 592 illegal Israeli settlements and outposts, while Israel unlawfully controlled about 42 percent of the territory.
It put the number of illegal Israeli settlers living in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, at around 780,000 as of the end of July, comprising 333,600 in settlements in East Jerusalem and 446,400 elsewhere in the occupied West Bank.
Attacks by the Israeli forces and illegal settlers in the occupied West Bank since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza have killed 1,182 Palestinians and injured more than 12,000 others, while around 24,000 have been arrested, according to official Palestinian figures.

China’s anti-corruption legal framework is about to extend beyond its borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

China’s anti-corruption legal framework is about to extend beyond its borders
A draft law aimed at combating cross-border corruption has been submitted for its first reading by the country’s top legislature
On Tuesday, the draft Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law was submitted for its first reading during the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People’s Congress (NPC), which runs until Friday.
The text of the bill is not yet available to the public.
Enacting the law is a vital initiative to complete China’s foreign-related legal framework, protect national interests, promote compliant overseas business growth and “enrich the legal ‘toolbox’ for fugitive repatriation, asset recovery and handling foreign-related corruption cases”, according to state news agency Xinhua.
The law codifies a decade of anti-corruption practices to close jurisdictional loopholes and target offshore financial crimes, aiming to resolve long-standing systemic hurdles, specifically the “difficulty in detecting, collecting evidence, repatriating illicit assets” and prosecuting offshore offences, it said.
Comprising six chapters and 47 articles, the draft law establishes key principles, scope and national positioning regarding corruption abroad.

World shares mostly gain and oil prices slip as the US raises pressure on Iran
BANGKOK (AP) — Shares were mostly higher Tuesday in Europe and Asia after U.S. stocks drifted to a mixed finish ahead of potentially market-moving events later in the week.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.7% to 9,164.60.
Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 0.9%, while the Sensex in India lost 0.2%.
On Monday, areas of the bond market that the U.S. Treasury Department has been trying to calm eased a bit, relieving pressure on stocks.
The S&P 500 slipped 0.3%, while the Dow industrials added 0.3%. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.8%.
Tech stocks led the decline. They’ve had big swings recently due to worries that the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology has sent prices too high and huge demand for AI chips will falter if AI doesn’t yield enough profits.
Chip giant Nvidia, a tremendous winner of the AI boom, lost 2.9% on Monday. It will deliver its quarterly earnings report on Wednesday and that could dictate the next big move for AI-related stocks. Micron Technology lost 5.8% and Broadcom fell 2.6%.
In the bond market, the yield of the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.69% from 4.74% late Friday, returning to where it was last week before the U.S. Treasury Department announced a surprise move to increase the size of its planned buybacks of Treasurys.
Longer-term Treasury yields climbed through the summer on worries about high inflation, huge government debts and other factors. High yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow, not just the government, and already have pushed up mortgage rates and hurt the housing industry.
“The latest discussion about using Treasury General Account cash to help finance purchases of longer-dated bonds gave the market something to chew on Monday, and it initially liked the taste. Long yields fell, and the curve flattened,” Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management said in a commentary.
“But there is a difference between forcing the bond market to blink for an afternoon and solving the underlying problem,” he said.
The Federal Reserve’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, is set to deliver a speech Friday at an annual economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, the backdrop for past policy announcements.
Analysts say Warsh is likely to talk about inflation and how the Fed plans to deal with it.
Oil prices are a major factor behind higher costs and Brent crude, the international standard, has been trading above the $72 per barrel level it was at before the war with Iran began in late February.
Early Tuesday, Brent crude fell 2% to $88.74 per barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil shed 2.2% to $83.14 per barrel.
Last month, Brent zigzagged between $72 and $102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. The new U.S. sanctions announced Monday helped drag the value of Iran’s currency, the rial, to a record low against the U.S. dollar.
In other dealings, the U.S. dollar rose to 159.30 Japanese yen from 159.10 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1670, up from $1.1667.

Hsinchu Zoo earns environmental education certification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:48:46 UTC
14:48:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hsinchu Zoo is turning its historic landmarks and everyday activities into opportunities for environmental education, from a Japanese-designed entrance gate to postcards made from hippopotamus droppings.
The zoo recently received certification as an environmental education facility, becoming the second zoo in Taiwan to earn the designation after Taipei Zoo. Under Taiwan’s Environmental Education Act, certified facilities provide environmental education through trained staff, educational programs, and other organized activities, according to Friendly Seed.
The National Environmental Research Academy said the certification recognizes the zoo’s role in connecting environmental education with Hsinchu’s history. Founded in 1936, Hsinchu Zoo is Taiwan’s oldest zoo still operating at its original site. Taipei Zoo, founded in 1914, moved from Yuanshan to its current location in Muzha in 1986, according to the Ministry of Environment.
Among the zoo’s most recognizable landmarks is its entrance gate. Designed by a Japanese architect and modeled on the entrance to Hagenbeck Zoo in Germany, the gate features cast-iron sculptures that remain intact and have become a symbol of Hsinchu Zoo’s history.
The grounds also contain one of the world’s few remaining hemispherical aviaries. Built in 1936, the structure once housed pink-backed pelicans and grey herons. Today, the former aviary has been converted into a children’s playground, according to AJ Travel.
Another historic feature is a stone monument erected in 1921. Its front bears an inscription meaning “infinite life,” written by Li Yi-qiao (李逸樵), a well-known Hsinchu calligrapher at the time. The inscription on the back conveys the idea that all things eventually return to emptiness, according to the Bureau of Cultural Heritage.
The zoo has also developed an environmental education course that turns one of its waste products—hippopotamus droppings—into postcards. After the plant-fiber-rich material undergoes high-temperature disinfection, participants knead it and shape it into postcards with a grassy scent.

Fire severely damages hall at Taipei’s Zhinan Temple
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:48:29 UTC
14:48:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A major fire severely damaged the Lingxiao Hall of Taipei’s Zhinan Temple in Wenshan District late Monday, with firefighters battling the blaze for more than four hours before extinguishing it shortly after midnight.
No injuries were reported. The fire broke out at about 8 p.m. Monday and was extinguished just after midnight, according to the Taipei City Fire Department. The blaze was concentrated on the first and second floors of the three-story Lingxiao Hall, which contains extensive wooden materials and flammable decorations, per UDN.
More than 100 firefighters and emergency personnel were mobilized, along with 34 fire and emergency vehicles. Firefighters also used drones to monitor the blaze and drew water from a pool at the temple to maintain their supply because of the temple’s mountainous location and limited access to water.
The first floor of the hall was almost completely destroyed, while about one-third of the second floor was damaged. A preliminary assessment found minor cracking around a stairwell, but officials said the main structural frame was undamaged and the building remained structurally safe.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) inspected the site Tuesday morning and thanked firefighters and volunteer firefighters for their efforts. He said the lack of casualties was fortunate and pledged city government assistance with the temple’s recovery and reconstruction, per CNA.
Chiang ordered the formation of a cross-department task force to assist with the restoration process. The city will conduct a structural safety assessment after the fire investigation and determine which portions of the building should be preserved and which may need to be removed. Officials will also document the site’s historical and cultural features before reconstruction begins.
“Zhinan Temple is one of Taipei’s most iconic temples,” Chiang said, adding that it holds memories for many residents and worshippers. He pledged that the city government would work alongside the temple throughout the restoration and reconstruction process.
Zhinan Temple was established in the late Qing Dynasty and is one of Taipei’s best-known Taoist temples. The temple complex includes several major halls and is located near Zhinan Temple Station on the Maokong Gondola.
Temple Chair Kao Chao-wen (高超文) said the temple would not close following the fire. Only Lingxiao Hall has been cordoned off, while visitors can continue to worship at the main hall and Daxiong Hall. Access routes have been adjusted to keep visitors away from the damaged area, per CNA.
Temple officials are expected to discuss a restoration and reconstruction schedule as the investigation and structural assessment proceed. The Taipei City Government describes the temple as an important religious and cultural landmark.

Japan’s famous bonfire monkey zoo to close for major revamp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:47:55 KST

Japan’s famous bonfire monkey zoo to close for major revamp
During the closure, the zoo plans to use social media to post updates on its 700 monkeys and hold members-only events
Home to about 700 monkeys of around 50 species, the facility in Inuyama, Aichi prefecture, will open only on weekends and holidays from September, and close its gates from October 19. During the closure, it plans to use social media to post updates on the monkeys and hold events open only to registered members.
The zoo’s iconic bonfires date back to 1959, three years after it opened with funding from Nagoya Railroad, when staff burned trees that had fallen in a massive typhoon and resident monkeys were seen gathering around the fire.
It later became the first facility in Japan to keep mountain gorillas. Working with partners, including Kyoto University’s Institute for the Evolutionary Origins of Human Behaviour, it is regarded as one of the world’s leading primate care and research facilities.
Since 2014, the zoo has been run by a Kyoto University-linked non-profit foundation. Operating costs have been covered by admission fees and donations solicited under the name “Goshien” – a Japanese play on words combining “support” and “monkey”.

AfD could take power in German state for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:47:01 UTC
14:47:01 KST

Joerg Urban, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state of Saxony, speaks to voters at an AfD campaign rally prior to state elections in Saxony-Anhalt on Aug. 24, 2026 in Naumburg, Germany. (Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
Germany is preparing for the possibility that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) could lead a state government for the first time, as the party holds a wide polling lead ahead of the Sept. 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt.
About 1.7 million people are eligible to vote in the eastern state.
Recent polls put the AfD at between 41 and 43 percent, well ahead of the governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which stands at between 22 and 24 percent.
With several smaller parties polling close to Germany’s 5-percent electoral threshold, that level of support could give the AfD an outright majority of seats, although the outcome remains uncertain.
If the party secures enough seats to govern alone, its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund could become Germany’s first AfD state premier since the party was founded in 2013.
The prospect has prompted federal and state officials to consider how an AfD-led administration should be handled in sensitive areas, particularly intelligence sharing.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified by the state’s domestic intelligence service as a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization.
The party rejects the designation and is challenging it in court.
Thuringia Interior Minister Georg Maier has called for an AfD-led administration to be denied access to intelligence concerning right-wing extremist groups and counterespionage.
Maier said a state could not be excluded entirely from Germany’s joint intelligence network but argued that internal barriers could be introduced to restrict access to certain information.
He cited security concerns over the AfD’s contacts with Russia.
An AfD state premier would also participate in meetings of Germany’s 16 state leaders and their talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Saxony-Anhalt is scheduled to assume the rotating chair of the Conference of Minister-Presidents in October, although it remains unclear whether a new state government will be formed by then.
The election will also test Germany’s political “firewall,” under which other parties rule out coalitions or structured cooperation with the AfD. With no prospective coalition partner, the party’s route to government largely depends on winning enough seats to govern alone.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel criticized the firewall during an interview with public broadcaster ZDF on Aug. 23, calling it “the most undemocratic thing there is.”
Weidel said the AfD would enter government first at the state level and later nationally.
She also backed closing Germany’s borders and leaving the Schengen Area, defended her party’s position favoring an exit from the euro and rejected further measures targeting climate change.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt campaign calls for a “180-degree turn” in migration policy, including tighter deportation rules and greater use of detention pending removal.
