‘Grain’ revolution: How lost varieties of rice are coming back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:44:23 UTC
14:44:23 KST

Decades after disappearing from Indian fields and kitchens, heirloom paddy is making a comeback.
Biryani made with Kaima instead of Basmati, payesh made with Badshahbhog, risotto made with Assam’s Bora. With heirloom rice vanishing from Indian kitchens faster than they could be documented, this seemed, until not very long ago, nothing more than nostalgia. The Green Revolution’s push for high-yield monoculture had, over the years, pushed out many old types of rice. But now, several of those varieties, thought long gone, are staging a comeback — thanks to the efforts of farmers, conservationists, NGOs, restaurateurs, and a bit of help from some state govts.
Guardians of the grain
In coastal Karnataka’s Nettanige village, Padma Shri awardee Sathyanarayana Beleri — everyone calls him ‘Seeding Sathya’ — nurtures more than 100 traditional paddy varieties in grow bags outside his house. It’s a small selection from his vast collection of over 650 seed varieties, collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.He has strains of flood-resistant Edekunhi and Nereguli, the medicinal Dodda Byra Nellu, and Kalanamak (also called ‘Buddha Rice’). He’s distributed seeds to hundreds of farmers across Karnataka and Kerala, as well as to agricultural universities nationwide. “Rice”, he says, “can be cultivated in grow bags, just like vegetables at home.
As climate change reshapes agriculture, conserving traditional, climate-resilient varieties is no longer a choice. It is a necessity.”
Sathyanarayana Beleri with some of the more than 650 seed varieties he has collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.
Further inland, entire families have turned conservation into a generational commitment. In Belthangady taluk, the Rao family has conserved 180-190 traditional varieties on 5.5 acres since B K Deva Rao started a seed bank in 1988. His son, Parameshwar Rao, points to a benefit beyond biodiversity. “Paddy cultivation is among the best forms of groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting,” he says. “Strong field bunds can retain water for nearly a week. Even two cropping cycles can substantially improve the groundwater table.” Their prized variety, Kayame — a red rice — “has a flavour rarely found in modern commercial varieties,” he adds.Some 1,300km away in Chhattisgarh, Khemlal Dewangan, a maths teacher in Rajnandgaon district, started farming traditional paddy around 15 years ago. Dewangan started with a handful of desi strains. He now has a collection of around 70 varieties.His seed collection has grown through a nationwide network of farmers — brought together on WhatsApp — who test small quantities in their fields. “I now receive 10-15 enquiries a day from social media and word of mouth,” he says.For him, the appeal goes beyond the market: he says traditional varieties are healthier, as they take longer to mature, absorbing more soil nutrients.
Roots of a revival
None of this happened by accident. Back in 2004, the UN’s second International Year of Rice, Kerala-based NGO Thanal decided something had to be done about India’s vanishing rice varieties. They launched the Save Our Rice campaign through a workshop in Kumbalangi village. Thanal teamed up with Tamil Nadu’s CREATE (a non-profit organisation) to run it, and the campaign took root in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Bengal, later spreading into Chhattisgarh.
Members of CREATE educate farmers about heirloom rice varieties on a farm in Tamil Nadu.
India had over one lakh varieties of rice in 1966, but by the time the campaign started, that number had dropped to around 30,000 — most locked away in university seed banks, rather than growing in farmers’ fields. The campaign has had a big impact on southern states. “In the last 15-16 years, there has been a revival of traditional seeds in these states,” says Jayakumar C, executive director at Thanal. “Today, there are more than 25 or 30 farmers or groups doing traditional seeds in different parts of Kerala. Thanal’s own centre in Wayanad now holds around 320- 330 varieties of rice.”That demand has started showing up in the market. Thanal runs a regular shop now in Thiruvananthapuram. Jayakumar says Kaima (also called Jeerakasala or Jeeraga Samba), a traditional variety, has become popular for biryani. Brands have caught on, too. Thondi, from a Wayanad farmer-producer company, sells online and via courier across Kerala’s cities, even as Mappila Chamba has built a following.“Traditional rice tends to be more filling,” says Jayakumar. You feel full after eating less, unlike white rice hybrids. Also, the longer shelf life and taste after cooking is winning over urban households, especially the older people.”
When state stepped in
In Tamil Nadu, govt push gave the revival momentum. According to Suresh Kanna, project director at CREATE Trust, state govt began promoting six native varieties some 10 years ago under the State Heritage Rice Mission: Mappillai Samba, Karuppu Kavuni, Thooyamalli, Poongar, Kaattuyaanam and Kichili Samba. “Today, they are liked by consumers and can be seen in organic shops across the state. They also fetch good income for the farmers. A Kavuni farmer can get up to Rs 200 for a kilo. My calculation is that more than one lakh farmers in the state are now cultivating traditional paddy varieties,” Kanna says.Even in Karnataka, grassroots efforts are now finding institutional backing. KVK Dakshina Kannada has begun field trials of 10 traditional varieties sourced from Beleri, aiming to identify strains suited to the coastal region, and reintroduce them into local food systems. Karnataka’s agriculture department has documented 2,164 traditional landraces (local, traditional varieties that evolved through natural and human selection to adapt to a specific geographic and climatic environment) across 20 crops, with paddy topping the list at 1,469 varieties, under its Conservation and Promotion of Landraces Programme. Rs 1.3 crore in incentives went to 490 farmers in 2025-26 for viable seed samples. The effort centres on custodian farmers who “continued cultivating them on small patches of land,” as department director GT Puthra puts it.The department is now supporting GI registration for varieties including Kagga paddy, Rajmudi paddy, Bijapur Jola, Joni Bella and Kumbi Mudli, and plans incentives for 15 “forgotten treasure” shops.
Farm to fork, fork to fame
A few restaurants are actively championing rare, indigenous rice over commercial varieties. Edible Archives in Goa works with regional grains like Thavala Kannan from Wayanad (a red rice from Palakkad, whose name means “frog’s eyes” in Malayalam), and Pokkali, which brings a distinct coastal terroir.The Kolkata-based Amar Khamar, both a heritage-grain retail brand and restaurant, is entirely built around Bengal’s native rice. Its signature is ‘Chhuti-r Bhat’, an 11-course meal following the traditional sequence of a Bengali meal, centred on heirloom varieties like Sugondhi Chine Kamini Aatap.
‘Chhuti-r Bhat’ in Kolkata’s Amar Khamar, which is an 11-course meal centred on heirloom rice varieties.
That influence has spread to other restaurants in the city. Sienna Cafe sources Chine Kamini, Radha Tilok, Kanakchur and Tulaipanji Atop from Amar Khamar; Yokocho, a Japanese alleyway-inspired bar and BBQ, draws on Kanakchur, Tulaipanji Atop and Karpurkanti; Red Bari incorporates Shatia, Mallifulo and Khejur Chhari.Juhi Punwani, head of kitchen operations at Amar Khamar, has built a career around collecting the many myths and stories behind Bengal’s native rice varieties. “Gobindobhog is not the only heritage rice in Bengal,” she says. A rice called Radhuni Pagol literally means “the cook gone crazy”, after lore that its fragrance once filled a kitchen so completely that the cook couldn’t think of anything else.Tulaipanji of North Bengal gets its name from how the cooked rice turns light and airy like cotton (tula); Khejur Chhari is named for the date palm its grains resemble; Radha Tilok’s dark-tipped grain evokes Radha’s tilak mark. “Every rice here has a beautiful story and a journey, and that’s what we’re trying to showcase,” says Punwani, whose team has worked to bring back over 100 varieties, keeping around 50 in active rotation.
A look at select traditional rice varieties and the regions they are associated with across India.
This past summer, that ambition crossed continents, as Amar Khamar toured France and Germany. In Paris, working with sommelier Rajat Parr, the team built an 80-guest, 10-course tasting menu entirely around rice. Kanakchur turned up as fritters with brown butter hollandaise, Sundarbansgrown Karpurkanti and Chine Kamini appeared as aatapan alongside a jackfruit-seed mung dal, Barddhaman’s Mohansal was served boiled, the meal closing with a Jhargram Fine Black Rice phirni.In Stuttgart, the team built a fully vegan Bengali tasting menu, rice carrying the meal from a humble jhal muri to a coconut-milk Badshahbhog payesh for dessert. A separate 200-guest winery event tested whether the format could scale — from Karpurkanti-paired lentils, a Chine Kamini peas pulao to Sunday lamb curry and Badshahbhog milk-rice. “None of this would be possible without the relationships we have built with a network of farmers,” says Punwani, who executed the menu in Europe.
The traceability problem
But as heritage rice travels from the farm into retail shelves, a different problem emerges: knowing whether what’s being sold is really what it claims to be. One store has built its entire business around solving exactly that. In Chennai’s Mylapore sits a store unlike any other. Spirit of the Earth calls itself a “retail store and experience centre”, where customers come to see, touch, feel and know the story of every rice. Opened in 2017, it’s the retail face of a project that Sheela Balaji, chairperson of NGO AIM For Seva, began over a decade ago, built on a principle she believes the heritage-rice surge often misses: traceability.“Unfortunately, certain grains are being sold as certain varieties, which is inaccurate,” says Balaji.“The minute you say heritage rice, people will just come and buy it. But who is taking accountability? How do you know if it’s really diabetic friendly? So, I started this project more than a decade ago, first and foremost by building a seed bank. All the rice that you see in our store is grown from our farm in Manjakkudi, a village in Tiruvarur.”
The 40-acre operation has grown as neighbouring farmers joined in, alongside a seed bank built from years of Balaji’s fieldwork with growers in Manipur, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.For Balaji, the mission is beyond nutrition or nostalgia. “Rice in our culture is Lakshmi,” she says. “And reintroducing its forgotten names and forms, one customer at a time, is as much about restoring that reverence as it is about the grain itself.”
Sheela Balaji and Parameshwar Rao explain the importance of rice and paddy cultivation.
Sneha Bhura is an Assistant Editor with The Times of India. She loves exploring stories at the intersection of culture and technology. She is also a published poet and podcaster. Her debut poetry collection 'Velvet Grapes' was released in 2021.

US widens Iran sanctions as Tehran threatens to halt Gulf oil flows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:42:05 UTC
14:42:05 KST

The United States on Aug. 24 launched a broad economic campaign against Iran, sanctioning nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels and warning third countries that continued dealings with Tehran could expose them to U.S. measures.
Iran responded by threatening to halt oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere in the Persian Gulf if other countries supported Washington’s campaign.
The Treasury Department said Operation Economic Outcast expanded the scope for secondary sanctions in five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington was “entering the endgame” and described the campaign as an “economic D-Day.”
“Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said.
The campaign puts pressure on governments, companies and financial institutions that continue to facilitate Iranian oil sales or financial transactions.
Bessent accused Iran’s trading partners of buying and transporting its petroleum, channeling funds through exchange houses and free-trade zones, tolerating ship-to-ship fuel transfers and allowing Tehran to use their banking and transport systems.
He said each country had been given a deadline to end activities identified by Washington, without disclosing the time frames. Failure to comply would prompt unilateral action by the Treasury, he added.
Financial institutions found to be facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on Iran’s behalf could also be cut off from the U.S. dollar system.
The Treasury said the latest sanctions targeted networks involved in procuring nuclear and missile technology, a cyber group directed by Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security and oil revenue networks operating through brokers, companies and shadow-fleet vessels.
The networks operated in several jurisdictions, including the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore, Switzerland and Europe, it said.
China, Iran’s largest oil customer, rejected Washington’s pressure campaign. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said sanctions would heighten tensions and serve no one’s interests, urging restraint and a return to dialogue.
Beijing would closely follow developments and take measures to protect its legitimate rights and interests, he added.
Tehran, meanwhile, warned other countries against joining the U.S. campaign.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said that if the economic pressure continued, “not a single drop of oil will be exported” through the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the Persian Gulf.
Iran would regard any country’s participation in or support for Washington’s campaign as “an act of war,” he added.
Iranian lawmakers have also moved forward with plans to charge vessels using the Strait of Hormuz. Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee on Aug. 23 approved a provision allowing fees for navigation, environmental, fuel, insurance, security and other services.
The proposal must still be approved by the full parliament and reviewed by the Guardian Council before it can take effect.

The mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which stretches across roughly 3,488 km.The 24th round of talks was held in August last year, when the two sides held what Beijing described as candid and in-depth discussions and reached several common understandings.The upcoming round assumes significance as India and China seek to stabilise ties following years of tensions along the Line of Actual Control.The discussions come amid efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to gradually improve bilateral relations after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash and the prolonged military stand-off in eastern Ladakh severely strained ties.Doval and Wang had also met in June in New Delhi on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting. NSA underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building trust and better understanding between the two sides. The discussions were constructive and forward-looking."The latest talks also come amid efforts by the two countries to build on a series of high-level engagements between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The leaders had welcomed positive momentum and steady progress in bilateral relations during their meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin last year, after their previous meeting in Kazan in October 2024.
They had reaffirmed that India and China are development partners rather than rivals and that differences should not be allowed to become disputes."A stable relationship and cooperation between India and China and their 2.8 billion peoples on the basis of mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity are necessary for the growth and development of the two countries, as well as for a multipolar world and a multi-polar Asia befitting the trends of the 21st century," the MEA had said after the leaders' meeting.Despite the gradual improvement in ties, differences over the boundary and Arunachal Pradesh remain sensitive issues between New Delhi and Beijing.Both Doval and Wang are designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism. While the process has not resolved the long-running border dispute, officials on both sides continue to regard it as an important channel for managing tensions and maintaining communication.The talks also come ahead of Xi's expected visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit on September 12-13, which could provide an opportunity for another meeting between Xi and PM Modi and further discussions on the bilateral relationship.

13:39:08 CST
14:39:08 KST

BELGRADE, Aug. 25 (Xinhua) -- The global governance system can draw inspiration from China's major global initiatives in a multipolar world, a former senior UN official told Xinhua in a recent interview.
"China's four initiatives give together a very important set of values and principles that, in my opinion, ought to be applied to the current system that we have in order to transform it," said Vuk Jeremic, who served as president of the UN General Assembly (2012-2013) and foreign minister of Serbia (2007-2012).
Jeremic currently leads the Center for International Relations and Sustainable Development, a global public policy think tank based in Belgrade.
He was referring to a series of major global initiatives proposed by China: the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative and the Global Governance Initiative.
Reviewing the evolution of the international landscape, Jeremic said the world is no longer unipolar. "There is no single center of power that dominates all others," he said. The world has moved toward multipolarity, he noted, but a new multipolar world order has yet to be fully established.
Jeremic said the emergence of a multipolar world does not mean a more cooperative international system.
He outlined three possible forms of multipolarity: competitive, managed and cooperative. Competitive multipolarity would see major powers compete fiercely without recognizing each other's legitimacy, increasing the risk of conflict. Managed multipolarity would involve competition within agreed rules and red lines to prevent misunderstandings and escalation.
Cooperative multipolarity, meanwhile, would see major powers recognize each other's existence, legitimacy and rights and work together to address common challenges such as climate change and the regulation of advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence.
"This third multipolar version, cooperative multipolarity, is something that we should all hope for," he said.
Jeremic also spoke highly of China's development over recent decades, describing it as "the most successful exercise in the history of human development."
He cited lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty and increasing opportunities to participate in economic and social development as major achievements. He also highlighted China's technological achievements, noting that the country has become a leading tech power.
It is in this broader context, Jeremic said, that China's four global initiatives have particular significance.
He identified the four initiatives as important components of China's approach to global challenges, stressing how the Global Governance Initiative is people-centered and action-oriented.
Global governance, he said, should be "not just for governments around the world, not just for certain blocs, but for the people."
"For somebody who comes from a very small country, this respect for international law and the sovereign equality of nations that is deeply embedded in the Global Governance Initiative is something very appealing," he said.
In his view, these principles are particularly relevant, given that the existing multilateral system faces significant challenges and that international institutions fail to better reflect today's realities.
"We do have a multilateral system that is not terribly functional these days," he said. "We need to change it, we need to reform it."
Though transforming the international system would be a lengthy process, Jeremic said China's global initiatives provide principles for countries worldwide to explore a more cooperative multipolarity. ■

‘Constitutional monstrosity’: P Chidambaram attacks One Nation, One Election Bill

‘Constitutional monstrosity’: P Chidambaram attacks One Nation, One Election Bill
Edited by: Yashasvi Vasistha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 25, 2026, 11:09 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
File photo: Congress MP P Chidambaram
NEW DELHI: Senior Congress leader and Rajya Sabha member P Chidambaram on Tuesday said simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies cannot be held in 2029 even if Parliament passes the proposed One Nation, One Election (ONOE) legislation.Chidambaram, who appeared before the Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) examining the ONOE Bills, said his basic submission before the panel was that the proposed legislation violated the basic features of the Constitution, particularly parliamentary democracy in a federal country.
In a post on X, Chidambaram said he was not permitted to disclose his evidence before the JPC but outlined the thrust of his argument.“I am grateful for the opportunity to present my views to the JPC on O.N.O.E. I am not at liberty to disclose my evidence to the JPC but the basic thrust of my deposition was that the Bill violated the basic features of the Constitution, especially the tenets of parliamentary democracy in a federal country,” he wrote.
Chidambaram disputes 2029 timeline
Chidambaram also rejected the reported assertion by JPC chairman PP Chaudhary that simultaneous elections could be held in 2029.
“I have read the reported statement of the Chairman, JPC, that simultaneous elections are possible in 2029 I am afraid his view is wrong and goes against the text of the Bill,” he said.According to Chidambaram, the Bill provides that the “appointed date” can only be a date that comes after a general election. Since the next Lok Sabha election is due in 2029, he argued that simultaneous polls cannot be conducted in that year.“Even if the Bill is passed (which is very unlikely), the 'appointed date' under the Bill can only be a date 'after a general election'. The next general election will take place in 2029. Hence, simultaneous elections are not possible in 2029, which is a blessing,” he said.Chidambaram added that the Congress and other Opposition parties would launch a nationwide campaign against the legislation, calling it a “Constitutional monstrosity in parliamentary democracy in a federal country.”
JPC receives suggestions on deferring state polls
Meanwhile, the parliamentary committee examining the ONOE legislation received several suggestions during its deliberations on Monday.According to sources cited by news agency ANI, two public policy institutions proposed replacing subjective discretion in deciding whether to defer state assembly elections with defined and judicially traceable grounds, along with fixed outer limits for such deferrals.The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024, seeks to facilitate the proposed synchronisation of Lok Sabha and state assembly elections. The Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024, forms part of the broader legislative framework for implementing simultaneous polls.Both Bills were introduced in the Lok Sabha on December 17, 2024, and subsequently referred to the JPC for detailed examination.The panel has since held meetings with subject-matter experts and undertaken study visits, with its most recent study visit taking place in Lucknow in July.
Chidambaram had opposed Bills before panel
Chidambaram had appeared before the JPC on Monday and strongly opposed the proposed simultaneous-election framework.He argued that curtailing the five-year tenure of elected legislatures would violate the Constitution's basic structure.He also said he could not support the Bills on grounds of conscience and contended that the government did not have the two-thirds majority required to pass the proposed constitutional amendments, according to sources cited by news agency PTI.JPC chairman PP Chaudhary said Chidambaram had provided “good inputs” but noted that he represented a particular political party. Chaudhary maintained that the proposal to hold simultaneous elections was not against the basic structure of the Constitution.
The ONOE Bills were formulated after a high-level committee headed by former President Ram Nath Kovind recommended holding Lok Sabha, state assembly and local body elections simultaneously in a phased manner.Historically, Lok Sabha and state assembly elections were held together from 1951-52 until the cycle was disrupted by premature dissolutions of some state assemblies in 1968 and 1969, followed by the early dissolution of the Fourth Lok Sabha in 1970.

US removes Syria from state sponsors of terrorism list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:36:52 UTC
14:36:52 KST

The United States on Aug. 24 formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism and lifted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham’s (HTS) remaining U.S. terrorist designation.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio authorized the rescission after the mandatory 45-day congressional notification period ended.
He also revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front, also known as HTS, as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organization.
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) simultaneously removed HTS from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List.
The State Department had already revoked HTS’s separate designation as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in July 2025.
Syria had been on the state sponsors list since December 1979. The designation carried restrictions on U.S. assistance, defense exports and sales, certain dual-use exports and financial dealings.
Rubio said the decisions reflected steps and commitments by President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government to distance Syria from international terrorism. He said the changes removed “the final major barriers” to private-sector investment and supported Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy.
Al-Sharaa welcomed the decision, saying Syria was leaving behind a painful chapter and moving toward development and reconstruction. He thanked U.S. President Donald Trump and countries that had supported Syria.
Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani called the decision historic, saying the designation had been linked to the policies of the ousted Assad government and had never been the Syrian people’s choice.
Türkiye’s Ambassador to Syria Nuh Yılmaz said the move had removed “the final obstacle” to Syria’s integration with the world and would support stability and development in both Syria and the wider region.

‘Petty grievances’ and an alleged troublemaker: unsealed Murdoch court documents give rare glimpse into bitter succession battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:33:18 UTC
14:33:18 KST

A year ago, Rupert Murdoch resolved the long-running fight over which of his children would control his sprawling media empire, ending a bitter legal battle and anointing his eldest son, Lachlan, as his successor.
Now, court documents have offered a rare glimpse into the family’s clashes before the decision, revealing the patriarch’s view of son James as a troublemaker who had to be ousted from the business and detailing tensions between Murdoch’s four eldest children and their airing of “petty grievances” about their father.
A crucial decision by a Nevada judicial officer in late 2024, recently made public, exposes the friction among Murdoch’s heirs and includes direct references to the HBO drama series Succession, which was purportedly inspired by the media family.
The reasoning of the probate commissioner, Edmund Gorman, sheds light on the motive behind Murdoch’s attempt to modify a family trust and put his eldest son, Lachlan, in charge of the media empire.
The bitter legal battle ended when a deal was reached last year.
Murdoch testified at length about his intended legacy, according to the Nevada decision, which he said included preserving Fox and News Corp as what he described as alternative conservative voices in the media.
“They were great assets for the family and I thought they were important in the English-speaking world, certainly in the United States,” Murdoch said, according to comments included in the decision.
In correspondence released to the court, the 95-year-old said it would be a disaster if the assets fell into the “wrong hands” and that Fox and News Corp’s voice were “essential for democracies”.
Murdoch had encouraged Lachlan to buy out his siblings’ stakes as early as 2019 so he would take over after his father’s death. Each was willing to sell but Lachlan did not offer them enough money, the commissioner found.
James drew heavy media attention when he quit the News board in July 2020, citing disagreements over editorial content. He had previously criticised coverage of climate change in the family’s outlets.
According to the published decision, Murdoch told the court he believed James was “making trouble” and “creating speculation” about succession at the company.
The Murdoch family interests include numerous media assets, including Fox News, the Wall Street Journal, The Times in the UK and a suite of mastheads in Australia including The Australian, news.com.au and News24 (formerly Sky).
Murdoch told the court James should be cut off from the trust controlling the family stake in the companies because he and his sisters, Prudence and Elisabeth, had planned to oust Lachlan and change the companies’ direction after the patriarch’s death.
As evidence for the supposed scheme, Rupert cited a memo written by Elisabeth’s representative on the trust after watching the Succession episode where patriarch Logan Roy dies and his business is thrown into chaos. The commissioner found that memo in fact appeared to suggest appointing a mediator a to ensure a “sensible outcome”.
Lachlan had fuelled Rupert’s “false assumption” about James’s behaviour and “falsely told his father, without proof” that James had spoken to Australian reporter Paddy Manning for his book The Successor, the commissioner found.
Lachlan did not tell Rupert that his own lieutenant, the Australia Post chair Siobhan McKenna, had provided more than 14 hours of interviews for that book with Lachlan’s permission. The commissioner elsewhere said Lachlan had showed a “lack of candor with the parties and on the witness stand”.
Fox did not respond when contacted for comment on behalf of Lachlan.
Family history
The court documents reveal the strain that had marked family dealings for some years, with each of the four older Murdoch siblings resigning from the family companies at least once. Rupert also has two other children – Chloe and Grace – with his third wife, Wendi Deng, who were not involved in the court case.
The four older children spoke to a family counsellor in 2010 but Lachlan said the siblings “all ended up hating each other” after the process of airing their “petty grievances” against their father.
Lachlan said James had “stormed out” after learning Murdoch wanted to replace him with Lachlan as chief executive of 21st Century Fox in 2015, resulting in a compromise that was a “disaster from day one”.
Elisabeth told the court the family had last been on “relatively good speaking terms” after her 2017 wedding. She said the siblings all kept friendly relations except for Lachlan and James.
On the morning of a December 2023 meeting to amend the trust and carry out the plan, Lachlan texted his sister: “Hey Lizzy. I really appreciate your support. Today is about Dad’s wishes and confirming all of our support for him and for his wishes. It shouldn’t be difficult or controversial. Love you, Lachlan”.
Murdoch had said the amendments should be carried out because Lachlan was “committed to my legacy”.
He added: “I love each of my children, and my support of Lachlan is not intended to suggest otherwise. But these companies need a designated leader and Lachlan is that leader.”
The proposal failed, sparking court action, before the 2025 deal saw Lachlan secure control of the sprawling media empire after Elisabeth, James and Prudence received an estimated $US1.1bn each for their shares in the business.

OMA/AMO and OPEN Architecture Design Opening Exhibitions for Powerhouse Parramatta in Sydney, Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Powerhouse Parramatta, a new museum and cultural institution on the banks of the Parramatta River in Western Sydney, Australia, will open to the public on Saturday, November 7, 2026. The 30,000-square-meter building has been designed by Franco-Japanese firm Moreau Kusunoki as lead designer, with Australian firm Genton as local architect and Arup as engineer. Moreau Kusunoki won the design competition for the project in 2019, with completion initially planned for 2025. Powerhouse Parramatta is the first state cultural organization located in Western Sydney, a region whose population includes communities from more than 170 countries. At opening, the museum will present five exhibitions.
The museum has been organized around seven Presentation Spaces, each with a distinct layout intended to accommodate a changing program of exhibitions. The building also includes retail spaces, cafés and restaurants, and several dedicated facilities: a residential learning program designed to host 10,000 students per year; a space for programming related to food history, culture, science, and technology; a rooftop observatory; an "Indigenous garden"; and residential apartments for up to 30 researchers, academics, and industry or community leaders in residence. Powerhouse Parramatta is part of Powerhouse, Australia's largest museum group. Powerhouse Parramatta forms part of an infrastructure renewal program that also includes the redevelopment of Powerhouse Ultimo, expanded facilities at Powerhouse Castle Hill, and ongoing heritage restoration work at Sydney Observatory.
The opening exhibition program at Powerhouse Parramatta will present more than 3,000 objects, including 1,600 drawn from the Powerhouse Collection alongside loans from national and international institutions. The program includes more than 45 new commissions from artists and designers across 14 countries, among them seven Community Commissions developed with First Nations practitioners. Two of the five opening exhibitions, Task Eternal and The Mall, have been designed in collaboration with architecture practices OPEN Architecture and OMA/AMO.
Related Article
Australian Pavilion Explores Multi-Dwelling Housing Through "Lived In" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
Task Eternal, designed by OPEN Architecture, traces the history of human flight, from First Nations sky knowledges and early aviation to contemporary aerospace technology. Drawing on Ted Chiang's short story The Tower of Babylon, the exhibition presents more than 850 objects, with loans from NASA, the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, the British Museum, MIT, and the Australian Space Agency. Among the objects on display is the "black box" flight recorder, a device originally developed in Australia to record aircraft data. The exhibition also includes James Turrell's Shangri La (Over the Hump) (2026), an immersive installation using cycles of changing color across the gallery space.
The Mall, developed by OMA/AMO, led by David Gianotten, Gabriel Duarte, and Sylvia Chan, examines the shopping mall as an architectural and urban typology, looking at how malls have both absorbed and generated changes in urban life, technology, and patterns of consumption. Its point of departure is Western Sydney's retail history, including Westfield Parramatta, at one point Australia's largest shopping mall, and the region's role in developing a transport-integrated retail model later applied elsewhere. Installed within a black-box gallery, the exhibition is organized around five thematic nodes, Desire, Arcade, Transaction, Ideal City, and Forum, each assigned a distinct spatial geometry derived from OMA/AMO's research into 101 malls worldwide. The nodes are arranged without a fixed sequence on a continuous ground plane referencing the suburban parking lot, allowing visitors to move between them non-linearly.
The exhibition draws on more than 560 objects from the Powerhouse Collection and international loans, together with 18 new commissions. Among the objects included are the archive of architect Victor Gruen, an early designer of the enclosed shopping mall in the United States; material on Australian brands originating from beach, skate, and street culture; a co-commission with M+ in Hong Kong featuring South Korean artist Ayoung Kim; archival loans from Levi's, Nike, Patagonia, Speedo, and Woolworths; and a new installation by Vert Design reinterpreting the Roselands Raindrop Fountain in southwest Sydney. The exhibition is accompanied by five publications described by OMA/AMO as "bookazines," positioned between exhibition catalogue and magazine format.
In Norway, the Oslo Architecture Triennale 2026 announced its program for its ninth edition under the theme "What if Nature Comes First?". The event will take place from September 17 to October 1 at Sofienberg Church in Oslo in a two-week festival format. OPEN Architecture recently designed Lina Bo Bardi's first exhibition in China at the PSA contemporary art museum in Huangpu, while OMA, led by partner Jason Long, together with San Francisco-based Y.A. Studio, completed 730 Stanyan, a mixed-use affordable housing development in San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury neighborhood.

A women’s shelter for refugees in Poland fights for survival as anti-Ukrainian sentiment rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:23:02 UTC
14:23:02 KST

A women’s shelter for refugees in Poland fights for survival as anti-Ukrainian sentiment rises
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — When Nastya Podorozhnya’s relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms.
Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began. But days before Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she rushed back to Ukraine to help her sister and nieces get out.
As she returned to Poland alongside an influx of refugees in the war’s first days, she witnessed the outpouring of support from Polish volunteers. But she also spotted a risk: Ukrainian women accepting help from strangers could become vulnerable to human traffickers.
That was when she decided to found Martynka, a helpline and support group for female Ukrainian refugees escaping gender-based violence.
Four years later, she is struggling to keep the organization afloat. Funding for refugee support is drying up, hostility toward Ukrainians is growing, and Poland still lacks a long-term integration strategy. As war fatigue deepens, politicians are increasingly exploiting anti-refugee sentiment for political gain.
The shift is being felt by groups such as Martynka. While fundraising was relatively easy in the first months of the war, international donors have since turned their attention to other global crises.
Martynka’s shelter, located in an inconspicuous two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow, has hosted more than 100 women and children. Women receive help to escape abusers and access medical care, psychological support, jobs and housing.
“It often starts with me having tea in this very kitchen with the women and they tell me what happened to them and I say ‘girl, same,’” Podorozhnya told The Associated Press during an interview in the Krakow shelter, referring to her own experience of a man trying to rape her on a street in Poland in 2016.
As Podorozhnya and her colleagues struggle to raise enough money to keep the shelter open, she says calls for donations frequently trigger a torrent of online abuse.
“It’s because I’m Ukrainian,” she said.
Ukrainian refugees contribute to Poland’s economy
Around 3.5 million Ukrainians fled to Poland in the first weeks of the war, according to the U.N. Poles greeted them at train stations and opened their homes to them, while the government granted refugees access to jobs and social security benefits.
The two countries share a long history of brutality at the hands of Russia, and Poland remains a key ally to Ukraine in the war.
By the end of 2022, the number of Ukrainian refugees in Poland had stabilized at around 1 million. Those who stayed were rapidly absorbed into the labor market: More than 70% found employment, and a Deloitte study estimated that they contributed 2.7% of Poland’s gross domestic product in 2024.
In addition to the refugees, most of whom are women and children, more than 1 million Ukrainians were already living in Poland before the war, primarily as economic migrants.
Historical grievances resurface
The refugees have increasingly become targets of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric. In research published this year, Ukrainian migrants interviewed by Olena Babakova, a researcher at Warsaw’s Vistula University, identified the 2025 Polish presidential campaign as the period when anti-Ukrainian feeling intensified, as it became a common theme for all parties, not just the far right.
Karol Nawrocki, representing the national-conservative camp and who eventually won the presidency, promised legislation that would prioritize Polish citizens over Ukrainians when accessing public services. Rafał Trzaskowski, the liberal candidate, proposed restricting child welfare benefits for Ukrainians.
As tensions increased, historical grievances between the countries resurfaced.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyydecided to name a military unit after a Ukrainian paramilitary organization accused of massacring Poles during World War II, causing outrage in Poland. Nawrocki responded by withdrawing a state honor awarded to Zelenskyy, further escalating the tensions.
“And it’s not only negative feelings, Ukrainians really experience hostile conversations and attacks,” Babakova told the AP.
According to data from the Polish police, 180 Ukrainian citizens were victims of prejudice-motivated crimes by mid-July, a significant increase compared with 275 for the whole of 2025 and 267 in 2024.
In response to multiple media reports of Ukrainians beaten on Polish streets over the summer, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in late July that “we must wage war on violence and hatred.”
Help for vulnerable refugees is decreasing
The Polish government has been steadily cutting support for Ukrainian refugees, saying that many have stabilized their situation.
Poland’s ombudsman has warned that the changes disproportionately affect the most vulnerable groups, including single mothers with several children, older people and those with chronic illnesses or disabilities. Because most Ukrainian men of military age, between 23 and 60, are prohibited from leaving the country, single mothers are overrepresented among the refugees.
Yuliia Repenko from the Ukrainian House said that her nongovernmental organization, which provides help to Ukrainians, was “increasingly supporting people who are particularly vulnerable to exclusion.”
The Polish government has defended its decision to cut back aid to Ukrainian refugees. Katarzyna Nowakowska, Poland’s deputy minister for family, labor and social policy, told the AP that the most vulnerable applicants still receive direct help from the state and any other refugees needing support should turn to social workers.
As the Polish government has been scaling back its support, international aid has also declined, further limiting options. Data from the U.N. refugee agency shows a steady drop since 2022 in the funding provided by international donors for Ukrainians, with only half the agency’s identified needs financed this year, compared with 94% in 2022.
“Financial supporters have moved on from helping Ukrainian refugees, but the war is still ongoing,” said Sonia Novytska, a Martynka helpline worker. “If anything, it has become deadlier since the start.”
Martynka received about 1,800 requests for help last year, and staff expect that number to increase, Novytska said. Not only victims of violence contact the helpline now, but also mothers struggling to provide food and shelter for their children.
“What Poles need to understand is that we are helping the people that could otherwise become homeless in their neighborhoods, the people who might start abusing substances out of despair they can’t make ends meet,” Podorozhnya said.
“Martynka does the job of the Polish state,” she said.

Six months into Iran war, almost half of global oil flows from war zones
Unknown

14:13:45 KST

Six months into Iran war, almost half of global oil flows from war zones
LONDON Aug 25 - Almost half the world's oil comes from countries affected by conflict in 2026, Reuters calculations show, underscoring that current disruptions have eclipsed previous energy crises.
Six months ago, U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran triggered what has become the largest oil supply crisis on record, with no clear end in sight.
At the same time, the Russia-Ukraine war has forced production and refining cuts, including in nearby Kazakhstan this year.
Ongoing conflict in Libya and U.S. restrictions on Venezuelan oil exports at the start of the year have added further strain.
Together, countries affected by those conflicts produced about 45 million barrels per day of oil based on 2025 output, accounting for more than 43% of global supply, according to Reuters calculations using International Energy Agency data.
The disruptions have increased the world's reliance on U.S. oil supplies, though that too has occasionally been disrupted by severe weather.
Not all of this year's supply disruptions happened at the same time.
With Saudi Arabia re-routing oil to the Red Sea and Gulf exporters sneaking oil secretly out of the Strait of Hormuz, the current Gulf oil disruption stands at around 5 million to 7 million bpd, according to analysts' estimates.
But risks to total flows remain high, as attacks in the Red Sea and near Egypt's Suez Canal in July demonstrated.
The conflicts in the Gulf and Ukraine have also cut global refining capacity by about a tenth.
Ukraine has targeted much of Russia's refining network, striking plants as far away as Omsk, about 2,700 km (1,680 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory.
Russia is grappling with fuel shortages and has banned gasoline and diesel exports, tightening global fuel markets.
Higher fuel prices have become a key driver of inflation, contributing to higher borrowing costs and helping to push U.S. debt to a record $40 trillion.
U.S. diesel prices have climbed to record levels despite refiners running at peak capacity.
The IEA has released record volumes from emergency stockpiles to help cushion the supply shock. Those releases are now largely complete, even as global inventories continue to decline. REUTERS

25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining the Straits of Malacca and Singapore (SOMS) as free, open and safe international shipping lanes, an official statement said.
At the 17th Co-operation Forum held Tuesday in Singapore, the three nations affirmed the status of the SOMS as a Strait Used for International Navigation where the right of transit passage applies, as enshrined in the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and reflected in customary international law.
The littoral states also reaffirmed the important roles played by user states, international organizations, the maritime industry and other stakeholders in sharing responsibility for and contributing to the safety of navigation and environmental protection in the SOMS.
"All three littoral states have reaffirmed their recognition that keeping the waterways safe, secure and open was in everyone’s best interests," said Singapore Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow.
In his opening remarks at the forum, Siow said the Strait of Malacca and the Singapore Strait are a "shining" example of what countries can achieve through close collaboration, a statement from his ministry said.
"For over half a century, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore collaborated closely to improve navigational safety in our waters, including in areas with unresolved maritime boundaries," he said.
“Even when there were differences in views, we did not allow these to paralyze cooperation,” he said, adding that “it is not only the littoral states that benefited. Nearly a quarter of the world’s seaborne trade that passes through the Straits of Malacca and Singapore go through here."

Construction safety design needed to reduce fatal accidents in Hong Kong: experts
City’s poor industrial safety record, including 15 fatalities so far this year, marked by bad habits and broader systemic and planning issues
Hong Kong should make safety design a part of all building development plans and address the culture of rushing work at construction sites, industry leaders have said after the city recorded 15 fatal industrial accidents earlier this year.
Their calls followed the warning by Construction Industry Council chairman Thomas Ho On-sing on Monday that the number of such accidents was on the rise despite stiffer penalties, reflecting that a safety culture had failed to take root.
Ho pointed out that up to 70 to 80 per cent of accidents at worksites were caused by bad habits and poor mindsets, while all 15 fatal accidents were triggered by the pressure to finish projects quickly, which he described as among the deadliest factors on construction sites.
Chau Sze-kit, chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Industry Employees General Union, said on Tuesday that safety awareness had improved but had yet to become second nature in a sector where “rushing culture” was still prevalent.
“For instance, the media recently exposed workers on exterior scaffolding without wearing safety belts or hooking on to independent lifeline ropes. This is a clear case of safety measures not being properly implemented. Ultimately, we need to embed a safety-first culture,” he said.
Chau said the issue stemmed from both worker habits and a lack of management supervision, while the provision of safety tools and improved design at the outset of construction would also minimise risks.

Shortage of engineers becomes a bottleneck for Ukraine’s defence tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:06:00 UTC
14:06:00 KST

Shortage of engineers becomes a bottleneck for Ukraine’s defence tech
- Ukraine's defence tech industry faces a severe engineer shortage, limiting the ability to quickly respond to frontline innovation needs.
- The labour gap is worsened by population decline, war impacts, and a lack of qualified candidates despite rapid workforce growth.
- Companies train inexperienced workers and boost salaries, but specialised skills remain scarce, threatening long-term defence innovation and production scaling.
AI generated
KYIV – The speed of innovation on the Ukrainian battlefield means frontline troops may need a new drone design within weeks – but the country’s defence industry faces a critical labour shortage that threatens to derail that pace.
Tens of billions of dollars in investments and wartime demand have fuelled the creation of thousands of defence companies in Ukraine, but the supply of workers has failed to keep up.
Yurii Faraponov, chief operating officer of BlueBird Tech, said his company can’t respond to some frontline requests because he doesn’t have enough engineers.
Another company recently poached a production manager by offering him three times his previous salary, along with paid housing, said Sergii Vysotskyi, vice-president of the National Association of Ukrainian Defence Industries.
Some companies are tracking down retired specialists and begging them to return to work.
The labour shortage is emerging as one of the biggest bottlenecks to expanding Ukrainian weapons production and accelerating innovation, industry insiders say.
“The market is experiencing something akin to internal cannibalism: we keep reaching out to the same people over and over and using every tool” to recruit them, said Marta Khrypiak, defence tech lead at the Lobby X recruitment agency.
Ukraine’s working-age population had been shrinking for decades and fell even more sharply after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, as millions fled abroad and others joined the military.
In defence tech, the shortage cuts directly into Ukraine’s bet that technology will offset its manpower disadvantage on the battlefield.
An April survey of 27 defence tech companies by the CORE Team recruitment agency found that the firms had grown their workforce by more than 50 per cent – collectively hiring thousands of people – in one year.
All expected to expand further, but said there was a lack of qualified candidates.
Even before the war, technical and vocational education had became less popular and many specialists left for better-paid work abroad, Vysotskyi said.
The number of professionals is rising as people retrain, said CORE Team chief executive officer Anna Korol, but the industry is growing much faster.
Some specialities – hardware developers, radio-frequency and antenna specialists, chemists needed for explosives manufacturing – are so scarce that recruiters say they effectively know all available candidates.
“You can’t recruit many people through job postings anymore – everyone has already been snapped up,” Vysotskyi said.
The lack of people is particularly damaging to innovation, several industry representatives said, as weapons become more sophisticated and require more specialised expertise.
Scaling suffers as well.
Even when a company can find enough welders and assemblers, for instance, there are too few production managers and process engineers to oversee and expand manufacturing lines, Vysotskyi said.
When a company needs to deliver on a tight deadline, job titles can become irrelevant: accountants and human resources workers may be pulled in to help assemble drones or load shipments, Khrypiak said.
There is no work-life balance, she added, with long hours at production sites targeted by Russian strikes.
That leads to fewer applicants: defence tech vacancies drew just an average of 1.5 to 3.8 applications in July on DOU.ua, a popular tech job board, compared with dozens for civilian software roles.
But workers in the industry care that their ultimate customer is a soldier, Faraponov said.
“When you compare your pace of work with the pace of the military, you don’t really feel like complaining,” he added.
The sense of purpose often drives people to the industry, according to recruiters, but there are tangible perks too.
Almost nine in 10 companies had raised salaries over the previous year, according to the CORE Team survey, to stay competitive.
Companies are aggressively headhunting specialists at home and trying to return others from overseas, industry insiders say.
People with rare expertise sometimes work for multiple manufacturers at once.
Military-aged men at defence companies also get an exemption from the draft.
And career growth opportunities are unparalleled for Ukraine, recruiters say.
Faraponov, for instance, worked in marketing before joining BlueBird Tech in 2024 to assemble drones in a garage-like workshop.
Within two years, as the company expanded, Faraponov led production at a factory and then became the company’s chief operating officer.
Such advancement is not uncommon.
Raising a new generation of engineers
Companies, unable to find experienced employees, increasingly take people with no tech background, then train them.
Assembly workers can be trained in weeks, said Maryna Shvydchenko, human resources director at Vyriy Drone.
The company runs an academy to prepare people with no relevant experience for production jobs, then grows many of them into managers and team leaders.
Training research and development employees takes longer, which puts a premium on university-educated specialists.
Since 2022, Ukrainian universities have been offering or reviving defence-related degree programmes.
All 32 first graduates of one such programme – master’s in unmanned aerial vehicles at the Kyiv School of Economics – were immediately snapped up by the UAV industry, according to Ivan Ostroumov, the programme’s head.
Although defence-tech-adjacent majors saw an uptick in enrolment across universities since the full-scale invasion in 2022, the gains have not kept pace with the industry’s growing demand.
In 2025, according to government data, only 671 students nationwide started bachelor’s degrees in aerospace engineering, which encompasses drone and missile manufacturing, and 464 chose chemical engineering, badly needed for explosives manufacturing.
“Obviously, it’s never too late because Russia will not disappear from the agenda as our enemy,” Vysotskyi said.
“As long as that existential threat exists, we will always need a very strong, technologically advanced defence industry, which requires a skilled workforce.” BLOOMBERG

‘Never seen this level of objection’: Scotland pushes back against datacentre boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

In a village 21 miles north of Edinburgh, a real estate consultancy plans to build a datacentre larger than the village itself – 35 metres high, with an area larger than 100 football pitches.
Billed as the second-biggest datacentre in the world, the development in Auchertool, Fife, has attracted 1,600 objections.
“The public pressure is huge,” said David Torrance, a member of the Scottish parliament representing the village. “I’ve never seen this level of objection to a local plan, and I have been in politics for 25 years.”
Similar concerns are being echoed across Scotland, next to gargantuan planned developments in towns such as Airdrie and Larbert. In a matter of weeks, as the Scottish parliament comes back into session, the growing opposition could pose a challenge to Britain’s AI strategy.
“The Scottish government is inching towards a moratorium,” said Kat Jones, director of the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland. “MSPs return to parliament next week, after a summer in their constituencies where they have been hearing the concerns of local people about proposed hyperscale datacentres. They will be expecting action.”
For months, UK officials have been encouraging would-be datacentre developers to consider Scotland. In April, Fintan Slye, the chief executive of the UK’s National Energy System Operator (Neso), told a London audience to look north: “If in the audience you have a big datacentre and you want to go to Scotland, please come talk to me, we will help you,” he said.
“They are coming up here because we are energy-rich, and we are water-rich, and England is in drought and the grid is struggling,” said Torrance.
But Scotland, it turns out, isn’t having it. The proposal for Auchtertool is a behemoth: drawings show the 600MW datacentre towering over the village, dwarfing old stone houses and blocking the view of fields and forests.
“How can you possibly ask people to accept that?” Torrance said. “You can see why the public is objecting.”
Scotland has already started to take steps that could mean the Auchtertool datacentre – and dozens of others – may never be built.
This week, Scotland’s minister for public finance issued a new set of directions to regulate datacentres in the country. The first of these requires planning authorities to notify the government when they receive an application for a datacentre larger than 50MW – in other words, anything more than a twelfth of the size of Auchtertool.
The minister has also required that certain datacentres, including Auchtertool, submit an environmental impact assessment. Their developers had previously argued that they were exempt.
In some senses, these are “obvious, bare-minimum” rules, said Jones. They mean that Scotland is starting to closely follow developments that stand to drastically reshape the landscape and resource consumption of the entire country.
The fact that giant datacentres can currently be built across Britain with little strategy and without government knowledge is a feature of an old and idiosyncratic planning regime; no one foresaw that giant tech companies would wish to litter the world with buildings the size of large monuments.
But these restrictions are just the start. The Scottish parliament will return at the end of this month. Three days after the session commences, in early September, campaigners plan a massive demonstration against datacentres in Edinburgh.
That demonstration will aim higher. Campaigners have been calling for Scotland to put in place a full moratorium on datacentre development, to give the public and authorities time to examine the plans that are in the pipeline. This summer, the national council of the Scottish National party passed a motion to freeze all new datacentre projects that have not received planning permission.
Several weeks ago, Police Scotland warned another datacentre developer that public anger over datacentres could lead to incursions and posed a security risk, in what appeared to be the first-ever such warning in the UK.
A moratorium on datacentres could soon become policy. At the least, “you’ll see a lot more restrictions – and stronger guidance,” said Torrance.
Datacentre developers have other plans. Data Vita, the company building the UK’s AI growth zone in Lanarkshire, has recently been awarded an investment package which includes a £202m guarantee from the National Wealth Fund – although the Guardian’s investigations have revealed that its plans to power itself do not stand up.
Meanwhile, Mark Wilson, chief executive of ILI Group, the company building the datacentre in Auchtertool, spoke to the BBC’s Scotcast this week and defended its plans, suggesting that Torrance’s angry constituents were perhaps ill-informed.
“I understand how people can think in a rural area,” he said. “There’s a lot of misinformation out there, it’s mainly coming from overseas, from America.”
His company was part of a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” for Scotland to “create long-term economic benefit”, he said, through the jobs created by building datacentres. He conceded that most of the datacentre developments currently in the planning pipeline in Scotland were unlikely to be built.
“Scotland can be No1,” he said. “We can become a global hub for datacentres in Scotland.”

Canadians do not seek a trade war – but nor will we be bullied by Donald Trump | Jen Gerson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

The Canadians are exceedingly angry. I realise this can sometimes be difficult for foreigners to deduce, given our national struggle to express the full range of human emotion outside ice hockey riots. However, let me assure you that the prime minister Canadians saw take the stage on Saturday morning in the wake of the collapse in trade negotiations with the US was a Mark Carney practically vibrating with fury.
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” he said, in a rare press conference that was as candid and clear as he ever tends to be. “That’s fine … We’ve got the reserves, we’ve got the resilience, we’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus. We’re gonna respond, we’re going to focus on what we can control and what we’re going to build.”
Canada walked out of negotiations, with a deal apparently on the verge of completion, mere hours before 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian exports were due to kick in.
Dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs, scheduled to take effect on 8 September, will follow in turn. In a statement, Carney said that last-minute demands from the US were “uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” The US denied this, insisting that it was Canadians who made last-minute demands.
In subsequent interviews with Bloomberg, Canadian ambassador to the US Mark Wiseman said there was no specific item that put a deal out of reach; rather, it was a range of issues in which the text that ultimately wound up on the page – or, at least the interpretation of that text – did not align with what the Canadians thought they had agreed to. The most contentious issues appear to be related to tariffs on autos, digital and cultural policy, and the US claiming the right to veto Canada’s attempts to form trade alliances with other countries. Meanwhile, Canadians have no reason to trust this administration not to unilaterally impose new tariffs on a whim – which it has done, repeatedly, and as recently as this week.
In short, Carney noted, sometimes the US signature on trade deals is “written in pencil”.
Canadian voters, who were pensive about the prospect of any new deal with the US in the first place, have come out strongly in support of the prime minister. Despite the fact that the deal’s collapse will almost certainly entail painful economic penalties, the mood is one of sustained and general anger toward the US not born merely of trade irritants – very few Canadians have opinions about rules of origin tariffs on auto parts, or softwood lumber protections, or supply managed dairy quotas. In cordial times, these are the ordinary frictions between close friends and neighbours.
Rather, it’s an emotion born of a real and visceral sense of betrayal: that the people we trusted with shared security and military obligations, that the nation with which we allowed ourselves to grow economically interdependent, has turned on us. They are using ordinary trade irritants as an excuse to exercise mafioso-style dominance in the pursuit of our subjugation and maybe outright annexation. We know very well that this isn’t about trade.
We are being trained to know our place in the new world order that the so-called Dunroe doctrine is seeking to impose on the western hemisphere.
So how, exactly, are any of us supposed to respond when the US secretary of transportation, Sean Duffy, goes on Fox News in the aftermath of the collapse to say things like: “We provide their security for them and they take advantage of us? President Trump was the first one to go and say ‘that’s not the kind of relationship friends should have’.”
The US does not provide Canadian security – although many commentators, including myself, do criticise our lax military spending. The North American Aerospace Defense Command, or Norad, is a fully integrated entity of both the Canadian and US military. We have our own military, and our own police forces.
How are we supposed to respond, exactly, when our large and once-admired neighbour to the south repeatedly threatens to make us the “51st state”? Or when he posts gag photos of the whole of North America covered in a US flag – provocations we’re supposed to take “seriously but not literally”, as if that makes these threats less horrific or more acceptable.
What does one do when one’s closest “friend” and “ally” repeatedly threatens to disregard border treaties? Or when the US’s actual behaviour aligns perfectly with the president’s threat to use “economic force“ to push us into becoming an American state?
We don’t want to be an American state. And even if we did, we certainly wouldn’t want to be a state of whatever the US is choosing to become right now.
There is not a single Canadian who wants to start a war with the US. No country in Canada’s position storms out of a trade negotiation unless it has to. No country as small and dependent on the US tells the modern imperium to get lost, and risks the consequences thereof, unless there is no other option.
What Carney – and Canada, for that matter – are trying to signal across the Atlantic is that the America we all built our expectations around is over. We cannot plan around the hope of a return to normal, even if Democrats regain power in Washington.
Canada’s location and US-integrated economy mean that we will be the first to face the reality of whatever the US becomes. And if it is coming for us, no European ally – including the UK – can expect to remain untouched, regardless of whatever “special relationship” you imagine may insulate you.
Personally, I simply cannot fathom the commentators and politicians in the UK who fail to understand this. Do you honestly imagine yourselves to be closer to the US militarily, geographically, economically, or culturally than Canada? Guys, we are a little America, albeit with a steadier political system and the king on the money. If they are willing to vassalise us, what sentiment of history or tradition remains to protect you?
A fundamental break in American values and objectives is not a problem that can be contained. It’s not a condition that can be ignored or wished away. Carney is serious when he talks about a historic “rupture in the world order”, as he did at Davos early this year.
Canadians understand that maintaining our sovereignty and independence will entail consequences and sacrifices. We did not bring this trade war on ourselves; we have merely refused to comply in advance to the unreasonable demands of a bad-faith actor. We will be punished for it. We have accepted this. If nothing else, let the US’s retaliation be a warning to the rest of the western alliance. Run, run. Protect yourselves. Move faster.
- 
  Jen Gerson is a Canadian commentator and co-founder of The Line. She lives in Calgary, Alberta

As global drug giants grow cautious, can Chinese biotech keep cashing in on out-licensing?

As drug giants grow cautious, can Chinese biotech firms still cash in on licensing deals?
Out-licensing deals have overtaken IPOs as the primary lifeline for cash-starved Chinese drug makers, analysts say
Record-breaking cross-border deals helped make some formerly loss-making Chinese biotech companies profitable in the first half of the year, but multinational drugmakers are now signalling plans to tighten deal budgets.
Analysts said deals with global partners had overtaken initial public offerings and pre-IPO fundraising as the main funding option for cash-starved Chinese biotech firms wanting to advance the discovery, clinical development and regulatory approval of new drugs. Yet questions remained over whether reliance on overseas licensing income was sustainable in the long run.
“Chinese biotech assets remain highly cost-effective relative to global peers,” said Cui Cui, head of healthcare research for Asia at Jefferies, adding that if major pharmaceutical companies became more selective about their expenditures to acquire new drugs, “Chinese biotech assets may look even more attractive”.
“This is quite sizeable when compared to the IPO proceeds,” said Tony Ren, head of Asia healthcare research at Macquarie Capital.
Healthcare and drug companies raised HK$14.1 billion (US$1.8 billion) via 11 first-half listings in Hong Kong, according to Deloitte, while six biotech and healthcare firms went public on mainland China’s A-share market, raising a combined 2.12 billion yuan, according to EY.

Tejahswi yadav targets Bihar CM over BPSC official remark
NEW DELHI: Bihar leader of opposition and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav has demanded an apology from BPSC examination controller Rajesh Kumar over his "dog-barking" remark against protesting students. While RJD scion also took a sharp dig at chief minister Samrat Choudhary, alleging official's language "mirrors the CM's language."Tejashwi said immediate action should be taken against the official, warning that such comments could set a wrong precedent in Bihar and encourage officials to speak disrespectfully to students and the public.Speaking to news agency ANI, Tejashwi criticised the Bihar government over the ongoing protests linked to the 70th BPSC examination. He said the examination controller’s remarks reflected the “language of the chief minister”.“This official should be removed immediately and made to apologise,” Tejashwi said. He alleged that students and young people were being ignored and that repeated exam-related controversies had not led to anyone being held accountable.Tejashwi also accused the government of failing to fix responsibility for repeated cancellations, alleged paper leaks and irregularities in competitive examinations.
'Elephant walks, dogs bark'
The row began after BPSC Examination Controller Rajesh Kumar was asked about allegations of irregularities and paper leaks.Responding to questions, Kumar reportedly said: “Haathi chale bazaar, kutta bhaunke hazaar” - meaning, “An elephant walks through the market while a thousand dogs bark.”The remark angered protesting students, who raised slogans against the official and intensified their criticism of the commission.Students have been protesting at Patna's Gardanibagh over the 70th BPSC examination, demanding its cancellation over alleged irregularities and paper leaks.Their protest has also focused on the proposed Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 (TRE-4). Students are opposing the plan to hold the examination in two phases across Bihar and are demanding that the official TRE-4 notification be released.
Tejashwi has also written to Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary, asking the government to engage with the protesters and address their concerns instead of ignoring them.He has demanded that the TRE-4 examination be conducted in a single phase across the state.Tejashwi also called for an end to what he described as discrimination against Hindi-speaking candidates in the BPSC Civil Services Main examination and interview.Among his other demands are:
Complete transparency in competitive examinations, including those conducted by the BPSC, BSSC and for police recruitment.
A high-level independent probe into alleged irregularities in past examinations.
Strict action against recruitment “mafias” involved in exam-related wrongdoing.
Time-bound schedules for pending exams, including BSSC Intermediate, CGL, ASO, BSO, Librarian and Accountant recruitment exams.
The RJD leader said the government must act quickly and hold discussions with the protesting students to find a solution to the ongoing dispute.

LOS ANGELES (AP) — Angel Reese broke the WNBA single-game rebounding record with 26 while also breaking the league’s season record for rebounds as the Atlanta Dream beat the Los Angeles Sparks 78-71 on Monday night.
Reese surpassed Chamique Holdsclaw’s record of 24 rebounds, set on May 23, 2003 for Washington.
The Dream star has 458 rebounds this season, seven more than A’ja Wilson’s mark set in 2024. Atlanta still has six games remaining in the regular season.
“I’m just in awe watching her rebound,” teammate Allisha Gray said after the game. “That’s a talent.”
Reese finished with 11 points. She secured her WNBA-leading 27th double-double of the season on a basket with 13.9 seconds left in the game.
The Dream have won four straight games — all on the road.
Gray led Atlanta (25-13) with 20 points. Rhyne Howard added 18 points to eclipse 3,000 for her career. Gray set an Atlanta record for field goals in a season with 247.
Nneka Ogwumike had 27 points and 16 rebounds for Los Angeles (13-25), which has lost nine straight games in the series. Dearica Hamby and Cameron Brink each scored 15 points.
Atlanta trailed 37-36 at halftime before starting the third quarter on a 9-2 run. The Dream also began the fourth on a 9-2 run to make it 71-57 with 6:57 left.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wagon Group General Manager Hung Yu-hang (洪郁航) said on Monday that the company’s Keelung–Ishigaki ferry route will be reduced from two trips per week to one beginning in October, the off-season for Ishigaki Island tourism.
Hung said that from October through February 2027, the ferry will depart Keelung Port on Thursdays and leave Ishigaki on Sundays, according to CNA. From March 2027, during the peak tourist season, service is expected to return to twice a week.
Hung said that if passenger numbers increase, more roundtrips may be added. Current occupancy rates are stable, though typhoons affect overall volumes, he said.
The general manager also noted that many passengers have raised concerns about pricing, and that a revised pricing plan is expected to be released in September, per CNA.
The passenger-cargo vessel operating the route, the Yaima Maru, has a capacity of 545 passengers and 122 cabins. It began service on May 28.
According to the company’s website, the route offers seven cabin types. Ticket prices range from about NT$2,000 (US$63) for a basic room during the off-season to NT$10,500 for premium suites during peak travel periods.
