====================================================================================================

Trump’s Arctic saber-rattling boosts Iceland’s pro-EU campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Pro-EU campaigners have a handy boogeyman to win over Icelandic voters ahead of a crunch referendum on Saturday: U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump’s threats to annex Greenland — Iceland’s closest neighbor — have added a strong geopolitical dimension to a referendum on resuming membership talks with the EU, which might otherwise have focused on long-standing gripes with Brussels, such as mackerel quotas.
And Trump is not the only security risk in the North Atlantic.
With Russia and China both pushing to secure Arctic resources, questions about global alliances are becoming increasingly vital to the 270,000 Icelandic voters heading to the ballot boxes across the weather-beaten volcanic island.
Reykjavík’s former mayor, Dagur Eggertsson, a prominent figure in the pro-EU “Yes” campaign, said that Trump’s threats to Greenland were weighing on voters’ minds and sparking debate about Iceland’s strategic position.
“This issue is not settled,” the Social Democrat member of parliament said of U.S. ambitions to control Greenland, whose coast is less than 300 kilometers from Iceland. “Trump has been quite outspoken, not only last year, but again and again. This is something that people on the streets think about.”
While Trump has rowed back on some of his more bellicose posturing to seize Greenland at the beginning of the year, he still insisted at a NATO summit in Ankara in July that the territory “should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark.”
Facing that kind of regional tension, Eggertsson, who also chairs Iceland’s delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, echoed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in mapping out the stakes: “Small and middle powers need to stick together.”
In the case of Iceland, he insisted this meant closer ties to Europe. “The matter is more urgent now than before,” he said.
A question of sovereignty
The key theme looming over the Icelandic referendum is sovereignty. But it’s an issue that cuts two ways, and polls suggest the referendum is on a knife-edge. A Gallup poll in mid-August gave the “Yes” camp a wafer-thin advantage, with 51.5 percent support.
While “Yes” campaigners like Eggertsson stress the regional implications of threats to Greenland’s sovereignty, the “No” camp argues the EU could impinge on Icelandic sovereignty, particularly within the politically crucial spheres of fisheries and farming policy.
Indeed, it was fisheries quotas that were key to scuppering Iceland’s previous bid to join the EU, which was definitively halted in 2015.
Eiríkur Bergmann, a professor of politics at Bifröst University, explained that national sovereignty has been the core issue animating political debate in Iceland since its independence from Denmark in 1944.
“There are two camps, both tapping into the same heritage,” said Bergmann. “One is arguing that Iceland needs to join the European Union to enhance its sovereignty and guard its heritage of its independence struggle. Another camp, equally vocal, is cautioning against EU membership on the exact same grounds, arguing that it threatens Iceland’s sovereignty.”
Those sentiments on national independence and identity have a long pedigree. Iceland’s parliament, the Althing, is one of the oldest electoral assemblies in the world, dating back more than a millennium.
Strategically, the island is a NATO member and has a bilateral defense agreement with the U.S. dating back to 1951.
At the same time, Iceland is a member of the European Economic Area, and it’s estimated that it already adopts about three-quarters of the EU’s rules through this. It’s also part of the Schengen Area, allowing for passport-free travel with most EU countries.
The core consideration, then, for the referendum is whether it is worth moving beyond that EEA relationship.
Tumi Árnason, a 35-year-old musician living in the capital, said he was planning to vote in favor of entering into talks for EU membership.
“I am for seeing what kind of deal we can get,” said Árnason, citing the economy as his primary concern.
But the international situation did worry him: “I think that at this point siding with the EU would be preferable in this political climate. With the U.S. on one hand, and then Russia on the other, it’s a bit of a precarious situation.”
Hannah Sigurðardóttir, a 68-year-old employee of Iceland’s medicines agency, also raised concerns about the reliability of the U.S. as an ally.
“We can’t count on the U.S., like we did for a long time. I think we should [have] better ties to our friends and allies in Europe. We have a similar history, culture,” she said.
‘Forward Iceland’
Not everyone agrees with the need to gravitate toward Brussels.
Guðlaugur Þór Þórðarson, an MP with the conservative and pro-“No” Independence Party, thought that EEA membership was sufficient and that any swing closer to the EU would be misguided.
Sporting a pin reading Áfram Ísland, or Forward Iceland, the slogan of the “No” campaign, on the lapel of his gray suit jacket, Þórðarson condemned the U.S. president’s comments on Greenland.
“I think it’s, of course, outrageous what Trump is saying about Greenland,” said Þórðarson, who was Iceland’s foreign minister during Trump’s first term in office.
But he cautioned that U.S. administrations come and go.
“When it comes to defense and security, then the key things are the bilateral defense agreement with the U.S. and also being a member of NATO,” he said.
Former Reykjavík Mayor Eggertsson from the “Yes” campaign stressed that the concerns about Arctic security were not just about Trump.
“The Arctic has traditionally been described as a low-tension area when it comes to defense. This is changing because of climate change and melting ice caps, the possibility of new shipping routes opening up,” he said.
While this newfound perception that Iceland could be more vulnerable than previously thought has entered the public consciousness, it is more prosaic concerns that continue to dominate the debate.
Outside of the Reykjavík area, where about two-thirds of the country lives, voters are more likely to put a “No” on their ballots.
Selfoss is a town of 10,000 people about an hour’s drive southeast of Reykjavík. Farmers cultivating the black volcanic soil along the road to the town adorn their bales of hay with the “No” campaign’s Áfram Ísland slogan.
Ari Hrafn Elíasson, an 18-year-old builder from Selfoss, said he would vote against the accession talks.
“I’m going to vote no because the farmers want to vote no. In my opinion, they are the backbone of this country, farmers and fishermen. I’m going to listen to them,” he said.
Another Selfoss resident, 19-year-old fast food worker Dagmar Isabella, said she was in favor of the EU talks but stressed that foreign policy was not her main concern.
She said she was worried about the cost of living, particularly for rents and mortgages. She thought joining the euro could help get galloping inflation under control. Iceland’s July inflation was running at an annual rate of 5.6 percent, nearly double the euro area’s.
Talking about the euro, she said: “It’s a much more stable currency than the Icelandic krona.”

The Rabbitohs finish the regular season against Arrow's former club, the Titans, on the Gold Coast, before a clash with rivals the Roosters in Sydney.
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.
In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.
Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.
Arrow, in jersey number 23, has been named co-captain with Cameron Murray, who is listed to come off the bench.
It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.
The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.
The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.
The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.
Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.
The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.
"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.
"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."
The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.
The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.
Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.
Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

- Storms caused power outages for 2,800 homes, transport disruptions, and the cancellation of a Vuelta a Espana cycling race stage in the Aude department.
AI generated
POMAS, France – A tornado tore through a village in south-western France on Aug 24, injuring 41 people and damaging hundreds of homes, the authorities said.
The French authorities had placed swathes of the country’s south-west on orange alert for storms, and numerous areas were hit by power outages and transport chaos.
In the Aude department, officials cancelled the third stage of the Vuelta a Espana cycling race, which was being held in the area, when a hailstorm forced riders to seek shelter.
The tornado hit hardest in the village of Pomas, which has a population of 1,000, damaging an estimated 300 homes, in some cases ripping their roofs off.
More than 120 emergency workers were deployed to the scene, the local authorities said.
Fifteen of the injured were taken to hospital.
They included a pregnant woman who was hurt when her house collapsed on her, her husband told AFP.
The national weather service, Meteo-France, said winds had reached up to 117km an hour in the nearby village of Arquettes-en-Val.
Storms across southern France upended the transportation network, delaying trains, forcing road closures, and causing delays and cancellations at airports in Bordeaux, Marseille, Nice, Toulouse and even Paris to the north, said Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot.
An estimated 2,800 homes were left without electricity across 10 villages, officials said.
France sees several dozen tornadoes a year on average.
The impact of global warming on their frequency and intensity is unclear, according to Meteo-France. AFP

The US wants to make the fee for new H-1B visas permanent at $103,000
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25

The US wants to make the fee for new H-1B visas permanent at $103,000
Kyiv • UNN
The US Department of Homeland Security is proposing to make the fee for new H-1B visas permanent. Its legality is being challenged in court.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has proposed making permanent a fee of $103,265 for new H-1B work visas for highly skilled foreign workers. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Trump first introduced this fee temporarily last year. Its validity expires in September, but the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has proposed making it permanent. The rule could be finalized by the end of the year.
The H-1B program allows U.S. employers to hire foreign professionals in specialized fields. Each year, 65,000 such visas are provided, plus another 20,000 for workers with higher education degrees. Before Trump's decision, obtaining an H-1B visa usually cost between $2,000 and $5,000.
The fee will not apply to people who are already in the United States on student visas, or to extensions of existing H-1B visas.
The decision is being challenged in court
In June, a federal judge ruled that the fee was unlawful and barred the administration from collecting it. The decision is being appealed in an appeals court.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, several states, and a coalition of labor unions and employers are also opposed to the fee. They argue that the administration lacks the authority to impose such charges without congressional approval.
Supporters of H-1B, in turn, say that the program is necessary for U.S. companies to attract qualified professionals in fields where the United States is experiencing a labor shortage.

Nearly 1.5 million Haitians are currently displaced in a country of about 11 million, and more than five million are facing severe food insecurity, according to UN figures.
The crisis worsened in early 2024, when gangs launched a wave of violence that forced the unelected prime minister to resign.
Haiti has not held any elections since 2016. Its last president, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated in July 2021 and was not replaced.

Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
01:30:10 UTC
10:30:10 KST

Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi
The evolution of English is an unstoppable force and resisting its ‘dumbing down’ may be futile
“Nothing bad can happen. It can only good happen.” Donald J. Trump
It would be easy to write off the regular word salads of America’s 47th president as the increasingly incoherent ramblings of an elderly man in obvious mental and physical decline.
However, one can also argue that Trump’s seemingly dyslexic struggles with the English language reflect a deliberate disregard for grammar rules that resonates with his support base. It’s the level of language that up to half of Americans happily use and identify with, if you think about it.
Laugh if you will at his limited vocabulary, disrespect for formal syntax and contempt for punctuation, but they have never been detrimental to getting his message across as an effective public speaker and communicator.
His very lack of linguistic sophistication – simple words, short sentences, constant repetition, blunt delivery – makes maximum impact with minimum polish, grammar rules and hoity-toity talk be damned.
Trump’s dumbing down of the language is but a microcosm of a global shift towards hyper-simplified English usage, stripped bare of formalities and tuned to resonate on digital platforms. All without the encumbrance of archaic or arbitrary rules and the rigid structure that we are expected to adhere to without even remembering why we have to in the first place.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – The trade war between the US and Canada erupted into an extraordinary exchange of insults and threats between US President Donald Trump and Doug Ford, the leader of Ontario.
The White House put tariffs of 50 per cent on some Canadian goods on Aug 22 after trade talks collapsed.
That prompted Prime Minister Mark Carney to announce hours later that Canada will impose counter-tariffs.
He was backed strongly by Ford, whose province is on the front line of Trump’s tariffs as Canada’s auto and steel manufacturing heartland.
On Aug 22, the Ontario Premier likened Trump to a schoolyard bully who would “take your lunch money” and hat, and said Canada should be ready to use electricity and critical minerals that the US needs as leverage.
Then, on Aug 24, Trump threatened on social media to double tariffs on Canadian autos to 50 per cent to punish Carney’s decision to retaliate.
Ford was in the middle of a radio interview, and the host read out the US President’s entire post.
“He can kiss my a** as far as I’m concerned,” Ford said.
The war of words only spiralled from there.
Trump posted on Truth Social calling Ford “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford”.
That was a reference to Doug Ford’s younger sibling, who made global headlines in 2013 when, as mayor of Toronto, a video emerged of him smoking crack cocaine. He died of cancer in 2016.
The US President also called Ford the “Flunky” of “Governor” Carney, a jibe he returns to when relations sour, alongside saying Canada should be the 51st US state.
“Remember, much of the Electricity, Oil, and Gas that Canada gets is transported through the U.S.A.,” Trump added. “Someone should get these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”
That could be read as a veiled threat against Enbridge Inc pipelines that carry western Canadian crude through the Midwestern US, feeding refineries there before re-entering Canada again in Ontario.
Ford was read some of Trump’s comments at a press conference on a construction site on Aug 24.
He called Trump a “dictator” and repeated his previous insult before launching into a fresh tirade, as hard-hatted workers occasionally chuckled behind him.
“I’m not going to take any advice off a guy that’s the king of bankruptcies,” Ford said. “Your own people, President Trump, don’t even like you. And they’re going to speak loud and clear when it comes to the midterms.”
When asked again about Trump’s social media attacks, Ford said, “I’m not going to take the bait”, before deciding to take the bait.
“This guy’s a loser,” he said, adding: “I have more courage, more brains in my baby toe than he has in his whole body.”
It’s a reprise of a role Ford played a year ago as the Canadian who most gets under Trump’s skin.
Ford briefly imposed a surcharge on the electricity Ontario exports to New York, Michigan and Minnesota, prompting Trump to threaten to increase tariffs on Canadian steel to 50 per cent.
Ford quickly backed down.
Three months later, Trump put global steel tariffs at 50 per cent anyway.
Then, last October, Ford’s government ran TV commercials in the US using an address of former president Ronald Reagan speaking out against tariffs.
That led Trump to terminate trade talks with Canada.
Negotiations over one of the world’s biggest trading relationships went quiet for months, but Ford defended it as the “best ad that’s ever been run.”
In some ways, Ford and Trump are alike – both are teetotallers and populist conservative politicians with a background in business.
Both have even had recent controversies over their official aircraft.
In response to the trade war, Ford has emulated Trump’s famous red “Make America Great Again” baseball caps.
The Ontario Premier has donned a navy blue version emblazoned with “Canada Is Not For Sale”. BLOOMBERG

Trump administration plans to revoke B1, B2 visas of 200,000 asylum seekers
If the action happens, it will be the largest single mass revocation of visas in US history, AP reports.
The United States is preparing to cancel business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the country, according to the Associated Press news agency.
The AP, citing State Department documents and interviews with two US officials, reported on Monday that if the plan goes ahead, it would be the “largest single mass revocation of visas” in the country’s history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump administration has revoked over 175,000 visas: US State Department
- list 2 of 3US judge strikes down Trump immigrant visa ban affecting 75 countries
- list 3 of 3Trump administration seeks to formalise H-1B fee of more than $100,000
It said the State Department is expected to announce the action within the coming weeks, working in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
It would target so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026, whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum.
“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.
Officials cited by the AP said the revocations would not automatically trigger deportations.
Instead, most people with pending asylum cases would be shifted into a different immigration category, effectively stripping their business or tourist designation while their cases proceed.
In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the US and then apply for asylum.
“People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims,” Landau wrote on X. “Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law.”
Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants – demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.
In the past 18 months, the State Department has also revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunk driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against US policies, particularly in the Middle East.

2026-08-25
00:53:42 UTC
09:53:42 KST

Türkiye and Qatar have set a target of increasing their bilateral trade volume to $5 billion, Turkish Trade Minister Omer Bolat said following talks in Ankara.
Bolat met with Qatar's Minister of State for Foreign Trade, Ahmed bin Mohammed Al-Sayed, at the Trade Ministry to review bilateral commerce and investment ties.
"Türkiye-Qatar relations have truly made tremendous progress. Our total annual foreign trade increased 53-fold over the past 21 years, reaching $1.3 billion last year," Bolat told reporters after the meeting.
Trade between the two nations previously climbed to $2.5 billion during preparations for the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, driven largely by construction projects, he added.
Bolat noted that the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, which entered into force last year, will make a significant contribution towards achieving the $5 billion target.
Corporate investments
Turkish contractors have undertaken 206 projects worth a combined $21 billion in Qatar, Bolat said.
Approximately 1,116 Turkish companies currently operate across Qatar's construction, services, and manufacturing sectors.
Meanwhile, around 250 Qatari companies hold investments totalling $7.8 billion in Türkiye, covering finance, banking, energy, logistics, media, and agriculture.
Bolat added that Al-Sayed conveyed the Qatar Investment Authority's desire to expand its investments in Türkiye, with related initiatives underway.
Addressing regional logistics challenges, Bolat stated that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to regional conflict has created supply bottlenecks, underscoring the urgent need for alternative trade routes.
"The current circumstances have shown that alternative routes are greatly needed to avoid dependence solely on maritime transport and the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
Under a transit transportation agreement with Saudi Arabia that took effect on April 15, Turkish carriers are conducting intensive shipments to Gulf countries through Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, as well as via Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
"We will work together to establish these transit and trade corridors on a stronger and more stable basis," Bolat noted.

Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz start US Open mixed doubles vs. team with women’s doubles champ
NEW YORK (AP) — Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz will open the U.S. Open mixed doubles tournament against a team that features the reigning women’s doubles champion.
Williams and Alcaraz will face Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool on Tuesday in the first round of the championship, which will be Williams’ first match at the U.S. Open since 2022.
Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic might have an even tougher draw. The top seeds, based on having the lowest combined singles ranking in the 16-team field, face the team of Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten — who are the No. 1-ranked doubles players on their respective tours.
The first round and quarterfinals are Tuesday. The semifinals and final are Wednesday.
Williams and Alcaraz were drawn to face one of the teams that emerged from the qualifying tournament that was held Monday. That ended up being Routliffe and Glasspool, who won two matches, both requiring match tiebreakers, to secure their place in the main draw.
Routliffe teamed with Gabriela Dabrowski to beat Siniakova and Taylor Townsend for last year’s U.S. Open women’s doubles title. They also won the championship in 2023.
Sabalenka and Djokovic had been slated to play Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe. But Tiafoe withdrew from mixed doubles Monday after losing to Arthur Fils in the Cincinnati Open final on Sunday, opening the door for a team that lost in qualifying to nevertheless earn a spot.
Siniakova and Patten won both their matches to reach the main draw. Kristina Mladenovic and Marcelo Arevalo, who lost to Routliffe and Glasspool in their second match, got the remaining spot and will play Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik.
The eight-team qualifying tournament was added this year to give the traditional doubles specialists an opportunity to compete for the U.S. Open title. When the tournament was overhauled last year — with a $1 million prize for the winners — in an effort to get top singles players to compete, direct entry was based on singles rankings, essentially shutting out the players who largely focus on doubles.
Williams is not planning to play singles in New York. Alcaraz, who has been sidelined since April with a right wrist injury, will return to defend his singles title.

Colombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:34:47 UTC
09:34:47 KST

Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes.
In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes.
De la Espriella said the first joint operations involving the police and the migration authority should begin “this very week”.
“Let the coordinated operations begin to track down illegal immigrants: first, those committing crimes; second, those who have not regularised their status and who will have to be deported immediately,” de la Espriella said during a cabinet meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the Caribbean city that has in effect been turned into an alternative capital.
He echoed the “Americans first” rhetoric of his ally, US president Donald Trump, saying that from now on it would be “Colombians first, Colombians second and Colombians third”.
The Colombian president has joined other Trump-aligned leaders in the region who have also tightened migration rules, including Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast.
De la Espriella’s order is facing criticism from the opposition and human rights activists, who say it will end a migration policy that endured for more than a decade under both rightwing and leftwing governments and benefited above all migrants fleeing the humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Venezuela.
Although he used the anti-immigration rhetoric characteristic of other far-right candidates during his campaign, his platform focused chiefly on his promise to pursue an iron-fist policy against criminal groups.
In the same announcement, he also declared that all gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining, extortion and smuggling were “terrorists and we will treat them as such. Whatever happens, we will defeat them, by reason or by force.”
The president did not directly mention Venezuelans when discussing immigration, but they account for roughly 90% of all migrants in the country. Of the 2.8 million Venezuelans living in Colombia, about 848,000 are in an irregular situation, including 193,000 children and adolescents.
The leftwing senator María José Pizarro Rodríguez reposted the president’s announcement and asked whether he was “proposing a Colombian ICE against fellow Latin Americans”, in reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She added that the “order to deport irregular migrants is pure xenophobia and aporophobia”.
“Instead of persecuting people fleeing poverty and violence, regularise their status. There are thousands of migrants who work hard and contribute to the economies of the countries that receive them,” she wrote.
The Colombian newspaper El Tiempo reported that sources within the migration department believe the agency does not have enough staff to carry out the operations De la Espriella has promised.
Analysts have also noted that under Colombian law there is no such category as an “illegal” immigrant, as De la Espriella said, but rather migrants in an “irregular” situation, since being in the country without the proper documentation is not a crime.

DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:34:29 UTC
09:34:29 KST

DRC’s constitutional battle: The fight over the 2028 vote
President Tshisekedi’s reform push is fuelling a battle over DRC’s 2028 succession.
Kinshasa, DR Congo – President Felix Tshisekedi is due to leave office in 2028 under the current Constitution of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Yet with more than two years to go, a battle over the rules governing what happens when his mandate ends is already reshaping Congolese politics.
In May, Tshisekedi said he had not sought a third term but would accept one if the Congolese people wanted him to continue. The remarks revived opposition fears that constitutional reform could eventually open a path beyond the existing two-term limit.
Under the current constitution, the president is elected for five years, renewable once, while the number and length of presidential terms are protected from constitutional revision.
Tshisekedi’s camp says the country needs institutional reform. Opponents of the reform fear the process could ultimately be used to change the rules governing presidential succession.
The dispute is unfolding as the DRC fights a rebellion in the east led by M23, an armed group that operates within the broader Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition that controls Goma and Bukavu, the capitals of North Kivu and South Kivu.
With an opposition mobilisation planned for September and Tshisekedi preparing to outline an inclusive national dialogue, the confrontation is entering a critical phase.
The referendum battle
The confrontation accelerated in June when the Parliament of the Democratic Republic of the Congo passed legislation setting out conditions for organising a referendum.
The Constitutional Court ruled in July that the law complied with the constitution, while raising concerns about some of its provisions. On August 10, Tshisekedi formally asked the presidents of the National Assembly and Senate to reconsider the legislation in light of the court’s observations. The National Assembly said the fresh deliberation would be placed on the agenda for its September session.
The legislation provides for a constituent assembly followed by a referendum in the event of what it describes as a “major dysfunction” of state institutions.
Critics of the process say the mechanism could eventually be used to alter provisions that currently prevent Tshisekedi from seeking a third term. The government, meanwhile, has presented constitutional reform as a broader institutional issue rather than an explicit bid to extend the president’s tenure.
The main opposition group campaigning against the process is known as C64, or the Article 64 coalition. Its name refers to Article 64 of the DRC’s constitution, which calls on citizens to oppose anyone who takes power in violation of the constitutional order.
C64 says it will resist any attempt to use constitutional reform to extend Tshisekedi’s mandate beyond 2028. The coalition announced a nationwide mobilisation for September 15, with demonstrations in Kinshasa expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple, the seat of parliament.
Taking the fight to parliament
The dispute has already spilled onto the streets.
Thousands demonstrated in Goma and Bukavu on July 28 against proposed constitutional changes and any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s time in office.
In Kinshasa, protesters are expected to converge on the Palais du Peuple.
For C64, the destination is deliberate: the coalition wants to take its protest to the institution at the centre of the constitutional process.
Jean-Marc Kabund, a Congolese opposition politician, told Al Jazeera that no constitutional revision, referendum or legal manoeuvre should be allowed to circumvent the current constitution.
He warned that this happening while the country is at war could deepen divisions and threaten national cohesion.
A constitutional fight during a war
The constitutional dispute is unfolding alongside a conflict that has transformed eastern Congo.
M23 and the AFC have seized large areas of territory, including Goma and Bukavu. The Congolese government accuses Rwanda of supporting M23, a charge that Kigali denies.
The war is also raising questions about the 2028 elections.
Tshisekedi has warned that elections may not be possible if the fighting continues, arguing that it would be difficult to organise a credible vote while parts of the country remain outside government control.
Emmanuel Bugama, a Congolese political analyst based in Bunia, told Al Jazeera that national interests should come before political disputes.
“The nation’s best interests should take precedence over these political squabbles,” he said.
The view from Goma
In Goma, the argument is being watched from a city no longer under Kinshasa’s control.
Gentil Mulume, a civil society activist in Goma, told Al Jazeera that any constitutional change extending Tshisekedi’s mandate would not be recognised in territory controlled by M23 and the AFC.
“If Tshisekedi dares to amend this constitution to extend his term of office, it will not be recognised here,” he said.
Mulume said the dispute was part of a deeper divide between Kinshasa and the east. He argued that continued Tshisekedi rule could be viewed there as a form of domination and that self-determination should be part of the political debate.
His comments illustrate how a constitutional confrontation in Kinshasa is being interpreted in territory already beyond the government’s effective control.
What do ordinary Congolese know?
There is also a more basic question: how much do ordinary citizens understand about the proposed changes?
Kevin Kalala, a 30-year-old mobile-credit retailer in Kinshasa, told Al Jazeera that he does not know enough about the constitution to take a position.
“We do not know what our constitution entails,” he said. “The Congolese state should start by teaching us about our constitution.”
Kalala said citizens should first be shown which provisions need changing, why they need changing, and what the benefits would be.
“I am neither for nor against amending the constitution,” he said.
An offer of dialogue
As tensions rise, Tshisekedi has proposed an inclusive national dialogue involving political parties, civil society and religious groups.
While in Libreville, Gabon, on August 16, he said he would soon address the nation to set out his vision and the contours of the talks. The date and format of the dialogue have yet to be announced.
Tshisekedi has ruled out sitting with people he accuses of siding with Rwanda or the armed rebellion.
Martin Fayulu, who challenged Tshisekedi in the 2018 presidential election, has called for former President Joseph Kabila and Corneille Nangaa, the political leader of the AFC, to participate.
For now, the constitutional dispute is running alongside the war in the east and the uncertainty over the 2028 elections.
The question is no longer only whether the constitution will change. It is whether Congo’s political forces can agree on the rules for what happens when Tshisekedi’s current mandate ends.
“We are certainly heading towards one of the most decisive periods in our recent history,” Bugama told Al Jazeera. “The country is under the control of an armed group, whilst the government in Kinshasa is posturing over constitutional reform instead of tackling what matters most.”

Want to keep a big dog in Hong Kong? Experts share what you should know
Concerns about responsible handling of big dogs raised after attacks last week
Heat, humidity and crowded living spaces could pose challenges for Hongkongers hoping to keep large or aggressive dogs as pets, experts have said, urging potential owners to consider the needs of such animals before deciding to house them.
They issued the warning after a woman and two small canines were mauled in two separate attacks last week.
The woman was found collapsed in Ping Yeung Tsuen, hours after she was attacked at a dog training centre by a canine suspected of being a mixed-breed fighting dog. She was certified dead at the scene.
The smaller dogs were mauled to death in Yuen Long by an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) mastiff-type canine earlier that week.
Discussing the importance of correctly caring for big dogs, Lau Yun-yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Society for Pet Nutrition, said large canines, particularly those with thick coats, could face greater challenges in Hong Kong’s hot and humid climate.
“Dogs rely primarily on evaporative cooling through panting rather than sweating,” he said, adding that sustained high humidity could significantly reduce their ability to cool themselves.

California lawmakers vote to increase transparency over influencers’ paid political posts
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — The California Senate passed a bill Monday that would fine content creators who don’t disclose they were paid to post in support of a political candidate or issue on the ballot.
California, along with Texas, already requires content creators to include payment disclaimers on their political posts. The goal of this year’s bill is to better enforce the law. The legislation, which was authored by Democratic Assemblymember Marc Berman, will need a final vote in the Assembly before it can reach Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk. Newsom has until the end of September to sign or veto it.
“Voters should have a right to know whether or not campaigns are paying for the messaging that they’re seeing,” Berman said in an interview last month.
Under current law, the state’s campaign watchdog can seek a court order compelling an influencer to disclose that they were paid, but that process can take months. Berman’s bill would give the state’s Fair Political Practices Commission, which supports the proposal, the power to fine influencers and political committees if they are found to have violated the law, allowing the commission to bypass the court process. Content creators could face fines of up to $5,000 per violation, according to the commission.
The bill’s passage comes as federal efforts to pass disclosure requirements for influencers have yet to advance. Sen. Adam Schiff of California introduced a bill in Congress last month, but it hasn’t received a vote.

Nevada sues US government over cuts to Colorado River access

Nevada sues US government over cuts to Colorado River access
- Nevada has sued the US government to block planned cuts to its Colorado River water allocation, which could reduce its share by two-thirds and threaten Las Vegas's water supply.
- The federal plan cuts water use for lower-basin states Arizona, California, and Nevada by up to 3.7 billion cubic metres annually, while upper-basin states keep their current levels.
- The cuts respond to ongoing drought and overuse, with federal officials warning that without agreement, hydropower dams on the river could fail, and other states like Arizona may also file lawsuits.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES - Nevada on Aug 24 launched legal action against the administration of US President Donald Trump over a plan that would cut the state’s access to the vital Colorado River.
The river, which originates in the Rocky Mountains, makes farming possible in large tracts of the arid American south-west, and provides drinking water to the 40 million people who live there, including in cities like Phoenix.
But decades of over-use, coupled with years of drought, have put crippling strain on a watercourse whose management has always been based on an over-allocation of available resources.
Last week the federal government announced it was imposing cuts on the amount of water the so-called “lower-basin states” – Arizona, California and Nevada – can use, while leaving the allowances for the “upper basin states” of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming unchanged.
The plan envisages slashing the three states’ collective water consumption by up to 3.7 billion cubic metres per year until 2036 – the equivalent of 1.5 million Olympic-sized swimming pools.
Now Nevada has launched legal action seeking to block the change, which state officials say could reduce their allocation by two-thirds, potentially devastating the desert city of Las Vegas, which depends on the river for 90 per cent of its water.
“This isn’t about political posturing,” Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo, a Republican, said on Aug 24.
“This is a matter of survival for a community that represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
Federal officials say their plan to cut usage is necessary because the seven states that lie on the river have been unable to agree amongst themselves.
They say without an agreement, dams on the river that are used to generate hydropower could cease to function.
Experts say Nevada’s lawsuit, lodged in a US district court, is unlikely to be the only legal action, with Arizona – which faces the deepest cuts – expected to launch its own challenge.
The federal government directive and the resulting legal action come after Lake Powell and Lake Mead, America’s two largest reservoirs, and which are fed by the Colorado River, fell to record low levels.
Scientists say human behaviour, including the unchecked burning of fossil fuels, is warming the global climate and interrupting weather patterns.
This leads to more sustained droughts in some parts of the planet, and more ferocious storms in others. AFP

- list 1 of 3Tunisia recovers 11 bodies after boat carrying migrants sinks, 3 missing
- list 2 of 3Antigovernment protesters take to Tunisia’s streets for second month
- list 3 of 3Tunisia sees protests after migrant boat sinking kills eight
The migrant boat, believed to be headed towards Italy, sank late on Friday after setting off from a location between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane with 15 mostly young people on board. It sank about 14 nautical miles (26km) off the coast of Zarzis.
Only one person survived, having drifted at sea for about 48 hours before being rescued by a commercial vessel, according to Tunisian media.
The bodies of 12 people were recovered by Sunday, the Tunisian National Guard said.
The deaths have sparked a wave of grief and anger, triggering violent protests in Ben Guerdane on Sunday night. According to the Tunisian National Guard, some 14 people on the boat were from Ben Guerdane, and one was from Zarzis.
The protesters burned tyres and blocked roads, while police responded by firing tear gas to disperse the crowds. The protesters demanded better living conditions and economic development, saying a lack of opportunities and years of marginalisation are pushing young people to undertake dangerous sea crossings to Europe in search of a better life.
Mostafa Abdelkebir, the head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights, said those on board included seven members of the same family. He told the Reuters news agency on Monday that a hospital in Ben Guerdane has received at least 19 bodies of migrants recovered from the sea over the past two days.
It was not clear if all the bodies were from the boat that sank. Abdelkebir told Reuters that genetic testing was being carried out to identify the bodies and determine how many had been on board the boat.
Some in Tunisia have called for a national day of mourning over the deaths.
Imad Oulad Jibril, a lawmaker, on Sunday called it “the tragedy of a nation that sees its youth fleeing the hardships of the land only to be swallowed by the sea”.
The opposition Democratic Bloc party tied the sinking to Tunisia’s economic strains, saying: “When crossing the sea becomes easier than living in Tunisia, we must ask: Who is at fault?”
Tunisia has seen similar tragedies in recent years, including the Kerkennah disaster, in which more than 100 people died or went missing in 2018 after the sinking of a migrant boat. The incident led to the dismissal of the then-interior minister. In Zarzis in 2022, at least 18 people died after another migrant boat sank, sparking weeks of protests.
Tunisia’s southeastern coast lies just 145 km (90 miles) from the Italian island of Lampedusa.
The central Mediterranean is considered the deadliest migration route in the world, according to the International Organization for Migration, which says at least 821 migrants have died or gone missing on the route this year – more than double the toll over the same period last year.
Across the Mediterranean as a whole, at least 1,065 people have died or gone missing, according to the group.

US state probes OpenAI over rogue AI hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:17:00 KST

US state probes OpenAI over rogue AI hack
WASHINGTON – ChatGPT-maker OpenAI faces an investigation by the US state of Alabama after the company revealed in July that its models went rogue and hacked an artificial intelligence (AI) platform during testing.
In mid-July, two OpenAI models escaped their confined testing environment and gained access to the internet, where they found and attacked Hugging Face, a site AI developers use to store and share models and data sets.
The incident raised alarm about the dangers of AI systems acting autonomously and breaking guardrails set by human programmers to prevent safety violations.
In a 14-page order, the office of Alabama Attorney-General Steve Marshall demanded OpenAI hand over internal records about the July incident, along with a long list of other material, including the identity of every employee involved in the intrusion or in the testing that led to it.
The investigation comes in response to “the company’s complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards”, Marshall’s office alleged in a statement.
It is the first known state investigation into whether an AI system attacking another company’s infrastructure amounts to a violation of consumer protection law – a finding that would expose the company to major litigation across the US.
On Aug 3, Alabama and 14 other states wrote to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman asking the company to preserve records on the incident and halt any internal cybersecurity evaluations of its models.
OpenAI has not responded to that August request, a spokesperson for the Alabama attorney-general’s office told AFP.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
However, OpenAI said in a statement to the tech news site TechCrunch that it was “conducting a thorough review along with external advisers”.
“Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly,” it added. AFP

US Supreme Court hands Trump admin win in mail-in voting ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:15:36 UTC
09:15:36 KST

The Supreme Court has cleared the way for US President Donald Trump to move ahead with his executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much his administration can implement before the fast-approaching midterm elections.
The decision on Monday appears to leave room for additional court challenges that could further slow Trump's order.
And with some states beginning to send mail ballots to voters in just a few weeks, time is running short to impose major changes.
Mail balloting has long been a favourite target for the Trump administration, which said that it breeds fraud.
The case could be one of multiple voting-related challenges before the justices. The Justice Department had filed an emergency appeal asking the high court to allow work on implementing the changes before the midterms.
Trump's executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the US Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists.
'Rushed effort'
In June, Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the president lacked the authority to order changes in how states administer federal elections, noting that under the US Constitution, states have the role of determining voter-eligibility requirements.
The judge also noted that federal agencies lack the ability to compile accurate lists of citizens for each state.
The states contend that their claims are not hypothetical and that the administration's "rushed effort to change the rules of mail voting on the eve of the November midterms risks disenfranchising a substantial number of voters."
The judge rejected the administration's arguments, finding that the suit was not filed too soon and that the states had legal standing because they would face election administration disruption, compliance costs and a credible threat of criminal prosecution.

‘Honest leaders are the first step to a better future’: Cockroach hunger striker targets India’s political class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
00:00:42 UTC
09:00:42 KST

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles

UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles
Following his first international visit to Kyiv, the new UK leader seeks a multi-nation deal to secure vital interceptors for Ukraine
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he and other European leaders plan to travel to the US next month to lobby President Donald Trump to let Ukraine access some of its Patriot air defence missile stocks ahead of the winter.
“I’m looking forward to going to New York in September,” Burnham said in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv on Monday evening, referring to the coming UN General Assembly meeting in New York. It would be his first trip to the US since becoming prime minister.
“I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion,” he said. “Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
Burnham’s comments came on his first international visit since becoming premier, after chairing a meeting of Ukraine’s allies for the first time and holding a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky has made repeated pleas to European nations and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot missile interceptors and to replenish its stocks in time for winter, when Russia is expected to ramp up attacks on energy infrastructure again. The interceptors are the most potent weapons to shoot down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles.
Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current struggles defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to its low stockpile of interceptors are “fixable”.

How the French language contributed to the US-Canada trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:55:00 UTC

How the French language contributed to the US-Canada trade war
- The US-Canada trade war has escalated into a cultural conflict centered on protecting the French language and Quebec culture, which Canada views as fundamental rights.
- Canada faces new US tariffs worth US$20 billion and has vowed to retaliate equally, with strong support from Quebec residents for defending their cultural identity.
- Quebec's recent laws on French-language content and product labelling challenge US companies, while the US downplays language issues but objects to financial rules favouring Canadian competitors.
AI generated
MONTREAL – The trade war between the United States and Canada has taken on the flavour of a culture war after the collapse of negotiations last week.
According to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the dispute with the nation’s largest trading partner was not just about tariff demands but what he called unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”.
Those are not typical sticking points in trade negotiations, but emotive ones in Canada, particularly in the French-speaking eastern province of Quebec, which has long sought to preserve its distinct identity.
Carney said Canadian subsidies for Francophone culture, the role of Francophone online media and bilingual labeling of products sold in Canada were among the issues at stake.
He described these as “fundamental rights” and said there was “a huge gap between Canadian and American perspectives”.
The Prime Minister also contended that the US wanted to destroy Canada’s automotive, steel and aluminum industries, and restrict Canadian trade deals with other countries.
After the breakdown of talks, Canada now faces additional tariffs on some US$20 billion (S$25.4 billion) worth of its US exports and double tariffs on Canadian vehicles, while Carney has vowed to match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar”.
In Quebec, Carney’s decision to break off negotiations was widely supported.
A poll published on Aug 23 by the Angus Reid Institute found that 85 per cent of Quebecers supported the move – the highest approval rate among the 10 Canadian provinces.
“Our identity is not negotiable,” Quebec Premier Christine Frechette wrote on Aug 23 in a social media post.
She faces a re-election battle in October and is currently trailing in polls to the leader of a Quebec separatist party.
According to the Canadian media, Frechette said Washington wanted concessions on Quebec’s rules for appliances and instruction manuals, as well as its law promoting French-language cultural content.
Recent legislation by Quebec allows it to regulate how much French-language content digital platforms offer and how prominently it appears, which can add to the cost of doing business for US companies, the Montreal Gazette reported.
In an interview on Aug 24, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer played down the language issue in the trade talks as a “funny fake story”.
“What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada,” Greer told CNBC.
“But I understand why the Quebecois want to have French language content and all of that. And we think that’s a really valuable thing.” AFP

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that the US must change its approach toward Tehran, warning that reliance on coercion and “bullying” would only complicate diplomatic efforts.
“The US must correct its tone and approach in dealing with Iran, as relying on coercion and bullying will only complicate the implementation processes” for the Pakistan-brokered memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US, Pezeshkian said during a meeting with Pakistani Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir in Tehran on Monday, according to Iran’s Tasnim News Agency.
Pezeshkian described establishing lasting peace and security in the region along with cooperation and coordination among Muslim countries as a “fundamental necessity.”
Meanwhile, Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said "another defeat" for the US was in the offing, saying the Islamic Republic had a "two-year plan" to counter Washington's new sanctions.
"They have done everything they could to test the determination of the Iranian people and the country's officials, but they have failed every time. It seems they wished to suffer yet another defeat," Madanizadeh told state television.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he added.
Iran ‘dismisses’ pressure
Earlier in the day, Pakistan’s army chief met with Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, in Tehran, as Islamabad pushes to revive stalled direct talks between Iran and the US.
The meeting came during Munir’s ongoing visit to Tehran, where he is discussing new proposals with Iranian officials following fresh contacts with Washington, multiple Pakistani government sources told Anadolu.
According to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB, Qalibaf told Munir that Washington had repeatedly failed to honour its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
“The commitments of the parties under the memorandum of understanding are clear, and it was the US that, by failing to honour its commitments, prevented stability from being established in the region and provided another reason for distrust toward it,” he was quoted as saying.
Qalibaf, who is also heading Iran’s negotiating team, rejected the prospect of Tehran yielding to pressure and said Iran was pursuing the implementation of the memorandum’s terms.

U.S. Supreme Court lifts lower court ruling that blocks Trump's order to restrict mail-in voting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-25
07:45:17 CST
08:45:17 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday lifted a lower court's ruling that blocked part of U.S. President Donald Trump's executive order to restrict mail-in voting, but it remains to be seen whether such measures would be implemented before the November midterm election.
"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell," the nation's highest court said in a ruling.
"But the Order itself does not harm the States, so the District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement it. And for the reasons discussed, that injunction is likely to irreparably harm the Government if it remains in place while the appellate process runs its course," the court continued.
The ruling marks the latest court action in the legal fight over Trump's order rolled out in March, which calls for the Department of Homeland Security to develop state lists of adult U.S. citizens and for the United States Postal Service to obtain lists of eligible mail voters from states.
U.S. media believe that it remains to be seen whether such measures would be implemented before the November midterm election.
CNN report noted that additional legal challenges could hinder implementation of Trump's plan before the midterm elections.
"It remains unclear what impact the high court's order will actually have on eligible mail-in voters," according to a report from NPR.
"The legal fight is far from over, with a separate set of lawsuits led by Democrats and voting rights groups continuing to play out as this fall's election draws closer," the NPR report said. ■

Calls grow for US to deny visa to RSS chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:38:12 UTC
08:38:12 KST

More than 1,000 people across the US have written to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, calling on the State Department to deny or revoke a US visa for Mohan Bhagwat, the head of India’s right-wing Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS.
The letters, collected by the Indian American Muslim Council (IAMC) alongside allied organisations, call on Washington to cancel Bhagwat's scheduled August 29, appearance at Madison Square Garden in New York City amid widespread public opposition.
"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Indian Americans, and Madison Square Garden should not present him as though he does. The State Department has the authority to deny him a visa, and a federal commission has already recommended it. They must act before August 29," said Mohammed Jawad, President of the IAMC.
Sanctions calls
In March, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) recommended targeted sanctions against the RSS, including asset freezes and visa restrictions on its leadership, citing its involvement in "acts of extreme violence and intolerance against members of minority groups for decades."
The Congressional Research Service classifies the RSS as a "hardline Hindu nationalist" organisation.
Human Rights Watch has identified the RSS and its affiliates as "most responsible" for violence against Christians and "directly responsible" for the 2002 anti-Muslim violence in Gujarat.
International watchdogs, including Genocide Watch and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum's Early Warning Project, have repeatedly raised alarms over state-tolerated mob violence, bulldozer demolitions of Muslim properties, and the systemic disenfranchisement of India's religious minorities.
Global pushback
The US petition follows actions in Canada, where more than 40 civil society, human rights, and faith groups urged Ottawa to bar Bhagwat, and Canadian MPs called for a ban on the RSS.
The RSS, founded in 1925, serves as the ideological parent organisation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Amid mounting scrutiny, senior RSS leaders, including General Secretary Dattatreya Hosabale, have recently conducted outreach tours across the US, Britain, and Germany to counter international criticism and oppose calls for Global Magnitsky sanctions.
IAMC has urged Madison Square Garden management to cancel the event and has called on New York officials to condemn the platforming of the RSS leadership.

Details

After receiving the assignment concerning Verzilov, Flores contacted lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov. According to her, together they managed to postpone the operation, after which she fled Russia. Zakhvatov said that Flores contacted him in the summer of 2025, and that they managed to get her out of the country approximately 10 days ago.
Flores said that she spoke about her cooperation with the FSB in order to help other people in similar situations.

Mark Walter's TWG Global hires Goldman veteran Markowitz as top lawyer amid probe of insurers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:16:19 UTC
08:16:19 KST

TWG Global has tapped veteran Goldman Sachs lawyer David Markowitz to be its chief legal officer, as federal investigators probe how two insurers that are part of TWG CEO Mark Walter's sprawling business empire classified loans to companies the billionaire controls.
Markowitz, while at Goldman, was a major player in the team that negotiated settlements worth billions of dollars to resolve the corruption scandal involving Goldman and its Malaysian subsidiary in connection with the Malaysian state-owned development company 1MDB. The scandal led to criminal and regulatory cases alleging Foreign Corrupt Practices Act violations by the bank.
"We are pleased to welcome David to TWG Global," Walter, who also owns the Los Angeles Dodgers, said in a statement Monday.
"His deep legal experience and proven leadership will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen the legal framework that supports our growth and allows us to execute on our long-term strategic priorities," Walter said.
Walter has not been charged with wrongdoing in the insurance probe.
Bloomberg first reported Markowitz's hiring by TWG, which is a holding company with interests in financial services, insurance, artificial intelligence and technology, and sports and media.
Markowitz's hiring comes nearly two weeks after Walter shocked the sports world by agreeing to sell his controlling stake in the Los Angeles Lakers — which he acquired last October — to Joshua Kushner and Bob Iger in a deal that valued the basketball team at $12.5 billion.
That sale revived attention on the parallel investigations into Walter's businesses by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The probes are focused in part on Delaware Life Insurance Co. and its affiliate, Clear Spring Life and Annuity, two Group 1001 insurers ultimately controlled by Walter, and how they labeled about $20 billion in loans to companies that were part of Walter's empire in regulatory filings.
The insurers reclassified billions of dollars of investments as affiliated or related-party transactions after receiving grand jury subpoenas and conducting internal reviews. Lending to affiliates is not illegal.
But Delaware Life, in a reclassification of its audited 2025 financials, said its affiliated investments stood at about 42% of invested assets, up from the 3% originally stated.
TWG last week announced it had agreed to exchange up to $6.5 billion of affiliated investments held by Delaware Life Insurance Co. for an equal amount of nonaffiliated assets.
"Under the agreement, TWG Global takes on investments tied to the performance of affiliated entities and the insurers receive assets that are independent of any affiliate," TWG said in a statement.
Markowitz joined Goldman in 2011, and most recently was the bank's global co-head of litigation and regulatory proceedings.
Before that, Markowitz spent eight years at the Securities and Exchange Commission's enforcement division and later had senior roles in the New York Attorney General's Office.
"I have long admired TWG Global's unique position across some of the world's most cutting-edge industries and its ambitious vision for transforming category-defining businesses and building enduring value," Markowitz said in a statement.
"I look forward to working with the incredible leadership team and helping grow the company's existing legal structure," he said.
— CNBC's Kasey O'Brien contributed to this article.
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that TWG Global acquired the Los Angeles Lakers in October 2025. A previous version misstated the month the team was purchased.

US judge postpones Lockerbie bombing trial over new evidence
Defence granted time to review newly disclosed material days before jury selection for former Libyan agent accused in 1988 attack
A federal judge on Monday postponed a trial in the US for a former Libyan intelligence official charged in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103, citing the discovery of new evidence that defence lawyers want to examine in the nearly 40-year-old case.
Jury selection was scheduled to begin Wednesday for the federal trial of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi in Washington DC. His trial will be the first in the US for the December 21, 1988, bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people, most of them Americans.
US District Judge Dabney Friedrich’s order did not specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.
Al-Marimi’s lawyers say prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them on Saturday and added that their “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development”. Defence lawyer Laura Koenig, an assistant federal public defender, declined to elaborate in response to an Associated Press inquiry.
The judge scheduled a September 1 hearing in Washington to discuss the status of the case. Friedrich’s brief order cited the complex nature of the case, the newly discovered evidence and “the need for the defence to determine how best to defend this case” as reasons to postpone the trial.
Al-Marimi is charged in the US with making the bomb that downed the plane.

====================================================================================================

Literacy Owns AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
23:15:16 UTC
08:15:16 KST

Despite recent hiccups and doomsday warnings, AI will continue to develop and become part of our everyday lives in much the same way that the internet has since the dotcom bubble burst over 20 years ago. Fears that widespread use of AI will make many job functions obsolete are well founded, but it will also create many opportunities for people skilled in its operation, especially those who can clearly communicate instructions and break down ideas into text. These skills are more than AI literacy, they are skills that we acquire through reading, listening, writing, and speaking—advanced literacy skills.
We need to recognize what AI is good at and what makes it work best for us—how it can automate mundane tasks and streamline processes, but not replace perspective or lateral or critical thought.
AI won’t replace communication or critical thinking, but it is replacing many entry-level jobs.
To make the most of AI, language and critical thinking are prerequisites. You can’t construct prompts to give AI instructions without using precise language. Nor can you check output without careful and critical review. So, if we are to provide our next generation of AI natives with the skills they need for success, we should focus on developing advanced literacy in middle and high school and then increase our attention on humanities like English, World Languages, Linguistics, and Philosophy.
Courses combining AI and philosophy are surging in popularity in China, Hong Kong, and the Philippines, driven by the demand from employers for graduates who can understand and use generative technologies as well as critically evaluate them.
In France, philosophy is strictly compulsory for all students in their final year (Terminale) across general academic tracks, and university applicants must take a philosophy exam to pass the baccalauréat.
Just a few weeks ago, The Economist reported that AI companies are hiring philosophers in large numbers, as philosophy plays a key role in improving the reasoning ability, safety, and ethical judgment of AI models. According to data released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York earlier this year, the unemployment rate for computer science majors in the US was 7% as of 2024, but for philosophy majors it stood at just 5.1%.
This is not to say that all students need to focus on philosophy. Studying language and literature is another, more practical, route to acquiring many of the same valuable skills—comprehension, reasoning, argument, and communication.
While we must continue to focus on helping ALL children achieve basic literacy in the early grades, we also need to recognize the importance of developing ALL students’ literacy skills as they advance through their schooling and make the most of their linguistic assets.
To work effectively with the latest technological tools in their learning and their work, today’s students need to articulate complex ideas, concepts, and functions; understand detail and nuance; and produce output that speaks to our increasingly multilingual and multicultural society. Our educational policymakers need to react to a world where AI is the ubiquitous tool by encouraging students developing their communication and literacy skills throughout their elementary, high school, college, and work careers.
Daniel Ward

Britain and France pledge stronger support as Ukraine marks Independence Day
