Ukraine has issued a unique commemorative silver coin marking the 35th anniversary of Independence
Kyiv • UNN
The 20-hryvnia coin is made of .925 sterling silver, with a mintage of up to 5,000 pieces. Its design symbolizes the protection of Ukraine’s freedom.
On Ukraine’s Independence Day, August 24, 2026, the National Bank of Ukraine put into circulation a commemorative coin “To the 35th Anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence,” UNN reports, citing the NBU.
Details
The coin continues the “Ukrainian State” series and is dedicated to the 35th anniversary of the proclamation of Ukraine’s independence—one of the most important events in the modern history of Ukrainian statehood, which embodied the Ukrainian people’s thousand-year aspiration for freedom.
The presentation of this unique silver commemorative coin took place in the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. It was here that, 35 years ago, on August 24, 1991, the Act of Proclamation of Ukraine’s Independence was adopted.
“For the National Bank, every commemorative coin is an opportunity to speak through the language of symbols, remind people of what is important, and preserve memory. When we were looking for the image that most accurately embodies 35 years of Ukraine’s Independence, we chose a shield. It has been struck, but it has not broken; it has endured. This is a metaphor for Ukraine. And the hand of a Ukrainian warrior firmly holding this shield reminds us that independence is protected by people, by Ukrainian soldiers. They defend it for the sake of a future symbolized by a child’s drawing—simple, like all true values: a child, a heart, the sun, a home. We bow our heads before those who gave their lives for these values. We thank those who are defending them now,” emphasized Andriy Pyshnyy, Governor of the National Bank of Ukraine.
“Today demonstrated a very important component of our unity. Different parliamentarians, different people, different eras, but everyone has the same goal—to do everything so that Ukraine endures and Ukraine wins. This is the leitmotif for each of us. Great goals lie ahead of us, and we will certainly achieve them. And the grandeur of this moment must be preserved in symbols that will carry this information to future generations, including in Ukrainian currency,” noted Ruslan Stefanchuk, Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine.
About the coin’s design
The commemorative coin “To the 35th Anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence” has a face value of 20 hryvnias and is made of .925 sterling silver; its minting quality category is “special uncirculated,” and the weight of the precious metal in pure form is 62.2 g. The coin’s edge is smooth with recessed inscriptions. The coin is decorated with patination and selective gilding. Its mintage is up to 5 000 pieces.
The obverse of the coin depicts the hand of a serviceman holding a shield. At the top is an image of a child’s drawing that serves as a talisman for the defender. In the upper-left section is the inscription УКРАЇНА, while on the right are the small State Emblem of Ukraine, the year of minting—2026, the denomination 20, and the graphic hryvnia symbol ₴. The circular inscription reads: 35 РОКІВ БОРОТЬБИ ЗА МАЙБУТНЄ.
The reverse depicts the outer side of a shield with damage, symbolizing the struggle for the freedom and independence of the Ukrainian people.
Artist—Andriy Sahach.

China’s lunar ambitions took a hit after the country called off the launch of a spacecraft that it has aimed to make the first to ever land on the moon’s south pole.
Chang’e 7 was supposed to launch onboard a Long March 5 rocket on August 24, but the launch was scrubbed on Sunday evening, China’s Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said in a statement. Poor weather conditions linked to Typhoon Narra were likely a factor. As a result, the mission will be put on ice until at least 2027.
The decision to delay the mission was reached after extensive review, the CMSA said, and reflects the need for “absolute safety.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
China and the U.S. are in a race to send humans back to the moon, a feat that that U.S. accomplished in the 1960s and that has never been achieved by any other country. Chang’e 7 is to play to a crucial part in China’s ambitions: the probe is designed to search for frozen water in the Shackleton Crater, a pit that spans some 21 kilometers (13 miles) and sits beside the lunar south pole.
No spacecraft has ever landed in that region, which scientists consider to be among the likeliest places to find water on the moon. Locating water that can be used by humans is vital to establishing any long-term lunar presence. NASA and China are eyeing the region to establish a crewed base—and because this real estate is so precious, it matters who gets their first.
NASA plans to establish a lunar colony by 2036, while China hopes to begin construction of the International Lunar Research Station, a moon base built in collaboration with Russia, in 2031. The CMSA has stated it aims to put humans on the lunar surface no later than 2030, while NASA’s Artemis IV mission to land humans on the moon for the first time in more than half a century is tentatively scheduled for early 2028.

Trump Suddenly Wants a Summit With Kim Jong Un. Why Now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:56:00 UTC
23:56:00 KST

On August 16, President Donald Trump posted an old photograph of himself and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Truth Social, the social media platform he owns. The picture, taken during a meeting at the Demilitarized Zone in 2019, showed neither man smiling.
Hours later, Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with Kim as one reason. Two days after that, the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was pushing aides to arrange a face-to-face meeting with Kim as early as November, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.
For a relationship that went cold after the failed Hanoi summit in February 2019, and that stayed cold through the first year and a half of the second Trump term, the sudden urgency raises an obvious question: why now?
The most direct answer is domestic politics. The war Trump launched against Iran remains unresolved (and unpopular), with no clear victory on the horizon. Shifting the story away from Iran carries real appeal – and a North Korea summit would definitely steal the spotlight, judging by the furor the mere idea of such a summit has generated.
A summit with Kim on the sidelines of the Shenzhen gathering would land roughly two weeks after the November 3 midterm elections. That would let Trump announce a foreign policy win in the making without voters being able to judge the actual results of the summit (which, going by past efforts, may well be disappointing).
The payoff looks less obvious from the vantage of Pyongyang. Kim Jong Un has little incentive to help rescue Trump from sliding approval numbers tied to the drawn-out Iran war.
And then there’s the South Korea factor. Trump’s annoyance with Seoul was on display in the social media post that announced the drawdown of the allies’ joint military exercises.
South Korea pledged $350 billion in investment as part of a tariff deal reached last year, and the rollout has lagged badly. Trump is reportedly frustrated with the slow pace of the investment; South Korea has even been described as the slowest negotiating partner the administration has dealt with. Bolstering Trump’s irritation are commercial disputes involving American companies and what he views as insufficient South Korean support for U.S. priorities.
That frustration played into the decision to cut back the drills. Trump framed the move as a both favor to Kim and a jab at Seoul over its refusal to help with the Iran war. He called the joint exercises “costly” and said they “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” toward North Korea, which he described as “unthreatening and respectful” during his time in office.
In light of Trump’s recent remarks, the decision to scale back joint exercises and the summit push send a message to Pyongyang that goes beyond nostalgia for the summit heyday of 2018-19. Trump is signaling that it can bypass Seoul and deal with North Korea directly, at a moment when the alliance with South Korea is already strained over money.
Kim has reason to welcome exactly that signal. North Korea would likely prefer engaging Washington and Tokyo while bypassing Seoul entirely, a strategy that would divide the allies and isolate South Korea much as Seoul once isolated Pyongyang by establishing ties with Moscow and Beijing at the end of the Cold War.
But unlike the 2018-19 summits, North Korea has a new precondition: its nuclear weapons are not up for negotiation. Pyongyang wants assurances that a Trump-Kim summit in 2026 would not discuss denuclearization.
In 2023, North Korea amended its constitution to make its nuclear arsenal a permanent basic law of the state, closing off denuclearization as a negotiating outcome. Kim said last September that he saw no reason to avoid dialogue with Washington if it dropped its denuclearization demand, but that he would never trade away the arsenal to escape sanctions.
The refusal has not discouraged Trump. On August 18, he told reporters at the Oval Office that Kim had in fact responded to his request for a conversation. “Kim jong Un has always treated me with great respect,” Trump said, adding,” I understand him. He understands me.”
The answer from Pyongyang came a day later and it was far cooler. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of Kim Jong Un, said the reduced drills changed nothing and called their provocative character unaltered by a shorter schedule. She also denied that any direct communication between the two leaders had taken place.
The following day, North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea.
These signals from Pyongyang aren’t a full rejection of dialogue. Rather, North Korea is attempting to raise the price of reengagement. Kim stands to gain plenty: a peace declaration would let him claim a historic first. A formal end to the state of hostility or even fresh limits on South Korea-U.S. military drills would do much the same and Kim could likely secure those gains without touching his nuclear weapons.
A larger pattern may sit behind the individual moves. Trump has separately pursued a rapprochement with Russia over the war in Ukraine, at a moment when security cooperation among China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea has sharply increased. A July report from The Foundation for Defense of Democracies documented more than 600 instances of cooperation between what it called the “axis of aggressors” between 2019 and 2025.
Whether a North Korea summit is meant to fit into a wider attempt to loosen that alignment, rather than stand as a separate and narrower bid for a foreign policy headline, remains unconfirmed. But the diplomatic trend has changed the foundations for any Kim-Trump summit.
North Korea has deepened military and economic ties with Russia through troop deployments and arms sales tied to the war in Ukraine. It has also maintained trade ties with China that have blunted the effect of United Nations sanctions. That alignment gives Kim far less reason to negotiate away the arsenal than he had in 2018, when sanctions were straining the North Korean economy.
To sum up: Trump is desperate for a diplomatic storyline that not’s about Iran. South Korea is behind on its promised investments. And Kim is looking to make the most of both trends – without budging on the one thing that Washington has always wanted most from North Korea. Whether any of it produces a third act to the Singapore and Hanoi summits will depend on decisions still to come in Pyongyang, Seoul, and Beijing.

Surprise protests, GenZ outreach: Rahul Gandhi's new playbook after CJP's success

Surprise protests, GenZ outreach: Rahul Gandhi's new playbook after CJP's success
Priyanka Mukherjee / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 24, 2026, 23:23 IST
Comments

Text Size

Rahul Gandhi's new playbook shows a more persistent style, combining youth outreach, and surprise street protests.
NEW DELHI: "I will not leave till you lodge an FIR. He has pellet injuries on his body, has lost his eye, and we are demanding an FIR for this… I will go outside and sit there until you lodge an FIR. I will sit for 10 days, 20 days, 30 days, 50 days, six months. Your government will have a problem."There is a visible change in how Rahul Gandhi pushes through issues now. The leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha has a new weapon in his political arsenal: impromptu protests.
For the second time in a month, the Congress leader caught the authorities and, to some extent, even his own party, off guard by taking to the streets of the national capital without prior warning.When Rahul reached the DCP office in Delhi on August 21 demanding an FIR for Sahil Lochab, who sustained pellet injuries during the July 20 student protest, it was Act 2 of his new playbook of street protest politics.When the cops dilly-dallied, Rahul refused to budge and staged a sit-in protest outside the police station. Priyanka Gandhi Vadra joined him. Congress leaders began arriving. Rapid Action Force personnel were deployed outside.
A visit to a police office turned into a high-voltage political stand-off and, after six hours of dharna, Delhi Police registered an FIR over the pellet firing.
'Politics of anarchy'
The BJP reacted sharply, calling Rahul's sit-in the 'politics of anarchy'. It argued that an FIR relating to the wider July 20 incident already existed, an investigation was under way and the Congress leader was turning police procedure into a political spectacle.For Lochab, however, there was a sense of relief. His family had been trying to get his complaint registered since August 14, shuttling between police stations. The 19-year-old, who underwent surgery after pellets struck his right eye, finally had an FIR registered after Rahul’s intervention.
According to Lochab's lawyer, the police returned the complaint after reading it and made them wait for a long time.
For years, opponents have labelled Rahul Gandhi a 'part-time politician' who would raise an issue and then disappear. But this incident reinforced something that has changed about Rahul’s tactics over the past year. He is no longer content merely to raise an issue. He increasingly wants to enter it, stay with it and, if necessary, physically occupy the space.
Rahul's new playbook
The first display of this surprise street-politics instinct had come a month earlier during the NEET student protests.On July 21, a day after police used force to stop thousands of students attempting a 'Sansad Chalo' march over exam irregularities, Rahul suddenly headed towards Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s residence and staged a sit-in.Police had reportedly made arrangements anticipating a Congress protest at Vijay Chowk. Rahul went to Lok Kalyan Marg instead. The move caught security officials by surprise. Rahul, Priyanka and several other opposition leaders were later detained. The visual that immediately took over the news was hard to ignore: the leader of opposition physically struggling with police officers, being dragged away and getting a nosebleed in the chaos.
Police personnel detained Rahul Gandhi during a sit-in protest near the Prime Minister's residence.
That was Act 1.It came at a time when the Congress was desperately trying to make its presence felt, with Abhijeet Dipke’s Cockroach Janata Party and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk already leading a massive student protest against the NEET paper leak.Congress had initially kept its distance, preferring to run its own youth outreach campaign, 'Chhatron Ki Goonj'. But people asked a simple question: If Congress claimed to support student issues, why was it missing from the biggest student movement in Delhi?When the July 20 Jantar Mantar protest took place and massive outrage erupted over police action against the student protesters, Rahul's approach changed.The very next day, he moved to the front lines. He stood outside the Prime Minister's house, Congress leaders visited injured students, and police action became a major national debate. Rahul took the issue to Parliament and continued raising the pitch over injuries suffered by students.And when the larger protest began to recede from the headlines, Rahul stayed with one part of it: the use of pellet guns. He has affirmed that his party will keep raising the issue and demand accountability.
Rahul's changing style
The first major image makeover was when Rahul Gandhi embarked on the 'Bharat Jodo Yatra' from Kanyakumari to Kashmir in 2022. Sceptics and rivals wondered if he would complete the journey. By the time he reached Kashmir months later, after walking thousands of kilometres in his now-signature white T-shirt, one charge had become considerably harder to make: that Rahul was unwilling to put in the physical grind that it takes in politics.The yatra, on its own, did not help the Congress much. What it did was change the way Rahul himself was seen as a politician.For months, people saw him walking with the common public rather than delivering a scripted speech from a podium. He met farmers, labourers and students, stopped for conversations, entered homes and sat and ate with people.The yatra experience also laid the foundation for his growing social media popularity. His online presence today increasingly relies on short, conversational exchanges that can easily travel as reels and clips.The second shift came in 2024, when he became the leader of the opposition.Since then, we have seen a more combative Rahul Gandhi. Whether one agrees with his politics or the issues he raises, he appears considerably more comfortable with confrontation than he once did.Congress's protests in the Parliament complex have also become more visual and experimental under Rahul.He repeatedly joined opposition MPs at Makar Dwar over the Election Commission’s SIR exercise in Bihar, with MPs carrying 'vote chori' placards and demanding its rollback. The protest later moved beyond the Parliament gates, with Rahul and other opposition leaders marching towards the Election Commission before being stopped and detained.Rahul provokes ministers across the aisle and stays for the response. He takes an argument from the street into Parliament and, increasingly, carries it back outside again. This is also a part of his renewed Gen Z outreach.
'Chhatron Ki Goonj'
If Bharat Jodo helped Rahul Gandhi build the image of a politician who was more approachable and willing to listen, 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' took that idea to a more specific audience: Gen Z.The programme began in Kota, where students spoke about paper leaks, recruitment delays, coaching pressure and the uncertainty around exams and jobs. The format was less rally and more conversation, with Rahul asking questions, listening, and allowing individual experiences to shape the message. That made the outreach more relatable.His latest Pune edition further widened that outreach by putting young women at the centre of the conversation.
Rahul's call to 'smash the patriarchy' in a stadium full of women was a strong message that came with its own set of criticism. He spoke about different social expectations for boys and girls, cited the 'Manusmriti' while attacking the BJP-RSS worldview, and told women that they 'belong' to themselves rather than to fathers, husbands or sons, triggering huge applause from the crowd.While a large section of people lauded the focus on women, the ruling BJP immediately trained its guns on him and asked him to induct women ministers into the Karnataka cabinet, where Congress is in power.
The Jharkhand dilemma
Even as Rahul attacked the BJP over issues such as NEET and paper leaks, major student protests broke out in Jharkhand, where the Congress shares power in the Hemant Soren government. Soon after the Jantar Mantar agitation ended, aspirants took to the streets in Ranchi over alleged irregularities and paper leaks in JPSC and JSSC examinations.
The BJP MP dared Rahul Gandhi to take a decisive political stand instead of limiting his activism to social media platforms.
This time, the criticism was closer to home. Protesters targeted not just chief minister Hemant Soren but Rahul as well, pointing to the irony of him speaking for students nationally while Congress was part of the ruling alliance in Jharkhand. Effigies of both leaders were burnt, and Rahul was accused of not speaking about Jharkhand issues.Eventually, Rahul was forced to react and intervene. He asserted that Congress supported students protesting peacefully and said that dialogue was the only way forward.
Rahul Gandhi urged Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren to personally meet representatives of students protesting irregularities in state recruitment examinations and address their remaining concerns.
Rahul wrote an open letter to Soren, requesting the CM to personally meet the students and hear out their grievances. The Jharkhand government later accepted the students' demands.The episode helped Rahul avoid the charge of being selective on student issues, but it also showed the challenge of claiming an issue as your own: once you do that, you can be questioned even when the government under fire is run by an ally.
Has Rahul evolved as a leader?
For years, Rahul Gandhi was accused of being an inconsistent politician who would raise important issues and then disappear from the conversation. Rivals branded him as an “entitled leader” and took “Pappu” digs at him.
But the old image of Rahul as a reluctant politician is certainly harder to sustain today. From Bharat Jodo to 'Chhatron Ki Goonj', fiery parliamentary confrontations and surprise dharnas, he appears more comfortable playing on the front foot.However, his latest round of street protests seems to stem from the crisis that the opposition in general and Congress in particular faced as Abhijeet Dipke-led CJP mobilised youth in large numbers and forced the government to make Dharmendra Pradhan resign as Union education minister.Rahul has made his presence felt, but we will have to wait and see if his new politics translates into electoral success for the Congress.

She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.

‘We don’t need Canada’: Trump threatens to double auto tariffs after trade talks collapse
US tariffs on all Canadian cars and trucks, automotive parts and steel will be increased to 50% starting January 1, 2027, President Donald Trump said Monday, adding that the US does not “need” Canada after the collapse of trade talks. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his administration had been “patient” during negotiations, but Canada would not do a deal “at any price”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
US President Donald Trump said Monday that he would double tariffs on Canadian vehicles beginning in 2027, as the neighbouring countries spiral towards an escalating trade war.
"On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The current US tariff on autos stands at 25% for non-US content, while imported steel to the United States generally faces a 50% duty.
Trump's latest threat comes after the North American neighbours failed Friday to reach a deal to avert new 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on select Canadian goods.
Read moreTrump says Canada wants 'benefits of being a State, without being one' as trade war deepens
The White House had alleged "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in rolling out the duties.
Trump delayed their implementation by three days last week as Washington and Ottawa stepped up negotiations towards a trade pact.
Canada won't pay 'any price' for deal, Carney says
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Monday said Canada has been "pragmatic, patient and persevering" in an effort to reach an agreement with the US, but his priority was to get the best deal for his country, not a deal "at any price or any time frame".
"The goal of our trade negotiations with the United States has always been to get the best deal for Canadians, never a deal at any price or on any time frame," Carney told an event on investments in Canada's shipbuilding industry.
Following the collapse of trade talks, Carney announced retaliatory tariffs on the US.
Carney accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said “its signature was written in pencil”.
Resorting to the language of battle, he said his country had been “attacked” by the new American tariffs. “You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.
Read moreCanada vows to match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' after failed trade negotiations
But to Trump’s chief trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliation by its longtime partner.
“We’ve said enough, and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains,” the US trade representative told “Fox & Friends Weekend”.
Carney said Canada had been willing to drop remaining retaliatory tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos if the US substantially lowered its own, and to encourage provinces to restore US alcohol sales. But he said Washington’s final demands went too far. “They asked too much and offered too little,” Carney said.
Greer said the Republican administration was offering to cut tariffs on steel, autos and lumber, “things that are sensitive for them. And they’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”
As a result, he said, “We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.”
Carney said the US added last-minute terms that would have reduced tariff relief for Canadian-made vehicles, restricted Canada’s ability to strike trade deals with other countries and weakened protections for language, culture and sovereignty.
He said such demands were “unacceptable”.
The breakdown in negotiations marked a sharp reversal from two days earlier, when officials from the two countries sounded as if they were headed toward a compromise.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who leads Canada’s most populous province, praised Carney for rejecting the deal, saying it would have hurt Ontario’s auto, steel and manufacturing sectors. Ford urged Canada to use “every tool in our toolbox” to fight the US tariffs.
The moves also call into question the future of a North American trade agreement covering the United States, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.
Carney said the breakdown was “certainly not good news” for the review of that agreement and that the failed negotiations had given Canada “a new perspective” on what Washington wants from the broader economic relationship.
The political impact will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $880 billion worth of goods and services last year.
The US and Canada have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots such as Canadian softwood lumber imports and US access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow, they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile US-Canada border is undefended, and nearly 330,000 people and $2 billion worth of goods cross it every day; 800,000 Canadians live in the United States.
Trump’s approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Trump has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States and made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America’s 51st state.

Carney said Canada had recognised that “America has changed” and that the two countries would “not return to our old relationship”.

Iran discovers major gas field "Takhteh" in Fars province worth $45b
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran discovers major gas field "Takhteh" in Fars province worth $45b
TEHRAN- The Exploration Director of the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) has announced that the newly discovered "Takhteh" gas field in Fars Province has an estimated economic value of approximately $45 billion, describing it as one of the most significant gas discoveries in the country over the past two decades.
In an interview with Shana, Seyyed Mohieddin Jafari detailed the discovery of the Takhteh gas field, stating that it is located 10 kilometers northwest of the city of Khonj and approximately 35 kilometers from the old gas fields of "Shanul" and "Homa."
He explained that the total gas in place at this field amounts to 7,500 billion cubic feet. With a recovery factor of 72%, approximately 5,700 billion cubic feet of this volume is recoverable.
Jafari noted that the gas from the Takhteh field is sweet, emphasizing: "This gas does not require a sweetening process, so it will follow a shorter path in development and processing compared to sour gas fields."
Equivalent to 15 years of production from one phase of South Pars
Jafari stated that the recoverable gas from Takhteh is equivalent to about 15 years of production from a standard phase of South Pars, and added: "This reserve can play a significant role in meeting the country's gas demand."
He announced that the field is about 50 kilometers long and 4 kilometers wide, and described it as "one of the most complex exploration structures discovered in the last 20 years" in terms of geological complexities.
Referring to the field's geological challenges, Jafari explained: "Multiple layer repetitions and faulting in the upstream sections of the reservoir made exploration operations highly difficult. Nevertheless, exploratory drilling continued to a depth of about five kilometers underground, and upon entering the reservoir, a significant volume of gas was discovered in a thickness of approximately 450 meters."
20 million barrels of recoverable condensates
Jafari also reported the presence of 27 million barrels of gas condensates in the Takhteh field, noting that about 20 million barrels of this amount are recoverable. Combined with the gas reserves, this brings the field's economic value to around $40 billion.
Regarding the exploration timeline, he said: "The drilling of the Takhteh exploratory well alone took about 17 months. After completing exploration operations and conducting final tests, the obtained data were carefully analyzed."
The Exploration Director of NIOC further emphasized that the entire exploration process of the Takhteh field was carried out by Iranian personnel, stating: "All exploration stages—from geological studies and geophysical activities to drilling operations—were conducted using the capabilities of Iranian forces."
Jafari added: "The technology, equipment, and tools used in this operation are also Iranian. In technical, equipment, and engineering sectors, there was no need for foreign personnel or companies."
He described the Takhteh gas field as a fully Iranian discovery and stressed: "This achievement demonstrates that the country's technical, engineering, and specialized capacity in oil and gas exploration has reached a level where complex exploration projects can be successfully completed without reliance on foreign parties."

Prince Harry to leave board of African Parks conservation nonprofit
LONDON (AP) — Prince Harry is stepping down as a trustee of African Parks, a nonprofit organization that manages protected areas in partnership with authorities in 13 countries from Chad to Zimbabwe.
Harry, who last week announced he and his family were returning to live in the U.K., left the board of trustees after 10 years of service to the organization, a spokesperson for prince confirmed on Monday.
African Parks said in a statement dated Aug. 19 that the prince’s departure was part of a “governance refresh” in which a Kenyan Supreme Court justice and the president of AGRA, which helps small farmers in Africa, will join the board. The changes take effect Sept. 30.
Harry’s departure comes four months after the Indigenous rights group Survival International called on him to resign after it alleged human rights abuses by rangers employed by African Parks. Previously, the prince left Sentebale, the charity he co-founded to fight poverty and AIDS in southern Africa, in March 2025 after relations with the organization’s chair broke down.
“We extend our thanks to all the members of the Board who generously volunteer their time in support of our conservation mission — and particularly to The Duke of Sussex, for a decade of committed service to African Parks,” Vas Narasimhan, chair of the African Parks board, said in a statement.
Harry and his wife, Meghan, stepped aside from royal duties when they moved to the U.S. They will not return to royal duties and are expected to live in a non-royal residence outside London.

Venice Film Festival adds Gaza doc ‘NAZA’ to competition lineup
The Venice Film Festival has added a new documentary about the civilian toll of the Israel-Hamas war to its lineup. “NAZA,” from two of the filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning documentary “No Other Land,” will screen in the main competition, festival organizers said Monday.
According to the synopsis, the film was shot at night on Tel Aviv rooftops and focuses on the killings of Palestinian civilians. Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor co-directed “Naza,” which was produced by The Guardian and filmmakers behind “The Zone of Interest.” It’s the only documentary competing for the Golden Lion award.
Abraham and Szor were two of the four directors of the 2025 best documentary winner “No Other Land,” the story of Palestinian activists fighting to protect their communities from demolition by the Israeli military. A collaboration between Israeli and Palestinian filmmakers, it was made over four years between 2019 and 2023, wrapping production days before Hamas launched its deadly Oct. 7, 2023 attack on Israel that started the war in Gaza.
“Naza” builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and The Guardian.
The war was top of mind at last year’s festival as well, where thousands gathered for a large pro-Palestinian protest during one of the busiest nights in hopes of redirecting the spotlight from the movie stars to the real world. The subject was also prominent in the program: Kaouther Ben Hania’s “The Voice of Hind Rajab,” about the death of a 6-year-old girl attempting to flee Gaza City with her family in early 2024, won the festival’s Silver Lion award.
Ben Hania is part of the Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury that will be selecting the award winners at the festival, which begins on Sept. 2. Winners will be announced on Sept. 12.
Earlier this year, the Venice Biennale contemporary art exhibition opened with no Golden Lions after the jury quit in protest of Israel’s and Russia’s participation and loud protests outside their pavilions. In 2024 the artist and curators representing Israel at the Venice Biennale kept the Israeli pavilion exhibit closed, saying they would only open it if there were a ceasefire in Gaza.

Ontario’s premier: Canada should be ready to cut electricity, critical minerals as trade woes worsen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:53:01 UTC
23:53:01 KST

Canada set to announce retaliatory tariffs as Trump tells its leaders to ‘fall in line’
TORONTO (AP) — Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the United States on Tuesday after relations deteriorated sharply Monday, with President Donald Trump telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs and Prime Minister Mark Carney accusing Washington of trying to subordinate Canada.
Trump also threatened new 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel, while Carney said U.S. trade demands showed Washington wanted to “destroy our major industries,” including autos, steel and aluminum.
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and three other Cabinet ministers are also expected Tuesday morning to share details of supports for workers affected by tariffs. Carney said earlier Monday that Canada may need to move away from matching U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar and instead use more targeted retaliation aimed at protecting Canadian workers and businesses.
“An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States” is “not something we’re going to accept,” Carney said.
Carney was even more blunt in French.
“We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum,” Carney said. “That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal.”
The fiery words from both sides show how U.S.-Canada relations have deteriorated since Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, triggering the president’s threatened 50% tariffs the next day on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Canada and the United States share one of the world’s largest trading relationships, with deeply integrated supply chains across autos, energy, agriculture and manufacturing, making a prolonged trade fight potentially costly for businesses and workers on both sides of the border.
Carney cast doubt on the U.S.’s dependability, saying Canada was finding reliable partners “everywhere in the world, except in the United States. Except in the United States. And Russia.”
Trump unleashes personal attacks on Canadian leaders
On Monday, Trump came back with further tariffs, warning that he would impose them on Canada’s auto industry beginning next year.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticizing what he called the country’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.
Carney said Washington’s auto-sector proposals would gradually have the effect of dismantling Canadian production.
“This is the most successful automotive partnership in history,” Carney said, referring to the deeply integrated Canada-U.S. industry.
Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unleashed his own tirade. In an interview with The Associated Press, he said Trump had underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure.
“We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch; everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”
Trump responded in a social media post by attacking Ford personally, calling him “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford,” and once again referring to Canada’s prime minister as “Governor Carney.”
Ford dismissed the insults: “If you think an insult from him hurts me? Well, bring it on, buddy, I’m ready.”
Ford is a Progressive Conservative whose party differs from that of Carney, a Liberal, but the two underscore broad political unity in Canada over the trade fight with Trump.
Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity
Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario.
Critical minerals are increasingly important to U.S. national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.
Ford said Canada should also consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south.
“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”
Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides backed away.
Auto industry becomes a central battleground
Ford accused Trump of not simply seeking a better trade deal but aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.
Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state.
“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said.
The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the center of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other U.S. states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production.
Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump’s new threat of a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the center of the escalating dispute.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
Ford says he opposed preliminary deal
Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from negotiations, and that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement.
“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.”
Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty.
Carney said the dispute also exposed a deeper divide over language and culture, saying protections for French and Canadian culture that Washington views as trade irritants are considered fundamental rights in Canada.
“Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”
___
Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed from Washington.

Global Unicorn Summit opens in Hong Kong

HONG KONG, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Global Unicorn Summit opened in Hong Kong on Monday, connecting high-flying startups with each other as well as investors worldwide.
Addressing the opening ceremony, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region Chief Executive John Lee reaffirmed Hong Kong's commitment to nurturing emerging industries and improving the ecosystem for innovation.
The two flagship technology hubs in Hong Kong -- Hong Kong Science Park and Cyberport -- provide startups at various stages of development with comprehensive support, said Lee, noting that the city has fostered about 20 unicorn enterprises in the past decade.
Lee said that the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone will become a new world-class hub for innovation, which is home to more than 90 tech institutions.
For mainland startups and unicorn enterprises, Hong Kong serves as the ideal launchpad towards overseas markets and a strategic foothold in their global supply chains, said Lee. The city is also a premier hub for overseas innovation firms to explore the mainland market, he added.
The event is hosted by Hong Kong Ta Kung Wen Wei Media Group and attended by over 200 unicorns worldwide. ■

Istanbul court announces verdict in mayors’ case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:52:19 UTC
23:52:19 KST

An Istanbul court on Aug. 24 sentenced former Beşiktaş Mayor Rıza Akpolat to 23 years and three months in prison for bid-rigging, bribery and laundering criminal proceeds, as it delivered its verdict in a 200-defendant case involving seven mayors.
The Istanbul 1st High Criminal Court ordered Akpolat to remain in custody. He was separately acquitted of membership in a criminal organization and of official- and private-document forgery.
Seyhan Mayor Oya Tekin was sentenced to eight years and four months for taking bribes, while Avcılar Mayor Utku Caner Çaykara received six years and eight months on the same charge. Çaykara was acquitted on two other counts.
Adana Metropolitan Mayor Zeydan Karalar was sentenced to six years and three months for bribery and Ceyhan Mayor Kadir Aydar to five years and 10 months.
Former Esenyurt Mayor Ahmet Özer was given eight months and 10 days for negligent abuse of office, though the court deferred pronouncement of the judgment. Adıyaman Mayor Abdurrahman Tutdere was acquitted of bribery.
The court also barred the convicted mayors from public office for periods equal to half their respective prison terms.
Aziz İhsan Aktaş, whom prosecutors had accused of leading a criminal organization that bribed municipal officials to steer public tenders, and Baki Nugay were acquitted of establishing such an organization.
Defendants charged with membership or aiding the alleged group were also cleared.
Aktaş was given two years, eight months and 15 days for bid-rigging, but the pronouncement of the judgment was deferred.
He was also barred from public tenders for two years. The court imposed no punishment on the bribery charges after applying effective-remorse provisions.
Presiding judge Oğuzhan Gül said the evidence did not establish the chain of command, hierarchical ties and other elements required under legal precedent for a criminal organization. The verdict was unanimous and can be appealed.
Oya Tekin’s husband, Celal Tekin, was also sentenced to eight years and four months for bribery. Beşiktaş Deputy Mayor Alican Abacı received 18 years, six months and 22 days for bribery and laundering, while Akpolat’s wife, Yeşim Akpolat, was sentenced to four years and two months for laundering criminal proceeds.
The court ordered Akpolat, Oya Tekin and Celal Tekin to remain in custody and released Adıyaman Deputy Mayor Ceyhan Kayhan and Avcılar Deputy Mayor Erhan Daka.
The trial began on Jan. 27, with the verdict delivered at its 60th hearing.

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has emphasized the importance of consolidating and expanding the progress made in a Party-wide study and education campaign for establishing and practicing a correct understanding of governance performance.
Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a recent instruction, which was studied at a meeting of the CPC Central Leading Group for Party Building held on Monday.
Xi stressed that establishing and putting into practice a correct view of governance performance is a long-term task that requires sustained efforts.
Since the 18th CPC National Congress, the organization of study and education campaigns across the Party to address major and pressing issues in Party building has become an important institutional arrangement, Xi said, lauding the notable results achieved in the latest campaign.
Xi emphasized the need to regularly conduct education on the correct view of governance performance, guiding Party members and officials to always take responsibility, perform their duties and fulfill their obligations in accordance with such a view.
Efforts should also be made to improve differentiated assessment and evaluation systems, and establish a personnel selection and appointment orientation that values solid work and concrete results, Xi said.

BeiDou support tops 98 pct of China's H1 phone shipments as commercial adoption broadens
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:52:08 CST
23:52:08 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- More than 98 percent of the 133 million mobile phones shipped in China's domestic market in the first half (H1) of 2026 supported the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS), as this technology expands across consumer devices, transport and other industries, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Monday.
Over 14 million shared two-wheelers had adopted BeiDou independent positioning by the end of June, accounting for more than 90 percent of the country's total fleet.
These figures highlight the growing rollout of BeiDou, China's global satellite navigation system, across consumer and industrial applications.
At a media roundtable on large-scale BeiDou applications, Shi Huikang, deputy director of the MIIT's department of electronic information, said China has stepped up pilot programs, product promotion, standards development and ecosystem building in recent years to accelerate adoption.
China's domestic supply base has also continued to expand. By the end of 2025, cumulative shipments of domestically produced BeiDou-compatible chips and modules had approached 2.6 billion units, while the installed base of terminal products with BeiDou functions had exceeded 2.2 billion units, according to the ministry.
Authorities have also supported the development and commercialization of high-precision, interference-resistant and low-power products, helping improve performance and lower costs.
Deployment has also expanded across 39 pilot cities for large-scale BeiDou applications, which had introduced more than 12 million terminals using BeiDou independent positioning by the end of June.
In a number of cities, designated sectors including shared two-wheelers, taxis, government vehicles, agricultural machinery and police equipment have achieved 100-percent BeiDou adoption, the ministry said.
BeiDou's footprint is also expanding across major industries. China now has nearly 40 million BeiDou terminal devices in key sectors, where overall application penetration stands at about 90 percent. More than 160 million wearable devices support BeiDou positioning, while over 100 million passenger vehicles have been equipped with BeiDou-based positioning devices.
Industry data released in May revealed the scale of the broader market. China's satellite navigation industry generated 629 billion yuan (roughly 92.7 billion U.S. dollars) in output in 2025, up 9.24 percent year on year, according to a white paper released by the Global Navigation Satellite System and Location-Based Services Association of China.
The white paper also said BeiDou services and related products have been exported to more than 140 countries and regions worldwide. It said the sector is upgrading toward a broader BeiDou spatiotemporal industry integrating satellite navigation with mobile communications, indoor positioning and artificial intelligence.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the MIIT said it will work with other authorities to support breakthroughs in key technologies and their industrial application, while continuing pilot programs for large-scale BeiDou deployment.
The ministry also plans to foster a broader spatiotemporal information industry by promoting coordinated development across satellite positioning, navigation and timing, remote sensing, geographic information systems, communications and satellite internet. ■

====================================================================================================

Across China: Brazilian programmers infuse passion into Chinese humanoid robots
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
22:52:08 CST
23:52:08 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A group of Chinese-made humanoid robots competing for the ball on a soccer field immediately came to a halt when commanded to do so by 21-year-old Brazilian programmer Isabela Moura.
Moments earlier, the robots had been positioning themselves, tracking the ball and kicking autonomously, powered by algorithms developed by young Brazilian programmers and researchers.
For Moura, seeing her work drive Chinese humanoid robots on an international stage is both a validation of her programming skills and a reflection of her passion for robotics.
Moura is a member of Team Brazil, formed this year by young researchers from five Brazilian universities to compete in 5-on-5 humanoid robot soccer at the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG) in Beijing, which brings together 666 teams from 16 countries.
Hailing from Pernambuco in northeastern Brazil, Moura said her passion for humanoid robots was ignited when she joined RoboCIn, a robotics team at the Federal University of Pernambuco, about 18 months ago. In July, she made her first trip abroad to compete at RoboCup in the Republic of Korea before traveling to Beijing.
"It's a really great experience," she said, adding that the robots used by her team are made by Chinese company Booster Robotics, allowing the Brazilian participants to concentrate on software, artificial intelligence and game strategy rather than building a robot from scratch.
"Developing a robot from scratch would require a lot of time devoted to hardware, communications and embedded systems," Moura said. "With a ready-made Chinese platform, we can focus more on what we do best."
This division of work has given the Brazilian team an opportunity to see its algorithms tested on a real-world robotic platform.
"Seeing what we have developed over the past year actually working is extremely rewarding," Moura said.
The effect is also being felt back at the universities in Brazil. When the Chinese robots operate in laboratories, other students often stop to watch, take photos and record videos. Some have become interested in robotics as a result, Moura noted.
For Team Brazil, however, the competition means more than winning games.
"There is competition here, but competition is not the only reason we came," said Joao Aguiar, a member of Team Brazil and a graduate of FEI University Center, who also participated in the competition last year.
The Brazilian team recently played a friendly match against an Italian team. After the game, members of the two teams discussed different approaches to kicking and positioning robots on the field.
"We talk about what each team does differently," Aguiar said. "Through this kind of exchange, all the teams can improve."
With the Chinese teams, the exchange has developed into technical cooperation. A team from Tsinghua University participated in developing part of Team Brazil's code, while China Agricultural University provided support in areas including game strategy.
Cooperation has continued beyond the competition. "We stay in touch, exchange ideas about what we are working on and also discuss maintenance issues," Aguiar said, recalling the relationship he established with Chinese teams during his first visit to Beijing last year.
His experience in China has also deepened his understanding of the country's humanoid robotics industry. During his first trip to China, Aguiar had the opportunity to closely observe humanoid robots developed by Chinese teams.
"The level of development over the past three or four years has been impressive. You can see how robust, fast and intelligent these robots have become in different scenarios, like logistics, industry and pharmacies," he said.
According to Aguiar, Beijing brings together Chinese and international teams in venues where they can develop, train and test robots while exchanging experience and comparing technical solutions. The competition therefore serves not only as a sporting event, but also as a platform for research, development and international exchange.
Beijing, in addition, is strengthening the infrastructure supporting humanoid robotics. The city announced plans to build a training and evaluation base for humanoid robots this year, said Liu Wenqiang, Party secretary of the China Center for Information Industry Development, at a WHRG press conference.
"Beijing has become a hub for humanoid robotics over the past two years," Aguiar said.
For Flavio Tonidandel, coach of Team Brazil and director of Socialdroids Robotics, China's efforts to apply humanoid robots to increasingly complex and practical tasks are particularly noteworthy.
"We need to put robots through increasingly demanding and complex challenges so that they can serve society," he explained.
This approach is reflected in this year's WHRG. In addition to competitive events such as soccer and athletics, the showpiece features 21 scenario-based events covering nine types of real-world needs, namely household and hospitality services, industrial production, emergency response, library management, retail, office services, green-space inspection and vehicle charging.
China is now home to over 140 humanoid robot manufacturers. With an annual shipment volume of 14,400 units, the country now accounts for eight out of every ten humanoid robots produced globally.
Tonidandel believes that clear support policies, competitions such as the WHRG and a steady influx of new talent are important factors behind the rapid development of humanoid robotics in China.
"You see university students, researchers and engineers are all deeply involved in the development of these robots," he said.
As humanoid robots begin to enter real-world applications, Tonidandel also sees greater room for cooperation between Brazil and China.
"Brazilians are faced with some challenges that Chinese may not be, and vice versa. The algorithms we develop in Brazil need to be adapted to local needs in Brazil," he said.
In his view, such cooperation could allow Brazilian researchers to learn from advanced technologies while helping Chinese robots develop solutions that can be applied in more countries.
"This collaboration is very important for both sides. Ultimately, it might facilitate applications of humanoid robots around the world," he said. ■

Deregistering a child from their place of residence has become easier — consent from one of the parents can now be obtained through &quot;Diia&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:51:35 EEST
23:51:35 KST

Deregistering a child from their place of residence has become easier — consent from one of the parents can now be obtained through "Diia"
Kyiv • UNN
A child under 14 can be deregistered through "Diia" without the second parent being personally present. A Ukrainian birth certificate, tax identification number, and signature are required.
In Ukraine, deregistering a child from their place of residence has become easier — the consent of one parent can now be obtained online, UNN reports, citing the Diia government services portal.
A child under 14 can now be deregistered from their place of residence online via the Diia portal. One parent can provide consent to deregister the child remotely — their personal presence during the process is no longer required
Parents can use the service if:
✔️the child is under 14; from the age of 14, the application must be submitted independently;
✔️the child has a Ukrainian birth certificate;
✔️both parents are Ukrainian citizens;
✔️they have a tax identification number and Diia.Signature/e-signature.
How does it work?
After logging in to the Diia portal:
1️⃣Go to Services → Change of place of residence → Deregister from the place of residence.
2️⃣Check your details. If necessary, update them in your personal account.
3️⃣Indicate whether you have children and whether you are a person liable for military service.
4️⃣Choose whom you want to deregister: only the child or yourself together with the child.
5️⃣Check the address where you are currently registered.
6️⃣If you are deregistering the child, check their details and provide the details of the other parent.
7️⃣The other parent must provide consent online.
8️⃣Sign the application with a Diia.Signature or electronic signature and pay the administrative fee.
Important for persons liable for military service: you can deregister only the child. The service for simultaneously deregistering yourself and the child is currently unavailable online for persons liable for military service, but it can be obtained at a CNAP

The mission called for a prompt investigation and said attacks on U.N. peacekeepers may constitute war crimes under international law.

24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
 Amnesty International has urged Nigerian authorities to urgently secure the release of worshippers abducted during Friday prayers at a mosque in Niger State, warning of the growing threat posed by mass abductions across the country’s north.
The rights group made the call after terrorists attacked the Kpenya Mosque in Dekara District of Borgu Local Government Area on Aug. 21, abducting an unspecified number of worshippers.
Amnesty described the incident as particularly alarming because the victims were abducted while observing Friday prayers, adding that more than 80 people may have been taken during the attack.
“The Nigerian authorities must act urgently to ensure the safe rescue of the abducted worshippers,” the organization said in a statement Monday.
It also called on the government to address the broader wave of mass abductions targeting rural communities across northern Nigeria.
Amnesty said at least 1,100 people were abducted between January and April 2026, while noting that available figures vary and may significantly underestimate the actual scale of the problem.
The organization warned that victims of previous mass abductions had reported severe abuses, including torture, starvation, sexual violence and amputation.
The Niger State government confirmed the attack and said terrorists stormed the mosque while worshippers were observing Juma’at prayers.
State Commissioner for Information and Orientation Obed Nana said a joint security operation had been deployed to track the attackers and facilitate the rescue of the abducted worshippers.
“A joint security operation has been deployed to assess the situation, track the attackers, and facilitate the rescue of the abducted worshippers,” Nana told Anadolu.
The government declined to disclose further operational details, saying doing so could compromise ongoing rescue efforts, while urging residents to avoid spreading unverified figures.
The Kpenya attack occurred barely a week after an attack on worshippers in the Ungushi community in Sokoto State, where gunmen killed at least 32 people during Friday prayers, including the mosque’s imam.
Anadolu previously reported the Aug. 18 attack in Ungushi, highlighting growing insecurity affecting communities in northwestern Nigeria.
The latest incident adds to a series of attacks reported around the Borgu-Kainji corridor, an area where authorities and security analysts have raised concerns about armed groups operating around Kainji Lake National Park.

Iran-Cuba economic ties: Unlocking investment potential amid sanctions, legal reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

23:43:15 KST

Iran-Cuba economic ties: Unlocking investment potential amid sanctions, legal reform
TEHRAN- On a global stage increasingly defined by economic fragmentation and unilateral sanctions, two nations with decades of experience in navigating external pressures—Iran and Cuba—are actively seeking to deepen their bilateral economic ties. Recent high-level exchanges and business delegations signal a mutual determination to translate longstanding political solidarity into tangible commercial partnerships.
At the heart of these efforts lies a complex interplay of opportunity and obstacle: Cuba’s gradual opening to private sector participation, Iran’s resilient industrial base, and the persistent logistical and financial barriers that have thus far constrained substantive cooperation.
This report synthesizes the outcomes of two key diplomatic and business engagements—a meeting in Tehran between the Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce and the Cuban Ambassador, and a subsequent Iranian business delegation visit to Havana in late 2025. While the first part details bilateral discussions on frameworks and aspirations, the second part captures the delegation’s on-the-ground exploration of specific investment projects. Together, they paint a comprehensive picture of a partnership poised for growth, provided that regulatory transparency and payment mechanisms are adequately addressed.
Strategic dialogue in Tehran; laying the groundwork for cooperation
In a significant diplomatic exchange, Samad Hassanzadeh, Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture (ICCIMA), met with Jorge F. Lefebre Nicolás, the Cuban Ambassador in Tehran, at the place of ICCIMA on August 24, to assess the evolving landscape of Iran-Cuba economic relations. The meeting underscored a shared recognition that while political ties are robust, economic interaction remains below its potential, primarily due to logistical and monetary transfer challenges.
Hassanzadeh opened the dialogue by affirming Iran’s readiness to enter the Cuban market, contingent upon the resolution of two critical bottlenecks: transportation and financial settlements. He stated unequivocally that “if logistical and monetary transfer issues are resolved, Iranian investors will enter the Cuban market.” He identified several promising sectors for joint cooperation, including offshore farming, sugar production, automotive parts, and sanitary products. These areas, he noted, align with Iran’s industrial strengths and Cuba’s import substitution needs.
The Cuban Ambassador responded by detailing the significant legal and structural reforms underway in Cuba. He explained that intensified U.S. sanctions have compelled the Cuban government to overhaul its economic model, pivoting toward a more robust private sector. This shift, he emphasized, has now gained legal status, permitting private banks, exchange houses, and a broader role for foreign investment in previously state-dominated sectors. Ambassador Nicolás invited Iranian investors to consider opportunities in fuel supply and distribution—now managed by Cuba’s private sector—as well as hospitality, where Spanish companies once held sway, and agriculture, where Vietnam has already pioneered land-lease arrangements. He also highlighted mining (nickel and quartz), car rental services, and renewable energy as areas ripe for Iranian participation.
Legal reforms and the private sector as a catalyst
A central theme of the Tehran meeting was the changing legal framework in Cuba. Hassanzadeh stressed the need for written documentation of these new laws to enable the Iran Chamber of Commerce to disseminate accurate information to its members. He recalled previous negotiations with Cuban officials during his visit to Cuba, where proposals for specialized committees to address trade barriers were discussed but not yet implemented. He urged the Cuban side to provide formal investment packages and clear regulatory guidelines, noting that Iranians, having navigated forty years of sanctions-induced restrictions, are uniquely equipped to operate under constrained conditions. He framed economic engagement not merely as a profit-seeking venture but as a religious and moral duty to stand alongside other nations, improving living standards through mutual cooperation.
Ambassador Nicolás acknowledged that transportation remains the primary operational hurdle, yet he expressed confidence that solutions exist, including route reconfiguration and alternative payment corridors that avoid the dollar-based system. He proposed practical next steps: holding online B2B meetings through the embassy, organizing a delegation of interested Iranian companies to visit Cuba, and facilitating a reciprocal Cuban business mission to Iran. He stressed that Iranian companies unafraid of sanctions can operate in Cuba using any currency, and that the Cuban embassy stands ready to act as a bridge for market familiarization.
Sectoral opportunities and the call for concrete action
Hassanzadeh provided additional granularity on potential cooperation areas. He reported on his visits to Cuban farms and sugar production facilities, concluding that joint investment in sugarcane cultivation and sugar processing holds considerable promise. He also floated the idea of designating free trade zones in Cuba exclusively for Iranian products, which would serve as a distribution hub for the Caribbean and Latin American markets. Furthermore, he revealed that official invitations have been extended to Cuba’s Economy Minister, Industry Minister, and Chamber of Commerce President to visit Iran, hoping that such a high-level visit would expedite mutual understanding and deal-making.
The Cuban Ambassador reinforced these overtures by reiterating that Cuba’s new legal framework allows foreign investors to repatriate earnings, a critical assurance for any potential investor. He noted that even the supply and distribution of fuel—a strategic sector—has been privatized, demonstrating the depth of Cuba’s commitment to economic transformation. He concluded by underscoring that this is a favorable moment for Iranian companies, especially large chain enterprises, to enter the Cuban market, provided they move swiftly to understand the new investment laws.
Havana business delegation; from dialogue to due diligence
Moving from high-level political discourse to operational engagement, an Iranian business delegation led by ICCIMA Head Samad Hassanzadeh visited Havana in late November 2025 to explore concrete investment projects aimed at reviving Cuba's idle industrial capacity.
The delegation’s agenda was far more specific than the Tehran discussions, focusing on rehabilitiating dormant factories and establishing joint ventures in sectors where Iran possesses proven technical expertise. In meetings with Cuban officials, Hassanzadeh requested a comprehensive list of non-operational plants, particularly in sugar and cement, to guide Iranian companies seeking investment opportunities. He argued that Iran could play a pivotal role in restoring Cuba’s once-prominent sugar industry, leveraging Iranian machinery and agricultural technology. Similarly, he noted that joint cement production would be more cost-effective than continued imports, and Iranian investors were prepared to construct several cement plants, provided clear regulatory conditions and investment guarantees are established.
Industrial revival and mining as a long-term pillar
ICCIMA Deputy Head Ghadir Ghiyafeh expanded on the industrial front, describing mining as a cornerstone for enduring cooperation. He characterized Cuba as a resource-rich but underdeveloped mining market, where Iranian firms—with advanced technical expertise in mineral exploration, extraction, and processing—could contribute significantly. He specifically mentioned cobalt and nickel production, from geological surveys to processing, and noted that Iranian engineering companies are ready to assist in training Cuban specialists for a planned national steel plant. Khuzestan Steel Company has already signaled its readiness to collaborate. Ghiyafeh projected that a clear legal framework could help push bilateral trade volumes to one billion dollars within five years, targeting construction, roadbuilding, food industries, agriculture, and mining as preferred sectors for Iranian investors.
In a separate meeting with Cuba’s Minister of Domestic Trade, Hassanzadeh urged the preparation of a formal investment package tailored for Iranian companies. He reiterated Iran’s industrial depth across agriculture, mining, petrochemicals, tourism, and energy, but emphasized the necessity of transparent rules and investment security. The Cuban minister responded positively, stating that President Miguel Díaz-Canel had ordered ministries to identify opportunities for importing food, clothing, and consumer goods from Iran, following the 2025 Havana International Fair (FIHAV). The minister stressed that Cuba aims to boost domestic production as a buffer against U.S. sanctions and is prepared to support foreign investors willing to assume risk.
High-level endorsement and the way forward
The visit culminated in a symbolic yet significant moment during Iran National Day at FIHAV 2025. Hassanzadeh declared that the presence of Iranian manufacturers reflected a shared commitment to expanding cooperation, urging both countries to translate political ties into economic outcomes. He outlined additional areas for Iranian contribution, including dam construction, road and housing projects, hydropower development, and renewable energy. Cuba’s Industry Minister, Eloy Álvarez Martínez, echoed this sentiment, calling for practical cooperation to match political solidarity, citing the 2023 comprehensive cooperation agreement as an essential framework for small, medium, and large firms to form direct partnerships.
Most notably, President Miguel Díaz-Canel personally visited Iran’s pavilion at the fair, where he was received by Hassanzadeh, Ghiyafeh, and Iran’s Ambassador to Cuba, Zabihollah Naderi. The Cuban president engaged with representatives of Iranian companies, learning about their products and export capacities. He expressed hope that the exhibition would pave the way for enhanced mutual cooperation and emphasized that his government supports the expansion of economic exchanges and joint investments. His visit underscored the political will at the highest level to pursue tangible results, particularly in petrochemicals, food industries, industrial equipment, and commercial services.
A partnership at a crossroads
The convergence of diplomatic dialogue and business delegation activity reveals a clear trajectory: Iran and Cuba are not merely maintaining symbolic solidarity but are actively engineering a practical economic partnership. The Tehran meeting established the foundational principles—acknowledging legal changes, identifying sectoral opportunities, and agreeing on the necessity of resolving logistical and monetary hurdles. The Havana delegation then tested these principles against reality, identifying specific factories for rehabilitation, mining projects for development, and trade volumes to target.
Three critical takeaways emerge for both sides. First, the resolution of banking and transportation challenges is not just a technicality but the key that unlocks all other potential. Alternative payment mechanisms and shipping routes must be operationalized swiftly. Second, Cuba’s legal reforms must be translated into accessible, written investment guidelines that provide Iranian companies with the confidence to commit capital. Third, the high-level political endorsement, epitomized by President Díaz-Canel’s visit to Iran’s pavilion, must now be followed by bureaucratic efficiency—streamlined permits, clear repatriation rules, and responsive ministerial coordination.
If these conditions are met, the current phase of exploration can transition into a phase of execution. Iran’s industrial resilience, honed under forty years of sanctions, offers a natural complement to Cuba’s resource wealth and strategic location. Together, they have the potential to build a resilient economic corridor that defies external pressures and delivers tangible benefits—in sugar, cement, mining, pharmaceuticals, and beyond—for both nations. The path is clear; the time for decisive action is now.

Israel denied entry to two Swedish members of the European Parliament who had planned to travel to the occupied West Bank, turning them away at Ben Gurion Airport, Israeli authorities said Monday.
Jonas Sjostedt and Hanna Gedin, members of Sweden's Left Party, were turned away Sunday at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport, the primary gateway for visitors to the Palestinian territory.
Israel's foreign ministry said the pair had "consistently acted against Israel," including by calling for international legal proceedings against Israelis.
"On various public occasions, they have spread false accusations against Israel, including allegations of genocide, deliberate starvation and the intentional targeting of children and medical personnel," the ministry said in a statement. Israel consistently denies committing acts of war crimes, genocide and occupation of Palestine, despite clear evidence proving it, including ministers openly calling for the extermination of Palestinians.
Sjostedt in a Facebook post said that the two MEPs planned to meet human rights and charitable organizations, including Save the Children, and to see refugee camps.
"We continue to work against Israel's illegal occupation, the displacement of Palestinians, and genocide," Sjostedt wrote.
He added that Sweden had issued a protest.
But Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard, while noting the Swedish embassy assisted the pair, said that every country "has its own entry regulations" and that Sweden has a travel advisory in place for Israel and the Palestinian territories.
Rawhi Fattouh, president of the Palestinian National Council, the West Bank-based legislative body, called on European parliaments to speak out against the exclusion of critical voices.
The denial of entry is "an attempt to impose silence by force and turn criticism of the occupation into an accusation, in clear disregard for international law and the moral immunity afforded to parliamentary work", he said.

French president confirms enactment of law banning cellphones in high schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:39:52 UTC
23:39:52 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday said he is enacting a law banning cellphones in high schools starting with the new school year.
“Protecting children from the excesses of screens can no longer wait,” Macron said on US social media company X.
“A school without phones means reclaiming the serenity of learning,” he added.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said earlier Monday that the ban could take effect as soon as the new school year begins following Macron’s decision.
The legislation, aimed at protecting minors from risks associated with social media, was passed on July 21.
Its flagship provision, which sought to ban social media for children under 15, was blocked by the Constitutional Council.
Bregeon said the cellphone ban in high schools would nevertheless take effect under a “stable, consolidated and legislative” legal framework.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu will work on a new version of the social media provisions that takes into account the Constitutional Council’s concerns, she said.
The government aims to establish a revised legal framework to protect children and young people by next spring, the spokesperson added.

Armenia may start EU accession bid in 'near future': PM Pashinyan

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:39:00 UTC
23:39:00 KST

Armenia could soon kick off preparations for the EU accession bid, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told lawmakers on Monday, despite warnings from Moscow not to pursue deeper European integration.
Armenia is formally allied with Moscow but has been building ties with the European Union for years, amid frustration over Russia's perceived failure to protect it during conflicts with neighboring Azerbaijan.
Russia, which has a military base in Armenia, still wields substantial influence over the small Caucasus country and counts it as a member of its Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).
"Armenia must first submit an official application for EU membership," Pashinyan told deputies.
"We may begin this process in the near future, especially given the urgent requests from our EAEU partners," he said.
Once the bid is lodged, Armenia would hold a referendum on membership, he added.
Russia has repeatedly called for such a vote, and the Kremlin has consistently warned that membership of both Western and Russian blocs is incompatible.
Asked about the former Soviet republic's EU aspirations on Monday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the trade, sanitary and customs rules of the two blocs did not match.
"I always recommend here that we keep in mind the experience of Türkiye and a number of other countries, whose applications were submitted decades and decades ago, yet they're still in the same situation today," Peskov said.
Türkiye, Armenia's old rival, has been waiting to join the EU for nearly 40 years.
Pashinyan, who rose to power through street protests in 2018, was re-elected in June after hosting EU leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for a summit.
Moscow has stepped up pressure on Yerevan over its rapprochement with Brussels by imposing import curbs. In a warning to Armenia, President Vladimir Putin said in June that the "Ukrainian scenario" began with Kyiv's EU ambitions.
